paragraphs: Spreading activation offers an account of inference in which activity moves through a network and its resulting pattern carries meaning. In structured connectionist systems, the nodes can have recognizable semantic labels. This makes it possible to interpret an inference by examining which meaningful nodes become active and how activation travels among them.

The paper asks whether simple forms of this structured inference can also be achieved using connections learned by a distributed algorithm. In a distributed representation, the relevant information is carried across microfeatures rather than residing entirely in individually named conceptual nodes. The authors demonstrate inference by passing activation over the learned connection weights.

The result establishes a relationship between structured and distributed connectionist approaches for the simple inference setting studied. It shows how a network's distributed learned connections can support behavior associated with a more explicitly structured account. This matters because it connects a way of learning representations with a way of explaining inference, giving the two approaches a shared computational basis.
summary.tldr: Activation spreading over distributed learned weights can perform simple inference associated with structured connectionist networks.

title: Spreading Activation over Distributed Microfeatures

paragraphs: The paper connects neural network training with discriminative estimation for probabilistic recognition models. Discriminative training focuses on distinguishing competing interpretations of an input. The authors investigate how a network's output representation and training objective can make that approach mathematically consistent with the probabilities used by stochastic classifiers.

They modify a multilayer perceptron's output layer to produce valid probability distributions and replace squared error with a probability-based score. Under these changes, training becomes equivalent to maximum mutual information estimation. This establishes a precise connection between a neural training setup and an objective already used successfully with hidden Markov models for speech recognition.

The authors then extend the idea by constructing a network that performs the recognition calculations of a particular stochastic model. Training that network provides a way to train the underlying model parameters discriminatively. Their examples include an HMM-based word discriminator called Alphanet. The contribution is a route from a model's recognition computations to a network-based training procedure, grounded in a probabilistic interpretation of its outputs and objective.
summary.tldr: Probability-correct network outputs and a probability-based objective connect neural training to maximum mutual information estimation for stochastic recognizers.

title: Training Stochastic Model Recognition Algorithms as Networks can Lead to Maximum Mutual Information Estimation of Parameters

paragraphs: The paper explores two ways to combine neural classifiers with Hidden Markov Model speech recognizers. The shared aim is to improve discrimination between speech patterns while preserving the HMM's handling of temporal structure. The two approaches place the neural network at different stages of recognition.

In the first, a neural classifier performs additional discrimination after the HMM recognizer. On a small-vocabulary task, both radial basis function and backpropagation networks substantially reduce errors; the radial basis function system lowers the rate from 7.9 percent to 4.2 percent. On a larger-vocabulary task, neural classifiers do not reduce recognition error, although they outperform Gaussian, Gaussian mixture, and nearest-neighbor classifiers.

In the second approach, networks extract low-level acoustic-phonetic features. Radial basis function classifiers outperform Gaussian mixtures when classifying phonemes from individual ten-millisecond frames. However, the difference becomes small when scores are accumulated across complete phonetic segments with a single-node HMM. The findings show that gains in local discrimination depend on how those decisions are integrated over time.
summary.tldr: Neural classifiers improve some HMM speech-recognition decisions, but the gains vary with vocabulary size and temporal aggregation.

title: HMM Speech Recognition with Neural Net Discrimination

abstract: We describe a model of visual word recognition that accounts for several aspects of the temporal processing of sequences of briefly presented words. The model utilizes a new representation for writ(cid:173) ten words, based on dynamic time warping and multidimensional scaling. The visual input passes through cascaded perceptual, com(cid:173) parison, and detection stages. We describe how these dynamical processes can account for several aspects of word recognition, in(cid:173) cluding repetition priming and repetition blindness.

We describe how these dynamical processes can account for several aspects of word recognition, in(cid:173) cluding repetition priming and repetition blindness.

paragraphs: The paper models how people recognize words when they appear briefly in a sequence. Its central concern is timing: recognition depends on how processing unfolds across successive inputs. The authors use this perspective to explain repetition priming, where repetition helps recognition, and repetition blindness, where a repeated word can fail to be detected as another occurrence.

The model introduces a representation of written words built using dynamic time warping and multidimensional scaling. These methods provide the basis for representing relationships among word inputs. The representation then feeds a cascade of three processing stages concerned with perception, comparison, and detection, so recognition emerges through successive transformations of the visual signal.

The authors describe how the changing activity in this cascade can account for several temporal effects in word recognition. The approach matters because it places the helpful and disruptive effects of repetition within a shared processing framework. Its stated contribution is an account of these phenomena through interacting recognition processes that evolve over time.
summary.tldr: A staged dynamical model explains how briefly presented word sequences can produce both repetition priming and repetition blindness.

title: A dynamical model of priming and repetition blindness

The structure of the model is drawn from known experimental data while the learning principles come from recent work in the field of brain style computation. The model accounts for numerous properties of the owl's sound localization system, makes specific and testable predictions for future experi(cid:173) ments, and provides a theory of the developmental process.

paragraphs: This paper uses the owl's sound localization system to investigate how abstract principles of learning might operate in a biological neural system. The authors build a computational model of development, making the acquisition of the system's abilities part of the explanation. The central question concerns how learning principles can account for the organization of an actual sensory system.

The model combines two sources of constraints. Its structure comes from experimental knowledge about the owl, while its learning principles come from work on brain-style computation. This combination gives the theoretical learning rules a concrete biological setting. It also ties the proposed developmental explanation to properties that experiments have already established.

The authors report that the model accounts for numerous properties of sound localization and generates specific predictions that future experiments can test. Its contribution therefore includes both an explanation of existing observations and a proposed theory of development. The predictions matter because they provide a way to assess whether the modeled learning process captures how the biological system develops.
summary.tldr: A computational model connects learning principles with experimental knowledge to explain development in the owl's sound localization system.

title: A Connectionist Model of the Owl's Sound Localization System

paragraphs: Competitive learning needs a way for network units to develop different roles. The paper describes a difficulty with achieving this through neural activity: simple inhibition supports sparse representations, while decorrelation and factorization approaches supporting distributed representations are computationally unattractive. The authors seek competition compatible with information being represented across many units.

Their proposal places the competitive interaction in neural plasticity, the processes that change connections during learning. This shifts the mechanism responsible for differentiation toward how units learn. The abstract describes the resulting alternatives as diffuse and nonadaptive, and states that they support fully distributed representations. The distinction matters because differentiation need not depend on limiting activity to a small subset of units.

The authors apply the technique to their binary information-gain optimization algorithm for feature extraction, reporting that it simplifies and improves the method. They also propose that the approach could benefit other learning algorithms. The demonstrated contribution is the feature-extraction application; the broader idea is to use interactions in learning itself to organize distinct roles within a distributed representation.
summary.tldr: Mediating competition through plasticity supports distributed representations and simplifies an information-gain feature-learning algorithm.

title: Plasticity-Mediated Competitive Learning

abstract: Support Vector Learning Machines (SVM) are finding application in pattern recognition, regression estimation , and operator inver(cid:173) sion for ill-posed problems. Against this very general backdrop , any methods for improving the generalization performance, or for improving the speed in test phase, of SVMs are of increasing in(cid:173) terest. In this paper we combine two such techniques on a pattern recognition problem. The method for improving generalization per(cid:173) formance (the "virtual support vector" method) does so by incor(cid:173) porating known invariances of the problem. This method achieves a drop in the error rate on 10,000 NIST test digit images of 1.4% to 1.0%. The method for improving the speed (the "reduced set" method) does so by approximating the support vector decision sur(cid:173) face. We apply this method to achieve a factor of fifty speedup in test phase over the virtual support vector machine. The combined approach yields a machine which is both 22 times faster than the original machine, and which has better generalization performance, achieving 1.1 % error. The virtual support vector method is appli(cid:173) cable to any SVM problem with known invariances. The reduced set method is applicable to any support vector machine.

paragraphs: This paper combines two techniques that improve different aspects of a support vector machine. The virtual support vector method improves generalization by incorporating known invariances: changes to an input that should leave the correct prediction unchanged. The reduced set method speeds up prediction by approximating the machine's decision surface.

On 10,000 NIST test digit images, incorporating invariances lowers the error rate from 1.4% to 1.0%. Applying the reduced set method then makes prediction fifty times faster than with the virtual support vector machine. These results distinguish the accuracy benefit of incorporating problem knowledge from the speed benefit of simplifying the resulting decision computation.

The combined machine achieves 1.1% error and runs 22 times faster than the original machine. Thus, the final approximation retains an accuracy improvement while also reducing prediction cost. The two techniques have different stated scopes: virtual support vectors require known invariances in the problem, whereas the reduced set method applies to any support vector machine. Their combination shows how those complementary improvements can operate together.
summary.tldr: Combining known invariances with decision-surface approximation produces an SVM that is 22 times faster and more accurate than the original.

title: Improving the Accuracy and Speed of Support Vector Machines

abstract: In most neural network models, synapses are treated as static weights that change only on the slow time scales of learning. In fact, however, synapses are highly dynamic, and show use-dependent plasticity over a wide range of time scales. Moreover, synaptic transmission is an inherently stochastic process: a spike arriving at a presynaptic terminal triggers release of a vesicle of neurotransmitter from a release site with a probability that can be much less than one. Changes in release probability represent one of the main mechanisms by which synaptic efficacy is modulated in neural circuits. We propose and investigate a simple model for dynamic stochastic synapses that can easily be integrated into common models for neural computation. We show through computer simulations and rigorous theoretical analysis that this model for a dynamic stochastic synapse increases computational power in a nontrivial way. Our results may have implications for the process(cid:173) ing of time-varying signals by both biological and artificial neural networks. A synapse 8 carries out computations on spike trains, more precisely on trains of spikes from the presynaptic neuron. Each spike from the presynaptic neuron mayor may not trigger the release of a neurotransmitter-filled vesicle at the synapse. The probability of a vesicle release ranges from about 0.01 to almost 1. Furthermore this release probability is known to be strongly "history dependent" [Dobrunz and Stevens, 1997]. A spike causes an excitatory or inhibitory potential (EPSP or IPSP, respectively) in the postsynaptic neuron only when a vesicle is released. paragraphs: Neural-network models often describe a synapse as a weight that changes slowly through learning. This paper instead treats the synapse as a dynamic, probabilistic computing element. An incoming spike may trigger neurotransmitter release or fail to do so, and the probability of release depends on the synapse's history of use.

The proposed simple model can be incorporated into common neural-computation models. Its input is a sequence of spike times, and its output records the spikes that successfully cause release. Because that selection is stochastic and history-dependent, the synapse transforms a temporal signal through more than a fixed scaling of its strength.

Computer simulations and rigorous theoretical analysis show that the dynamic stochastic model increases computational power in a nontrivial way. This supports treating synaptic behavior as part of the computation itself. The implications concern time-varying signals in biological and artificial networks, where information in a spike sequence can interact with the changing state and release probability of the connection.
summary.tldr: History-dependent, probabilistic synapses add computational power by transforming spike trains through dynamic release behavior.

title: Dynamic Stochastic Synapses as Computational Units

abstract: This paper reports about an application of Bayes' inferred neu(cid:173) ral network classifiers in the field of automatic sleep staging. The reason for using Bayesian learning for this task is two-fold. First, Bayesian inference is known to embody regularization automati(cid:173) cally. Second, a side effect of Bayesian learning leads to larger variance of network outputs in regions without training data. This results in well known moderation effects, which can be used to detect outliers. In a 5 fold cross-validation experiment the full Bayesian solution found with R. Neals hybrid Monte Carlo algo(cid:173) rithm, was not better than a single maximum a-posteriori (MAP) solution found with D.J. MacKay's evidence approximation. In a second experiment we studied the properties of both solutions in rejecting classification of movement artefacts. Experiences with Bayesian Learning in a Real World Application

paragraphs: This paper applies Bayesian neural-network classifiers to automatic sleep staging. Two properties motivate the approach: Bayesian inference incorporates regularization, and network outputs can become more variable in regions unsupported by training data. That second behavior can moderate predictions and provide a basis for detecting unusual inputs.

The authors compare a full Bayesian solution obtained with hybrid Monte Carlo against a single maximum a posteriori solution obtained using an evidence approximation. In five-fold cross-validation, the full Bayesian solution does not outperform the single-solution approach. The result makes the comparison concrete for this application: the more extensive Bayesian treatment does not automatically yield better classification performance.

A second experiment examines how both solutions reject classification of movement artifacts. This addresses a different question from ordinary classification accuracy: whether the system can recognize inputs on which it should withhold a classification. Together, the experiments assess Bayesian learning through both its predictive performance and the potential usefulness of its behavior away from familiar training examples.
summary.tldr: In automatic sleep staging, full Bayesian neural-network inference did not outperform a single MAP solution in five-fold cross-validation.

title: Experiences with Bayesian Learning in a Real World Application

abstract: This paper formulates the problem of visual search as Bayesian inference and defines a Bayesian ensemble of problem instances . In particular, we address the problem of the detection of visual contours in noise/clutter by optimizing a global criterion which combines local intensity and geometry information. We analyze the convergence rates of A * search algorithms using results from information theory to bound the probability of rare events within the Bayesian ensemble. This analysis determines characteristics of the domain , which we call order parameters, that determine the convergence rates. It defines a probabilistic collection of search problems and evaluates candidate contours using a global criterion that combines local image intensity with geometry. This connects evidence at individual image locations with the overall shape of the contour being sought.

The authors analyze how quickly A* search algorithms converge on these problems. They use information theory to bound the probability of rare events within the defined collection of instances. The analysis identifies characteristics of the problem domain, called order parameters, that determine convergence rates. paragraphs: The paper presents a real-time vision system that recognizes actions and interactions as they unfold. It explores two settings: coordinated movements of both hands in Tai Chi and interactions among people in surveillance scenes. Both require interpreting linked movements over time, rather than treating each visible motion as an isolated event.

The system uses a Bayesian framework with feedback between bottom-up visual evidence and top-down interpretations. It compares hidden Markov models with coupled hidden Markov models for representing individual actions and interacting agents. Coupling provides a way to model dependencies between evolving processes. For a fixed amount of training, the coupled models are reported to be more accurate and efficient.

The authors also address limited training data by using synthetic agents to develop prior models of person-to-person interaction. These artificial agents supply expectations about possible interactions that the recognition system can incorporate. The contribution combines temporal modeling, feedback, and simulated behavior to support recognition when observed training examples are limited.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian vision system uses coupled temporal models and synthetic-agent priors to recognize coordinated human actions and interactions.

title: Graphical Models for Recognizing Human Interactions

The basic bounds are formulated for a fixed training set. Simpler expressions are obtained for sampling from an input distri(cid:173) bution which equals the weight function of the covariance kernel, yielding asymptotically tight results. The results are compared with numerical experiments.

paragraphs: This paper develops mathematical bounds on several kinds of Bayesian prediction error in Gaussian-process regression. The aim is to characterize prediction error through inequalities that constrain its possible size. A simple convexity lemma provides the starting point for deriving these results across the error measures considered.

The basic bounds apply to a fixed training set. This makes the actual collection of training examples the starting point of the analysis. The authors then obtain simpler expressions under an additional sampling condition: the distribution used to draw inputs equals the weight function associated with the covariance kernel. That relationship is part of the setting for the simplified results.

Under this sampling setup, the resulting bounds are asymptotically tight, meaning they approach the error behavior they are intended to describe in the relevant limit. The authors also compare their results with numerical experiments. The paper thus connects a general fixed-training-set analysis with simpler, tight asymptotic expressions available under the stated relationship between sampling and kernel weighting.
summary.tldr: Convexity-based bounds characterize Gaussian-process regression errors, with simpler asymptotically tight results under a specified sampling condition.

title: General Bounds on Bayes Errors for Regression with Gaussian Processes

abstract: We propose a method of approximate dynamic programming for Markov decision processes (MDPs) using algebraic decision diagrams (ADDs). We produce near-optimal value functions and policies with much lower time and space requirements than exact dynamic programming. Our method reduces the sizes of the intermediate value functions generated during value iteration by replacing the values at the terminals of the ADD with ranges of values. Our method is demonstrated on a class of large MDPs (with up to 34 billion states), and we compare the results with the optimal value functions.
originalAbstract: We propose a method of approximate dynamic programming for Markov decision processes (MDPs) using algebraic decision diagrams (ADDs). Our method reduces the sizes of the intermediate value functions generated during value iteration by replacing the values at the terminals of the ADD with ranges of values. Our method is demonstrated on a class of large MDPs (with up to 34 billion states), and we compare the results with the optimal value functions.

paragraphs: APRICODD addresses planning in Markov decision processes, where a system must choose actions across many possible states. Dynamic programming uses value functions to describe how desirable those states are and derive a policy for choosing actions. The paper seeks to make this computation practical when exact intermediate value functions demand too much time and memory.

The method represents value functions with algebraic decision diagrams. Its key approximation replaces the numerical values at diagram terminals with ranges of values. This reduces the sizes of the intermediate representations created during value iteration. The approximation thus acts on the objects that the planning computation repeatedly constructs, directly targeting their storage and processing requirements.

The authors report near-optimal value functions and policies with substantially lower time and space requirements than exact dynamic programming. They demonstrate the approach on a class of large problems containing up to 34 billion states and compare the approximate results with optimal value functions. These comparisons connect the computational savings to the quality of the resulting plans.
summary.tldr: APRICODD compresses intermediate value functions with decision diagrams to obtain near-optimal plans at much lower computational cost.

title: APRICODD: Approximate Policy Construction Using Decision Diagrams

abstract: The problem of learning a semantic representation of a text document from data is addressed, in the situation where a corpus of unlabeled paired documents is available, each pair being formed by a short En- glish document and its French translation. This representation can then be used for any retrieval, categorization or clustering task, both in a stan- dard and in a cross-lingual setting. By using kernel functions, in this case simple bag-of-words inner products, each part of the corpus is mapped to a high-dimensional space. The correlations between the two spaces are then learnt by using kernel Canonical Correlation Analysis. A set of directions is found in the ﬁrst and in the second space that are max- imally correlated. Since we assume the two representations are com- pletely independent apart from the semantic content, any correlation be- tween them should reﬂect some semantic similarity. Certain patterns of English words that relate to a speciﬁc meaning should correlate with cer- tain patterns of French words corresponding to the same meaning, across the corpus. Using the semantic representation obtained in this way we ﬁrst demonstrate that the correlations detected between the two versions of the corpus are signiﬁcantly higher than random, and hence that a rep- resentation based on such features does capture statistical patterns that should reﬂect semantic information. Then we use such representation both in cross-language and in single-language retrieval tasks, observing performance that is consistently and signiﬁcantly superior to LSI on the same data.

paragraphs: The paper learns document representations from paired English texts and their French translations without category labels. The translation pairs provide two expressions of shared content. The aim is to extract features useful for retrieval, categorization, or clustering, including tasks that connect documents across languages.

Each language is represented using kernel functions, specifically bag-of-words inner products. Kernel canonical correlation analysis then finds directions in the two representation spaces that correlate maximally. The semantic interpretation rests on an explicit assumption: the two representations are independent apart from their semantic content. Under that assumption, recurring correlations between English and French word patterns should reflect shared meaning.

The authors first show that the learned cross-language correlations are significantly greater than random, supporting the presence of statistical structure that should reflect semantic information. They then evaluate the representation in both single-language and cross-language retrieval. On the same data, performance is consistently and significantly better than latent semantic indexing. These results support translation-based correlation as a useful source of document features in the evaluated retrieval tasks.
summary.tldr: Kernel correlation analysis learns document features from English–French translation pairs and improves both single-language and cross-language retrieval over LSI on the evaluated data.

title: Inferring a Semantic Representation of Text via Cross-Language Correlation Analysis

abstract: We propose an approach to learning the semantics of images which al- lows us to automatically annotate an image with keywords and to retrieve images based on text queries. We do this using a formalism that models the generation of annotated images. We assume that every image is di- vided into regions, each described by a continuous-valued feature vector. Given a training set of images with annotations, we compute a joint prob- abilistic model of image features and words which allow us to predict the probability of generating a word given the image regions. This may be used to automatically annotate and retrieve images given a word as a query. Experiments show that our model signiﬁcantly outperforms the best of the previously reported results on the tasks of automatic image annotation and retrieval.

paragraphs: This paper learns a connection between image content and descriptive words so that a system can automatically annotate pictures and retrieve them using text. It starts from images that already have annotations, using these examples to learn how visual features and words occur together.

The method assumes that each image has been divided into regions, with each region represented by a vector of continuous numerical features. The authors build a joint probabilistic model of those features and the annotation words. Given an image's regions, the model can then estimate the probability of generating a particular word. This makes the connection between visual evidence and language explicit within one probabilistic framework.

The same learned relationship supports both applications: proposing words for an image and finding images relevant to a query word. Experiments show significant improvements over the best previously reported results on annotation and retrieval. These findings support the usefulness of jointly modeling image regions and words for both tasks under the paper's region-based representation.
summary.tldr: A joint probabilistic model of image regions and words improves automatic image annotation and text-based image retrieval.

title: A Model for Learning the Semantics of Pictures

abstract: Coreference analysis, also known as record linkage or identity uncer- tainty, is a difficult and important problem in natural language process- ing, databases, citation matching and many other tasks. This paper intro- duces several discriminative, conditional-probability models for coref- erence analysis, all examples of undirected graphical models. Unlike many historical approaches to coreference, the models presented here are relational--they do not assume that pairwise coreference decisions should be made independently from each other. Unlike other relational models of coreference that are generative, the conditional model here can incorporate a great variety of features of the input without having to be concerned about their dependencies--paralleling the advantages of con- ditional random fields over hidden Markov models. We present positive results on noun phrase coreference in two standard text data sets.

paragraphs: Coreference analysis asks whether different mentions or records refer to the same underlying entity. The paper introduces several conditional-probability models for this problem, with noun phrase coreference as the application. Its main concern is how to make identity decisions together while using a broad range of evidence from the input.

The models are undirected graphical models with relational dependencies. They therefore avoid assuming that every pairwise identity decision should be made independently. Decisions about different pairs can inform one another within a shared model. This is important because the task concerns relationships among mentions, rather than just a collection of isolated pair comparisons.

Their conditional formulation also accommodates many input features without requiring a generative account of the dependencies among those features. The authors relate this advantage to the distinction between conditional random fields and hidden Markov models. They report positive results on noun phrase coreference in two standard text datasets, supporting the usefulness of combining relational decisions with flexible input evidence.
summary.tldr: Conditional relational models combine dependent identity decisions with varied input features and show positive results on noun phrase coreference.

title: Conditional Models of Identity Uncertainty with Application to Noun Coreference

abstract: We describe a way of learning matrix representations of objects and relationships. The goal of learning is to allow multiplication of matrices to represent symbolic relationships between objects and symbolic relationships between relationships, which is the main novelty of the method. We demonstrate that this leads to excellent generalization in two different domains: modular arithmetic and family relationships. We show that the same system can learn first-order propositions such as $(2, 5) \member +\!3$ or $(Christopher, Penelope)\member has\_wife$, and higher-order propositions such as $(3, +\!3) \member plus$ and $(+\!3, -\!3) \member inverse$ or $(has\_husband, has\_wife)\in higher\_oppsex$. We further demonstrate that the system understands how higher-order propositions are related to first-order ones by showing that it can correctly answer questions about first-order propositions involving the relations $+\!3$ or $has\_wife$ even though it has not been trained on any first-order examples involving these relations.

paragraphs: This paper learns matrix representations for both objects and relationships. Matrix multiplication is used to express relationships between objects, but the distinctive step is to also represent relationships between relationships. This allows the same system to handle ordinary symbolic facts and higher-order facts about the relations those facts involve.

The authors demonstrate the approach in modular arithmetic and family relationships. A first-order fact might connect two numbers through adding three, or connect two people through a spouse relation. Higher-order facts can express that adding and subtracting three are inverse operations, or describe a relationship between the husband and wife relations.

The reported generalization includes correctly answering first-order questions involving adding three or the wife relation despite receiving no first-order training examples involving those relations. This shows that, in the demonstrations, higher-order information can support answers about object-level relationships. The contribution is a shared numerical representation that connects these two levels of symbolic knowledge, with strong reported generalization in both studied domains.
summary.tldr: Learned matrices connect object-level and higher-order relationships, enabling generalization to relations without direct first-order training examples.

title: Using matrices to model symbolic relationship

abstract: Given a corpus of news items consisting of images accompanied by text captions, we want to find out ` whos doing what, i.e. associate names and action verbs in the captions to the face and body pose of the persons in the images. We present a joint model for simultaneously solving the image-caption correspondences and learning visual appearance models for the face and pose classes occurring in the corpus. These models can then be used to recognize people and actions in novel images without captions. We demonstrate experimentally that our joint face and pose model solves the correspondence problem better than earlier models covering only the face, and that it can perform recognition of new uncaptioned images.

paragraphs: A news photograph and its caption provide related information, but they do not explicitly identify every correspondence. A name must be matched to a face, and an action verb must be associated with a person's body pose. This paper tackles those assignments together, aiming to determine who is pictured and what each person is doing.

The proposed joint model simultaneously learns image-caption correspondences and visual appearance models for the face and pose classes present in the corpus. Learning the assignments and the visual models within one formulation connects the identity and action tasks. The caption supplies names and verbs, while the image supplies the facial and pose evidence to be matched.

Experiments show that the joint face-and-pose model solves the correspondence task better than earlier models that cover faces alone. The learned visual models also recognize people and actions in new images without captions. This demonstrates that the paired image-text corpus can support both annotation of its own examples and recognition when textual assistance is absent.
summary.tldr: Jointly learning face, pose, name, and verb correspondences improves image-caption matching and supports recognition in uncaptioned images.

title: Who’s Doing What: Joint Modeling of Names and Verbs for Simultaneous Face and Pose Annotation

abstract: We propose a novel Bayesian nonparametric approach to learning with probabilistic deterministic finite automata (PDFA). We define and develop and sampler for a PDFA with an infinite number of states which we call the probabilistic deterministic infinite automata (PDIA). Posterior predictive inference in this model, given a finite training sequence, can be interpreted as averaging over multiple PDFAs of varying structure, where each PDFA is biased towards having few states. We suggest that our method for averaging over PDFAs is a novel approach to predictive distribution smoothing. We test PDIA inference both on PDFA structure learning and on both natural language and DNA data prediction tasks. The results suggest that the PDIA presents an attractive compromise between the computational cost of hidden Markov models and the storage requirements of hierarchically smoothed Markov models.

paragraphs: Learning a probabilistic automaton involves deciding both how it predicts sequences and what state structure it should have. This paper introduces a Bayesian nonparametric model with an infinite number of possible states, called a probabilistic deterministic infinite automaton. The authors also develop a sampler for inference in the model.

Given a finite training sequence, posterior prediction can be interpreted as averaging over multiple finite automata with different structures. Each candidate automaton is biased toward using few states. This allows structural uncertainty to enter prediction, and the authors suggest that averaging over automata offers a new approach to smoothing predictive distributions.

The model is tested on automaton structure learning and on prediction tasks involving natural language and DNA. Results suggest an attractive compromise between the computational cost of hidden Markov models and the storage requirements of hierarchically smoothed Markov models. The contribution therefore combines a flexible account of state structure with an empirically promising balance of prediction-related computational and storage demands.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian infinite-state automaton predicts by averaging over compact finite automata with different structures.

title: Probabilistic Deterministic Infinite Automata

abstract: We study the problem of identifying the best arm in each of the bandits in a multi-bandit multi-armed setting. We first propose an algorithm called Gap-based Exploration (GapE) that focuses on the arms whose mean is close to the mean of the best arm in the same bandit (i.e., small gap). We then introduce an algorithm, called GapE-V, which takes into account the variance of the arms in addition to their gap. We prove an upper-bound on the probability of error for both algorithms. Since GapE and GapE-V need to tune an exploration parameter that depends on the complexity of the problem, which is often unknown in advance, we also introduce variations of these algorithms that estimate this complexity online. Finally, we evaluate the performance of these algorithms and compare them to other allocation strategies on a number of synthetic problems.

paragraphs: The problem is to identify the best option in each of several bandit problems, where an option's quality is represented by its mean outcome. Sampling must be allocated across options to make those selections accurately. A central difficulty is distinguishing the best option from competitors whose means are very close.

The authors introduce Gap-based Exploration, or GapE, which focuses on options with small gaps relative to the best mean within their own bandit. A second algorithm, GapE-V, also accounts for outcome variance. The paper proves upper bounds on the probability of making an identification error for both algorithms.

Both methods require tuning an exploration parameter using problem complexity, which is often unknown beforehand. The authors therefore provide variants that estimate this complexity as sampling proceeds. Comparisons with other allocation strategies use synthetic problems. The contribution combines targeted sampling, error guarantees, and a way to address missing prior knowledge about how difficult the identification task will be.
summary.tldr: Gap-based sampling algorithms identify the best options across multiple bandits, with error bounds and variants that estimate difficulty online.

title: Multi-Bandit Best Arm Identification

abstract: Lifted inference algorithms exploit symmetries in probabilistic models to speed up inference. They show impressive performance when calculating unconditional probabilities in relational models, but often resort to non-lifted inference when computing conditional probabilities. The reason is that conditioning on evidence breaks many of the model's symmetries, which preempts standard lifting techniques. Recent theoretical results show, for example, that conditioning on evidence which corresponds to binary relations is #P-hard, suggesting that no lifting is to be expected in the worst case. In this paper, we balance this grim result by identifying the Boolean rank of the evidence as a key parameter for characterizing the complexity of conditioning in lifted inference. In particular, we show that conditioning on binary evidence with bounded Boolean rank is efficient. This opens up the possibility of approximating evidence by a low-rank Boolean matrix factorization, which we investigate both theoretically and empirically.

paragraphs: Lifted inference accelerates probabilistic reasoning by exploiting symmetries in relational models. Observed evidence can destroy those symmetries, making conditional probabilities much harder to compute than unconditional ones. Evidence describing binary relations is especially problematic: existing worst-case results classify conditioning on it as a computationally hard counting problem.

This paper identifies Boolean rank as a useful measure of the evidence's structure. It shows that conditioning on binary evidence is efficient when this rank is bounded. The result refines the worst-case picture by distinguishing structured evidence that remains manageable from arbitrary evidence covered by the hardness result.

That characterization also suggests an approximation strategy. Evidence can be approximated using a low-rank Boolean matrix factorization, potentially replacing a difficult conditioning problem with one whose evidence has the tractable structure. The authors investigate this possibility both theoretically and empirically. The contribution is a structural route to efficient conditioning and approximation; it does not remove the general worst-case difficulty of binary evidence.
summary.tldr: Bounded Boolean rank makes conditioning on binary evidence efficient and motivates low-rank approximations for lifted inference.

title: On the Complexity and Approximation of Binary Evidence in Lifted Inference

abstract: We address the problem of image collection summarization by learning mixtures of submodular functions. We argue that submodularity is very natural to this problem, and we show that a number of previously used scoring functions are submodular — a property not explicitly mentioned in these publications. We provide classes of submodular functions capturing the necessary properties of summaries, namely coverage, likelihood, and diversity. To learn mixtures of these submodular functions as scoring functions, we formulate summarization as a supervised learning problem using large-margin structured prediction. Furthermore, we introduce a novel evaluation metric, which we call V-ROUGE, for automatic summary scoring. While a similar metric called ROUGE has been successfully applied to document summarization [14], no such metric was known for quantifying the quality of image collection summaries. We provide a new dataset consisting of 14 real-world image collections along with many human-generated ground truth summaries collected using mechanical turk. We also extensively compare our method with previously explored methods for this problem and show that our learning approach outperforms all competitors on this new dataset. This paper provides, to our knowledge, the first systematic approach for quantifying the problem of image collection summarization, along with a new dataset of image collections and human summaries.

paragraphs: Summarizing an image collection requires selecting images that together make a useful summary. This paper learns a scoring function for that selection by combining submodular functions. The authors identify submodularity in several previously used scoring functions and introduce function classes addressing coverage, likelihood, and diversity.

They formulate summary selection as supervised learning through large-margin structured prediction. This allows the mixture of scoring functions to be learned from examples of summaries. The contribution therefore connects desirable properties of an image summary with a training procedure for deciding how those properties should contribute to its score.

The paper also introduces V-ROUGE, an automatic evaluation measure for image summaries, and a dataset of 14 real-world collections with many human-created reference summaries gathered through Mechanical Turk. On this new dataset, the learned approach outperforms all compared methods. The authors describe the combined modeling, evaluation, and dataset contribution as, to their knowledge, the first systematic approach to quantifying this problem. The reported performance advantage is specific to the new dataset and its comparisons.
summary.tldr: Learned mixtures of submodular scoring functions improve image-collection summaries on a new dataset with human references.

title: Learning Mixtures of Submodular Functions for Image Collection Summarization

abstract: Sparse-Group Lasso (SGL) has been shown to be a powerful regression technique for simultaneously discovering group and within-group sparse patterns by using a combination of the l1 and l2 norms. However, in large-scale applications, the complexity of the regularizers entails great computational challenges. In this paper, we propose a novel two-layer feature reduction method (TLFre) for SGL via a decomposition of its dual feasible set. The two-layer reduction is able to quickly identify the inactive groups and the inactive features, respectively, which are guaranteed to be absent from the sparse representation and can be removed from the optimization. Existing feature reduction methods are only applicable for sparse models with one sparsity-inducing regularizer. To our best knowledge, TLFre is the first one that is capable of dealing with multiple sparsity-inducing regularizers. Moreover, TLFre has a very low computational cost and can be integrated with any existing solvers. Experiments on both synthetic and real data sets show that TLFre improves the efficiency of SGL by orders of magnitude.

paragraphs: Sparse-Group Lasso selects both groups of features and individual features within groups by combining two sparsity-promoting penalties. This flexibility makes it useful for discovering layered sparse patterns, but the combined regularizers can make large optimization problems computationally demanding. The paper addresses that cost through feature reduction.

The proposed method, TLFre, decomposes the optimization problem's dual feasible set to identify variables that cannot appear in the final sparse representation. One layer identifies inactive groups; the other identifies inactive individual features. Because their absence is guaranteed, those groups and features can be removed from the optimization rather than merely assigned a low priority.

The authors describe the screening procedure as inexpensive and compatible with any existing solver. They also position it, to their knowledge, as the first feature-reduction method capable of handling multiple sparsity-inducing regularizers. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets report efficiency improvements of orders of magnitude. The practical contribution is a smaller optimization problem backed by safe elimination guarantees, allowing existing SGL solvers to benefit without replacing their core optimization procedures.
summary.tldr: Two-layer screening safely removes inactive groups and features from Sparse-Group Lasso, producing large empirical efficiency gains.

title: Two-Layer Feature Reduction for Sparse-Group Lasso via Decomposition of Convex Sets

abstract: Recently there has been substantial interest in spectral methods for learning dynamical systems. These methods are popular since they often offer a good tradeoffbetween computational and statistical efficiency. Unfortunately, they can be difficult to use and extend in practice: e.g., they can make it difficult to incorporateprior information such as sparsity or structure. To address this problem, we presenta new view of dynamical system learning: we show how to learn dynamical systems by solving a sequence of ordinary supervised learning problems, therebyallowing users to incorporate prior knowledge via standard techniques such asL 1 regularization. Many existing spectral methods are special cases of this newframework, using linear regression as the supervised learner. We demonstrate theeffectiveness of our framework by showing examples where nonlinear regressionor lasso let us learn better state representations than plain linear regression does;the correctness of these instances follows directly from our general analysis.

paragraphs: Spectral methods for learning dynamical systems can offer a useful balance of computational and statistical efficiency. However, adapting them to incorporate prior information, such as sparsity or other structure, can be awkward. This paper reformulates dynamical-system learning as a sequence of ordinary supervised-learning problems to make such adaptation easier.

The reformulation allows familiar supervised-learning tools to encode prior knowledge, including L1 regularization. Many existing spectral methods appear within the framework as cases that use linear regression. This gives them a shared interpretation while opening the supervised-learning component to alternatives that can express different assumptions about the desired representation.

The authors demonstrate examples in which nonlinear regression or lasso produces better state representations than plain linear regression. Their general analysis supplies correctness results for these instances. The contribution is therefore both a unification and an extension: it explains existing methods through standard prediction tasks and shows how changing those tasks' learners can improve representations in the examples studied, with theoretical support carried through the common framework.
summary.tldr: Recasting dynamical-system learning as supervised learning makes sparsity and nonlinear predictors available within a unified, theoretically supported framework.

title: Supervised Learning for Dynamical System Learning

abstract: We present and empirically evaluate an efficient algorithm that learns to aggregate the predictions of an ensemble of binary classifiers. The algorithm uses the structure of the ensemble predictions on unlabeled data to yield significant performance improvements. It does this without making assumptions on the structure or origin of the ensemble, without parameters, and as scalably as linear learning. We empirically demonstrate these performance gains with random forests.
originalAbstract: We present and empirically evaluate an efficient algorithm that learns to aggregate the predictions of an ensemble of binary classifiers. It does this without making assumptions on the structure or origin of the ensemble, without parameters, and as scalably as linear learning. We empirically demonstrate these performance gains with random forests.

paragraphs: An ensemble supplies several binary predictions for each example, creating an additional learning problem: how should those predictions be combined? This paper introduces an efficient algorithm that learns the aggregation. Its semi-supervised approach uses structure in the ensemble's predictions on unlabeled data to improve the combined result.

The method does not require assumptions about the ensemble's structure or where its classifiers came from. The authors also describe it as parameter-free and as scalable as linear learning. These properties make the aggregation procedure applicable without tailoring it to a particular way of constructing the ensemble.

Empirical evaluation with random forests demonstrates significant performance improvements. The central finding is that unlabeled examples can contribute useful information at the aggregation stage, through the pattern of predictions they elicit from the ensemble. The paper combines this empirical benefit with an efficient learning procedure, addressing the quality of the combined predictions and the computational practicality of learning how to combine them.
summary.tldr: A parameter-free aggregation algorithm uses ensemble predictions on unlabeled data to improve performance while scaling like linear learning.

title: Scalable Semi-Supervised Aggregation of Classifiers

abstract: The iterations of many sparse estimation algorithms are comprised of a fixed linear filter cascaded with a thresholding nonlinearity, which collectively resemble a typical neural network layer. Consequently, a lengthy sequence of algorithm iterations can be viewed as a deep network with shared, hand-crafted layer weights. It is therefore quite natural to examine the degree to which a learned network model might act as a viable surrogate for traditional sparse estimation in domains where ample training data is available. While the possibility of a reduced computational budget is readily apparent when a ceiling is imposed on the number of layers, our work primarily focuses on estimation accuracy. In particular, it is well-known that when a signal dictionary has coherent columns, as quantified by a large RIP constant, then most tractable iterative algorithms are unable to find maximally sparse representations. In contrast, we demonstrate both theoretically and empirically the potential for a trained deep network to recover minimal $\ell_0$-norm representations in regimes where existing methods fail. The resulting system, which can effectively learn novel iterative sparse estimation algorithms, is deployed on a practical photometric stereo estimation problem, where the goal is to remove sparse outliers that can disrupt the estimation of surface normals from a 3D scene.

paragraphs: Many sparse-estimation algorithms repeatedly apply a linear filter followed by thresholding. Each iteration resembles a neural-network layer, so a sequence of iterations can be viewed as a deep network with shared, hand-designed weights. This paper asks whether learning those computations from ample training data can improve sparse estimation, with accuracy as its main focus.

The difficult setting involves dictionaries whose columns are highly coherent, as reflected in a large restricted-isometry constant. In such settings, many tractable iterative methods fail to find representations using the fewest nonzero coefficients. The authors present theoretical and empirical evidence that trained deep networks can recover minimum-ℓ0 representations in regimes where existing methods fail.

The resulting system can effectively learn new iterative sparse-estimation procedures. It is applied to photometric stereo, where sparse outliers interfere with estimating surface normals in a three-dimensional scene. The contribution establishes the potential of learned estimators in challenging sparse-recovery regimes, rather than claiming that every trained network always finds the sparsest representation.
summary.tldr: Trained deep networks can recover maximally sparse representations in some regimes where conventional iterative methods fail.

title: Maximal Sparsity with Deep Networks?

abstract: In this paper we present a new algorithm for computing a low rank approximation of the product $A^TB$ by taking only a single pass of the two matrices $A$ and $B$. The straightforward way to do this is to (a) first sketch $A$ and $B$ individually, and then (b) find the top components using PCA on the sketch. Our algorithm in contrast retains additional summary information about $A,B$ (e.g. row and column norms etc.) and uses this additional information to obtain an improved approximation from the sketches. Our main analytical result establishes a comparable spectral norm guarantee to existing two-pass methods; in addition we also provide results from an Apache Spark implementation that shows better computational and statistical performance on real-world and synthetic evaluation datasets.

Our algorithm in contrast retains additional summary information about $A,B$ (e.g. row and column norms etc.) and uses this additional information to obtain an improved approximation from the sketches. paragraphs: The paper considers how to find a low-rank approximation of the matrix product AᵀB while reading each input matrix only once. A straightforward approach would compress A and B separately into sketches and then apply PCA to those summaries. The proposed algorithm keeps extra information during the same pass to improve the approximation.

That additional information includes summaries such as row and column norms. Rather than treating the sketches as the only available description of the inputs, the method uses these summaries alongside them. The central idea is that retaining a little more information about the original matrices can make the eventual product approximation more informative without requiring another pass.

The main theoretical result gives a spectral-norm guarantee comparable to existing two-pass methods. An Apache Spark implementation also shows better computational and statistical performance on the evaluated synthetic and real-world datasets. Together, the results support single-pass processing as a way to obtain a useful product approximation while preserving a strong error guarantee.
summary.tldr: Extra matrix summaries improve single-pass sketches of AᵀB, yielding an error guarantee comparable to two-pass methods.

title: Single Pass PCA of Matrix Products

abstract: We present the first general purpose framework for marginal maximum a posteriori estimation of probabilistic program variables. By using a series of code transformations, the evidence of any probabilistic program, and therefore of any graphical model, can be optimized with respect to an arbitrary subset of its sampled variables. To carry out this optimization, we develop the first Bayesian optimization package to directly exploit the source code of its target, leading to innovations in problem-independent hyperpriors, unbounded optimization, and implicit constraint satisfaction; delivering significant performance improvements over prominent existing packages. We present applications of our method to a number of tasks including engineering design and parameter optimization.

We present applications of our method to a number of tasks including engineering design and parameter optimization.

paragraphs: Probabilistic programs describe models through code containing sampled variables. This paper presents a general framework for marginal maximum a posteriori estimation: optimizing selected variables while accounting for uncertainty in others through marginalization. The aim is to make this optimization available across probabilistic programs rather than requiring a separate method for each model.

A sequence of code transformations makes the program's evidence optimizable with respect to an arbitrary subset of sampled variables. The authors then develop a Bayesian optimization package that directly uses the target program's source code. That access supports methods for problem-independent hyperpriors, searching unbounded domains, and satisfying constraints implicitly.

The important connection is between model representation and optimization: the program supplies structure that the optimizer can exploit. The abstract reports significant performance improvements over prominent existing packages and describes applications including engineering design and parameter optimization. It presents the framework as the first general-purpose approach of its kind, with the same program-based formulation extending to graphical models.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian optimization framework exploits probabilistic program source code to optimize selected variables while marginalizing others.

title: Bayesian Optimization for Probabilistic Programs

abstract: Social dynamics is concerned primarily with interactions among individuals and the resulting group behaviors, modeling the temporal evolution of social systems via the interactions of individuals within these systems. In particular, the availability of large-scale data from social networks and sensor networks offers an unprecedented opportunity to predict state-changing events at the individual level. Examples of such events include disease transmission, opinion transition in elections, and rumor propagation. Unlike previous research focusing on the collective effects of social systems, this study makes efficient inferences at the individual level. In order to cope with dynamic interactions among a large number of individuals, we introduce the stochastic kinetic model to capture adaptive transition probabilities and propose an efficient variational inference algorithm the complexity of which grows linearly — rather than exponentially— with the number of individuals. To validate this method, we have performed epidemic-dynamics experiments on wireless sensor network data collected from more than ten thousand people over three years. The proposed algorithm was used to track disease transmission and predict the probability of infection for each individual. Our results demonstrate that this method is more efficient than sampling while nonetheless achieving high accuracy.

paragraphs: Social dynamics connects interactions between individuals with changes across a population. This paper focuses on predicting individual state changes, such as infection or opinion transitions, using information about those interactions. Its objective is efficient inference about particular people within a large evolving system.

The authors introduce a stochastic kinetic model to capture adaptive transition probabilities. They pair it with a variational inference algorithm whose complexity grows linearly with the number of individuals rather than exponentially. This scaling property is central to handling dynamic interactions across large populations while retaining predictions at the individual level.

The method is evaluated through epidemic-dynamics experiments using wireless sensor network data collected from more than ten thousand people over three years. The algorithm tracks disease transmission and predicts each individual’s infection probability. The authors report greater efficiency than sampling while maintaining high accuracy. These results support using an interaction-based model with approximate inference to make detailed predictions at a scale where computational demands are a central concern.
summary.tldr: A stochastic kinetic model with linearly scaling variational inference predicts individual infection risk efficiently in large-population experiments.

title: Using Social Dynamics to Make Individual Predictions: Variational Inference with a Stochastic Kinetic Model

abstract: This paper deals with the unsupervised domain adaptation problem, where one wants to estimate a prediction function $f$ in a given target domain without any labeled sample by exploiting the knowledge available from a source domain where labels are known. Our work makes the following assumption: there exists a non-linear transformation between the joint feature/label space distributions of the two domain $\ps$ and $\pt$. We propose a solution of this problem with optimal transport, that allows to recover an estimated target $\pt^f=(X,f(X))$ by optimizing simultaneously the optimal coupling and $f$. We show that our method corresponds to the minimization of a bound on the target error, and provide an efficient algorithmic solution, for which convergence is proved. The versatility of our approach, both in terms of class of hypothesis or loss functions is demonstrated with real world classification and regression problems, for which we reach or surpass state-of-the-art results.

Our work makes the following assumption: there exists a non-linear transformation between the joint feature/label space distributions of the two domain $\ps$ and $\pt$. We propose a solution of this problem with optimal transport, that allows to recover an estimated target $\pt^f=(X,f(X))$ by optimizing simultaneously the optimal coupling and $f$. paragraphs: The paper addresses unsupervised domain adaptation: learning a predictor for a target domain that has no labeled examples by using a labeled source domain. Its stated assumption is that a nonlinear transformation relates the two domains’ joint distributions of features and labels. This places both the inputs and their associated prediction targets within the adaptation problem.

The proposed method uses optimal transport to jointly optimize a coupling between domains and the target prediction function. Because target labels are unavailable, the target joint distribution is estimated using features paired with the function’s predictions. Learning the correspondence and learning the predictor are therefore connected parts of the same optimization.

The authors show that their method minimizes a bound on target-domain error and provide an efficient algorithm with a convergence proof. They also demonstrate flexibility across hypothesis classes and loss functions through real-world classification and regression problems. On those evaluations, the method matches or exceeds state-of-the-art results, supporting its use under the proposed joint-distribution adaptation framework.
summary.tldr: Joint optimal transport learns a target predictor and cross-domain coupling together, assuming a nonlinear relationship between source and target feature-label distributions.

title: Joint distribution optimal transportation for domain adaptation

abstract: We propose a recurrent extension of the Ladder networks whose structure is motivated by the inference required in hierarchical latent variable models. We demonstrate that the recurrent Ladder is able to handle a wide variety of complex learning tasks that benefit from iterative inference and temporal modeling. The architecture shows close-to-optimal results on temporal modeling of video data, competitive results on music modeling, and improved perceptual grouping based on higher order abstractions, such as stochastic textures and motion cues. We present results for fully supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised tasks. The results suggest that the proposed architecture and principles are powerful tools for learning a hierarchy of abstractions, learning iterative inference and handling temporal information.

paragraphs: Some learning tasks benefit from repeatedly refining an interpretation, while others require tracking how information changes over time. This paper introduces a recurrent extension of Ladder networks to address both needs. Its structure is motivated by the inference processes needed in hierarchical latent-variable models, connecting recurrence to learning multiple levels of abstraction.

The architecture is tested on tasks involving temporal modeling and perceptual grouping. Reported results include near-optimal performance on video temporal modeling, competitive performance on music modeling, and improved grouping using higher-level information such as stochastic textures and motion cues. These applications examine different ways that iterative processing and temporal information can support learning.

The evaluation includes fully supervised, semi-supervised, and unsupervised tasks, so the architecture is investigated under different amounts of explicit teaching information. The findings suggest that recurrent Ladder networks provide useful principles for learning abstraction hierarchies, iterative inference, and temporal structure. That conclusion is supported by the reported variety of tasks rather than a claim that recurrence is optimal for every learning problem.
summary.tldr: Recurrent Ladder networks support iterative inference and temporal modeling across several tasks and supervision settings.

title: Recurrent Ladder Networks

abstract: Recently, the Probabilistic Sentential Decision Diagram (PSDD) has been proposed as a framework for systematically inducing and learning distributions over structured objects, including combinatorial objects such as permutations and rankings, paths and matchings on a graph, etc. In this paper, we study the scalability of such models in the context of representing and learning distributions over routes on a map. In particular, we introduce the notion of a hierarchical route distribution and show how they can be leveraged to construct tractable PSDDs over route distributions, allowing them to scale to larger maps. We illustrate the utility of our model empirically, in a route prediction task, showing how accuracy can be increased significantly compared to Markov models.

In particular, we introduce the notion of a hierarchical route distribution and show how they can be leveraged to construct tractable PSDDs over route distributions, allowing them to scale to larger maps. We illustrate the utility of our model empirically, in a route prediction task, showing how accuracy can be increased significantly compared to Markov models.

paragraphs: Probability models over structured objects must represent combinations such as complete routes, rankings, or graph matchings. Probabilistic Sentential Decision Diagrams, or PSDDs, provide a framework for learning distributions over such objects. This paper examines their scalability for routes on a map, asking how to retain manageable computation as the map becomes larger.

The authors introduce hierarchical route distributions and show how to use them to construct tractable PSDDs. The hierarchy gives route modeling an organization that supports scaling to larger maps. The contribution concerns both representing distributions over routes and learning them within a computationally manageable framework.

An empirical route-prediction task illustrates the model's usefulness, showing that prediction accuracy can increase significantly relative to Markov models. This result provides an application-level reason to pursue the hierarchical construction, beyond scalability alone. The paper connects a general framework for structured probability to a specific modeling domain, demonstrating how a hierarchy over routes can support tractable models with improved prediction in the reported evaluation.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical route distributions make PSDD route models tractable on larger maps and improve route prediction over Markov models in the reported evaluation.

title: Tractability in Structured Probability Spaces

abstract: The success of machine learning methods heavily relies on having an appropriate representation for data at hand. Traditionally, machine learning approaches relied on user-defined heuristics to extract features encoding structural information about data. However, recently there has been a surge in approaches that learn how to encode the data automatically in a low dimensional space. Exponential family embedding provides a probabilistic framework for learning low-dimensional representation for various types of high-dimensional data. Though successful in practice, theoretical underpinnings for exponential family embeddings have not been established. In this paper, we study the Gaussian embedding model and develop the first theoretical results for exponential family embedding models. First, we show that, under a mild condition, the embedding structure can be learned from one observation by leveraging the parameter sharing between different contexts even though the data are dependent with each other. Second, we study properties of two algorithms used for learning the embedding structure and establish convergence results for each of them. The first algorithm is based on a convex relaxation, while the other solved the non-convex formulation of the problem directly. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: Learning a useful low-dimensional representation can replace manually designed features for high-dimensional data. Exponential family embeddings provide a probabilistic framework for doing this, but the paper identifies a gap between their practical success and theoretical understanding. It studies Gaussian embeddings to establish theoretical results within this broader class of representation models.

The central result is that, under a mild condition, the embedding structure can be learned from one observation. The method draws on parameters shared across different contexts, allowing those contexts to contribute information even though the data are dependent. The one-observation claim is therefore tied to the structured sharing and condition in the result.

The paper also analyzes two learning algorithms and establishes convergence results for each. One works through a convex relaxation of the problem, while the other addresses the nonconvex formulation directly. Experiments demonstrate the approach's effectiveness. Together, these contributions address both whether the embedding structure can be learned from the available data and whether the proposed optimization procedures converge.
summary.tldr: Under a mild condition, shared parameters let Gaussian embedding structure be learned from one observation, with convergence results for two algorithms.

title: Provable Gaussian Embedding with One Observation

abstract: Finding minimum distortion of adversarial examples and thus certifying robustness in neural networks classifiers is known to be a challenging problem. Nevertheless, recently it has been shown to be possible to give a non-trivial certified lower bound of minimum distortion, and some recent progress has been made towards this direction by exploiting the piece-wise linear nature of ReLU activations. However, a generic robustness certification for \textit{general} activation functions still remains largely unexplored. To address this issue, in this paper we introduce CROWN, a general framework to certify robustness of neural networks with general activation functions. The novelty in our algorithm consists of bounding a given activation function with linear and quadratic functions, hence allowing it to tackle general activation functions including but not limited to the four popular choices: ReLU, tanh, sigmoid and arctan. In addition, we facilitate the search for a tighter certified lower bound by \textit{adaptively} selecting appropriate surrogates for each neuron activation. Experimental results show that CROWN on ReLU networks can notably improve the certified lower bounds compared to the current state-of-the-art algorithm Fast-Lin, while having comparable computational efficiency. Furthermore, CROWN also demonstrates its effectiveness and flexibility on networks with general activation functions, including tanh, sigmoid and arctan.

paragraphs: This paper addresses how to certify that an input cannot be turned into an adversarial example by a sufficiently small change. The goal is a certified lower bound on the minimum distortion needed to alter a neural classifier’s prediction. Such a bound gives a guaranteed region of robustness without requiring the exact minimum distortion to be found.

The authors introduce CROWN, which handles general activation functions by bounding them with linear and quadratic functions. It can work with ReLU, tanh, sigmoid, and arctan, among other choices. The method adaptively selects suitable bounding surrogates for individual neurons to seek tighter certificates, extending certification beyond approaches centered on ReLU’s piecewise-linear structure.

Experiments on ReLU networks show stronger certified lower bounds than Fast-Lin with comparable computational efficiency. Experiments with the other listed activations demonstrate the framework’s flexibility and effectiveness. These findings concern the strength and computational cost of robustness certificates: improving a lower bound means certifying a larger protected region, rather than establishing the exact location of the nearest adversarial example.
summary.tldr: CROWN certifies robustness across general activation functions using adaptive linear and quadratic bounds.

title: Efficient Neural Network Robustness Certification with General Activation Functions

abstract: From traditional Web search engines to virtual assistants and Web accelerators, services that rely on online information need to continually keep track of remote content changes by explicitly requesting content updates from remote sources (e.g., web pages). We propose a novel optimization objective for this setting that has several practically desirable properties, and efficient algorithms for it with optimality guarantees even in the face of mixed content change observability and initially unknown change model parameters. Experiments on 18.5M URLs crawled daily for 14 weeks show significant advantages of this approach over prior art.
