paragraphs: Services that depend on online information must repeatedly request remote content to discover changes. Search engines, virtual assistants, and web accelerators all face this scheduling problem. Their stored information can fall behind the remote source, so deciding when to request another update is part of keeping the service current.

The paper proposes a new optimization objective for this setting and efficient algorithms with optimality guarantees. The guarantees accommodate mixed observability of content changes and change-model parameters that are initially unknown. These features matter because the scheduling method must operate while information about the change process is incomplete, rather than assuming that every relevant parameter is available beforehand.

The authors evaluate the approach using 18.5 million URLs crawled daily over 14 weeks and report significant advantages over prior methods. The contribution links an objective for freshness-related scheduling to algorithms that retain guarantees under the stated information conditions. The large collection of observed URL histories provides empirical support for the proposed approach in online content updating.
summary.tldr: A new content-update scheduling objective and efficient algorithms offer optimality guarantees despite incomplete change observations and initially unknown parameters.

title: Staying up to Date with Online Content Changes Using Reinforcement Learning for Scheduling

abstract: Inferring the most likely configuration for a subset of variables of a joint distribution given the remaining ones -- which we refer to as co-generation -- is an important challenge that is computationally demanding for all but the simplest settings. This task has received a considerable amount of attention, particularly for classical ways of modeling distributions like structured prediction. In contrast, almost nothing is known about this task when considering recently proposed techniques for modeling high-dimensional distributions, particularly generative adversarial nets (GANs). Therefore, in this paper, we study the occurring challenges for co-generation with GANs. To address those challenges we develop an annealed importance sampling based Hamiltonian Monte Carlo co-generation algorithm. The presented approach significantly outperforms classical gradient based methods on a synthetic and on the CelebA and LSUN datasets.

paragraphs: A model of a joint distribution describes variables together, but using that model to fill in only some variables poses a separate problem. The paper calls this co-generation: holding the given variables fixed while seeking the most likely configuration of the remaining ones. This can be computationally demanding even when the distribution itself can be modeled.

The authors investigate co-generation specifically for generative adversarial networks. They distinguish this setting from classical distribution models, where related inference problems have received considerably more attention. The central challenge is therefore how to use a GAN for constrained inference, beyond its role in generating complete samples from a learned distribution.

To address the challenges they identify, the authors develop a co-generation algorithm combining annealed importance sampling with Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. They report substantial improvements over classical gradient-based methods on synthetic data and on CelebA and LSUN. The findings support this sampling-based approach for the evaluated co-generation problems, giving GANs a way to infer missing configurations conditioned on supplied information.
summary.tldr: An algorithm combining annealed importance sampling and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo improves conditional configuration inference with GANs in the reported evaluations.

title: Co-Generation with GANs using AIS based HMC

abstract: In this paper, we introduce STREETS, a novel traffic flow dataset from publicly available web cameras in the suburbs of Chicago, IL. We seek to address the limitations of existing datasets in this area. Many such datasets lack a coherent traffic network graph to describe the relationship between sensors. The datasets that do provide a graph depict traffic flow in urban population centers or highway systems and use costly sensors like induction loops. These contexts differ from that of a suburban traffic body. Our dataset provides over 4 million still images across 2.5 months and one hundred web cameras in suburban Lake County, IL. We divide the cameras into two distinct communities described by directed graphs and count vehicles to track traffic statistics. Our goal is to give researchers a benchmark dataset for exploring the capabilities of inexpensive and non-invasive sensors like web cameras to understand complex traffic bodies in communities of any size. We present benchmarking tasks and baseline results for one such task to guide how future work may use our dataset.

paragraphs: Traffic datasets often omit an explicit description of how sensors relate within a road network. Those that include such structure commonly focus on urban centers or highways and rely on costly sensors. STREETS addresses a different setting: suburban traffic observed through publicly available web cameras, paired with network information.

The dataset contains more than four million still images collected over 2.5 months from one hundred cameras in suburban Lake County, Illinois. The cameras are divided into two communities represented by directed graphs. Vehicle counts provide traffic statistics, connecting the image collection to measurements of traffic activity across the camera network.

The authors provide benchmark tasks and baseline results for one task to help researchers use the dataset. Their goal is to support investigation of inexpensive, non-invasive cameras for understanding traffic in communities of different sizes. The contribution is therefore both a large image resource and a structured suburban network setting in which researchers can study relationships among traffic observations.
summary.tldr: STREETS pairs over four million suburban traffic images with camera-network graphs and vehicle counts to support traffic-flow research.

title: STREETS: A Novel Camera Network Dataset for Traffic Flow

abstract: The literature on ranking from ordinal data is vast, and there are several ways to aggregate overall preferences from pairwise comparisons between objects. In particular, it is well-known that any Nash equilibrium of the zero-sum game induced by the preference matrix defines a natural solution concept (winning distribution over objects) known as a von Neumann winner. Many real-world problems, however, are inevitably multi-criteria, with different pairwise preferences governing the different criteria. In this work, we generalize the notion of a von Neumann winner to the multi-criteria setting by taking inspiration from Blackwell’s approachability. Our framework allows for non-linear aggregation of preferences across criteria, and generalizes the linearization-based approach from multi-objective optimization. From a theoretical standpoint, we show that the Blackwell winner of a multi-criteria problem instance can be computed as the solution to a convex optimization problem. Furthermore, given random samples of pairwise comparisons, we show that a simple, "plug-in" estimator achieves (near-)optimal minimax sample complexity. Finally, we showcase the practical utility of our framework in a user study on autonomous driving, where we find that the Blackwell winner outperforms the von Neumann winner for the overall preferences.

paragraphs: Pairwise comparisons can identify a winning distribution over objects through a game-theoretic solution called a von Neumann winner. Real decisions, however, often involve several criteria with different pairwise preferences. This paper extends the winning-distribution idea to that setting using inspiration from Blackwell's approachability.

The resulting Blackwell winner supports nonlinear aggregation across criteria and generalizes approaches based on linear combinations of objectives. This matters when the desired way of combining preferences cannot be captured adequately by a linear aggregation. The authors show that computing a Blackwell winner can be expressed as a convex optimization problem, providing a concrete computational formulation.

When preferences must be estimated from randomly sampled pairwise comparisons, a simple plug-in estimator achieves near-optimal minimax sample complexity. This means its sample requirements are close to the best possible in the stated worst-case framework. In an autonomous-driving user study, the Blackwell winner performs better than the von Neumann winner on overall preferences. That study illustrates the practical value of explicitly retaining multiple criteria in preference aggregation.
summary.tldr: The Blackwell winner extends game-theoretic preference aggregation to multiple criteria with convex computation and near-optimal statistical estimation.

title: Preference learning along multiple criteria: A game-theoretic perspective

abstract: Positive-unlabeled (PU) learning trains a binary classifier using only positive and unlabeled data. A common simplifying assumption is that the positive data is representative of the target positive class. This assumption rarely holds in practice due to temporal drift, domain shift, and/or adversarial manipulation. This paper shows that PU learning is possible even with arbitrarily non-representative positive data given unlabeled data from the source and target distributions. Our key insight is that only the negative class's distribution need be fixed. We integrate this into two statistically consistent methods to address arbitrary positive bias - one approach combines negative-unlabeled learning with unlabeled-unlabeled learning while the other uses a novel, recursive risk estimator. Experimental results demonstrate our methods' effectiveness across numerous real-world datasets and forms of positive bias, including disjoint positive class-conditional supports. Additionally, we propose a general, simplified approach to address PU risk estimation overfitting.

paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning builds a binary classifier from labeled positive examples and examples with unknown labels. A common assumption is that the labeled positives represent the positives the classifier will encounter. This paper addresses cases where that assumption fails, including shifts over time, changes between domains, and manipulation of the positive examples.

The authors show that even arbitrarily unrepresentative positive data can be used when unlabeled samples are available from both source and target distributions and the negative-class distribution remains fixed. That fixed-negative condition is central to the result. They develop two statistically consistent methods: one combines negative-unlabeled and unlabeled-unlabeled learning, while the other uses a recursive estimator of prediction risk.

Experiments span real-world datasets and different forms of positive bias, including cases where source and target positives occupy disjoint supports. The reported effectiveness shows how much positive-class mismatch the methods can accommodate under the stated setup. The paper also proposes a simplified general approach for addressing overfitting in PU risk estimation.
summary.tldr: PU learning can tolerate arbitrary positive-class shift with source and target unlabeled data when the negative-class distribution stays fixed.

title: Learning from Positive and Unlabeled Data with Arbitrary Positive Shift

abstract: Machine learning algorithms typically require abundant data under a stationary environment. However, environments are nonstationary in many real-world applications. Critical issues lie in how to effectively adapt models under an ever-changing environment. We propose a method for transferring knowledge from a source domain to a target domain via $\ell_1$ regularization in high dimension. We incorporate $\ell_1$ regularization of differences between source and target parameters in addition to an ordinary $\ell_1$ regularization. Hence, our method yields sparsity for both the estimates themselves and changes of the estimates. The proposed method has a tight estimation error bound under a stationary environment, and the estimate remains unchanged from the source estimate under small residuals. Moreover, the estimate is consistent with the underlying function, even when the source estimate is mistaken due to nonstationarity. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed method effectively balances stability and plasticity.

paragraphs: When an environment changes, a useful model must adapt without needlessly discarding what it already knows. This paper proposes transferring a high-dimensional model from a source domain to a target domain through two l1 penalties. One encourages sparse parameter estimates, while the other encourages sparse differences between source and target parameters.

The second penalty makes adaptation selective: the method favors changing only some parameters while retaining others. The authors establish a tight estimation-error bound in a stationary environment and show that the target estimate stays identical to the source estimate when residuals are small. This gives a precise condition under which the method preserves existing knowledge.

The analysis also establishes consistency with the underlying function even when environmental change has made the source estimate mistaken. Thus, the method can retain a suitable source model while still correcting an unsuitable one under the analyzed conditions. Empirical results support its ability to balance stability and plasticity, connecting those theoretical properties to the practical problem of deciding how much to change.
summary.tldr: Penalizing both model parameters and changes from a source model enables sparse adaptation while balancing retention and correction.

title: Transfer Learning via $\ell_1$ Regularization

abstract: Domain Adaptation (DA) enables transferring a learning machine from a labeled source domain to an unlabeled target one. While remarkable advances have been made, most of the existing DA methods focus on improving the target accuracy at inference. How to estimate the predictive uncertainty of DA models is vital for decision-making in safety-critical scenarios but remains the boundary to explore. In this paper, we delve into the open problem of Calibration in DA, which is extremely challenging due to the coexistence of domain shift and the lack of target labels. We first reveal the dilemma that DA models learn higher accuracy at the expense of well-calibrated probabilities. Driven by this finding, we propose Transferable Calibration (TransCal) to achieve more accurate calibration with lower bias and variance in a unified hyperparameter-free optimization framework. As a general post-hoc calibration method, TransCal can be easily applied to recalibrate existing DA methods. Its efficacy has been justified both theoretically and empirically.

paragraphs: Domain adaptation transfers a predictor from labeled source data to a target domain without labels. Most methods emphasize target accuracy, but a useful prediction also needs a meaningful confidence estimate. This paper examines calibration in that setting, where domain differences and missing target labels jointly make predictive uncertainty difficult to assess.

The authors identify a tension: adaptation models can improve accuracy while producing less well-calibrated probabilities. They propose Transferable Calibration, or TransCal, to address that problem through a unified optimization framework with lower bias and variance. The framework is described as hyperparameter-free, and its purpose is to improve calibration after a domain-adaptation model has been learned.

As a general post-hoc method, TransCal can recalibrate existing adaptation approaches. The paper supports its effectiveness with both theory and experiments. Its contribution is to treat confidence quality as a distinct requirement of successful transfer, showing that accuracy gains alone do not establish that a model's probabilities are dependable in the new domain.
summary.tldr: TransCal recalibrates domain-adaptation models through a hyperparameter-free framework designed to reduce calibration bias and variance.

title: Transferable Calibration with Lower Bias and Variance in Domain Adaptation

abstract: We revisit and extend model stitching (Lenc & Vedaldi 2015) as a methodology to study the internal representations of neural networks. Given two trained and frozen models $A$ and $B$, we consider a "stitched model" formed by connecting the bottom-layers of $A$ to the top-layers of $B$, with a simple trainable layer between them. We argue that model stitching is a powerful and perhaps under-appreciated tool, which reveals aspects of representations that measures such as centered kernel alignment (CKA) cannot. Through extensive experiments, we use model stitching to obtain quantitative verifications for intuitive statements such as "good networks learn similar representations", by demonstrating that good networks of the same architecture, but trained in very different ways (eg: supervised vs. self-supervised learning), can be stitched to each other without drop in performance. We also give evidence for the intuition that "more is better" by showing that representations learnt with (1) more data, (2) bigger width, or (3) more training time can be "plugged in" to weaker models to improve performance. Finally, our experiments reveal a new structural property of SGD which we call "stitching connectivity", akin to mode-connectivity: typical minima reached by SGD are all "stitching-connected" to each other.

paragraphs: This paper studies neural representations by testing whether parts of different trained networks can work together. A stitched model connects the lower layers of one frozen network to the upper layers of another through a simple trainable layer. The resulting performance measures how well one model’s representation can serve another model’s computation.

Experiments show that good networks with the same architecture can be stitched without losing performance even when trained in very different ways, including supervised and self-supervised learning. The authors argue that this functional test reveals aspects of representation similarity that measures such as centered kernel alignment do not capture.

Further experiments show that representations learned with more data, greater width, or longer training can improve weaker models when plugged into them. The authors also identify an empirical property called stitching connectivity: typical minima reached by stochastic gradient descent are connected through this stitching procedure. Together, these findings provide quantitative evidence for similarity and transferability among representations while examining their usefulness inside another network.
summary.tldr: Model stitching tests representation compatibility by joining frozen networks, revealing empirical similarity, transferable improvements, and connectivity among trained solutions.

title: Revisiting Model Stitching to Compare Neural Representations

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) agents often fail to generalize beyond their training environments. To alleviate this problem, recent work has proposed the use of data augmentation. However, different tasks tend to benefit from different types of augmentations and selecting the right one typically requires expert knowledge. In this paper, we introduce three approaches for automatically finding an effective augmentation for any RL task. These are combined with two novel regularization terms for the policy and value function, required to make the use of data augmentation theoretically sound for actor-critic algorithms. Our method achieves a new state-of-the-art on the Procgen benchmark and outperforms popular RL algorithms on DeepMind Control tasks with distractors. In addition, our agent learns policies and representations which are more robust to changes in the environment that are irrelevant for solving the task, such as the background.

paragraphs: A reinforcement learning agent can perform well during training yet struggle when its environment changes. Data augmentation can help, but different tasks benefit from different transformations of their training inputs. Selecting an effective transformation therefore often depends on expert knowledge. This paper studies how to automate that selection so augmentation can better support generalization.

The authors introduce three approaches for finding useful augmentations and combine them with two new regularization terms. These terms act on the policy and the value function, the two components used by actor-critic algorithms. According to the paper, this regularization is required to make augmentation theoretically sound in that setting, connecting the choice of transformed inputs to the learning objective.

The resulting method achieves a new state of the art on Procgen and outperforms popular reinforcement learning algorithms on DeepMind Control tasks containing distractors. The learned policies and representations also become more robust to environmental changes irrelevant to solving the task, such as background changes. These findings connect automated augmentation selection with improved resistance to distracting visual variation.
summary.tldr: Automatically selected augmentations, combined with policy and value regularization, improve reinforcement learning generalization and robustness to irrelevant environmental changes.

title: Automatic Data Augmentation for Generalization in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Evaluating the inherent difficulty of a given data-driven classification problem is important for establishing absolute benchmarks and evaluating progress in the field. To this end, a natural quantity to consider is the \emph{Bayes error}, which measures the optimal classification error theoretically achievable for a given data distribution. While generally an intractable quantity, we show that we can compute the exact Bayes error of generative models learned using normalizing flows. Our technique relies on a fundamental result, which states that the Bayes error is invariant under invertible transformation. Therefore, we can compute the exact Bayes error of the learned flow models by computing it for Gaussian base distributions, which can be done efficiently using Holmes-Diaconis-Ross integration. Moreover, we show that by varying the temperature of the learned flow models, we can generate synthetic datasets that closely resemble standard benchmark datasets, but with almost any desired Bayes error. We use our approach to conduct a thorough investigation of state-of-the-art classification models, and find that in some --- but not all --- cases, these models are capable of obtaining accuracy very near optimal. Finally, we use our method to evaluate the intrinsic "hardness" of standard benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: The paper develops a way to compare classification performance with the best accuracy theoretically possible for a data distribution. That reference is determined by Bayes error, which is usually difficult to compute. The authors show how to compute it exactly for generative distributions learned with normalizing flows, creating benchmarks with a known optimal error.

This lets the authors work with the flow models' Gaussian base distributions and use Holmes-Diaconis-Ross integration for efficient computation. These controlled datasets let the authors investigate how close leading classifiers come to the theoretical optimum. They find near-optimal accuracy in some cases, but not all, and use the method to assess the intrinsic difficulty of standard benchmarks. The exact error calculation applies to the learned generative models, providing a concrete reference for evaluating classifiers on those modeled distributions.
summary.tldr: Normalizing-flow models enable synthetic classification benchmarks with known Bayes error, revealing when classifiers approach optimal accuracy.

title: Evaluating State-of-the-Art Classification Models Against Bayes Optimality

abstract: We introduce the GANformer2 model, an iterative object-oriented transformer, explored for the task of generative modeling. The network incorporates strong and explicit structural priors, to reflect the compositional nature of visual scenes, and synthesizes images through a sequential process. It operates in two stages: a fast and lightweight planning phase, where we draft a high-level scene layout, followed by an attention-based execution phase, where the layout is being refined, evolving into a rich and detailed picture. Our model moves away from conventional black-box GAN architectures that feature a flat and monolithic latent space towards a transparent design that encourages efficiency, controllability and interpretability. We demonstrate GANformer2's strengths and qualities through a careful evaluation over a range of datasets, from multi-object CLEVR scenes to the challenging COCO images, showing it successfully achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of visual quality, diversity and consistency. Further experiments demonstrate the model's disentanglement and provide a deeper insight into its generative process, as it proceeds step-by-step from a rough initial sketch, to a detailed layout that accounts for objects' depths and dependencies, and up to the final high-resolution depiction of vibrant and intricate real-world scenes. See https://github.com/dorarad/gansformer for model implementation.

paragraphs: GANformer2 generates scenes through an iterative process organized around objects. Its design explicitly reflects the idea that a visual scene contains components with relationships to one another. By building this structure into the model, the authors aim to make image generation more efficient, controllable, and interpretable.

Generation has two stages. A lightweight planning stage drafts a high-level scene layout, and an attention-based execution stage refines that layout into a detailed image. The sequence progresses from a rough sketch toward a layout accounting for object depths and dependencies, then to the final depiction. This gives the generation process intermediate structure that can be examined.

Evaluations range from multi-object CLEVR scenes to COCO images. The authors report state-of-the-art results for visual quality, diversity, and consistency across their evaluation. Additional experiments examine disentanglement and reveal how the scene develops step by step. The findings support an explicitly compositional architecture as an effective approach to generating both structured scenes and complex real-world imagery.
summary.tldr: GANformer2 generates images by planning object-based scene layouts and progressively refining them with attention.

title: Compositional Transformers for Scene Generation

abstract: Effective control and prediction of dynamical systems require appropriate handling of continuous-time and discrete, event-triggered processes. Stochastic hybrid systems (SHSs), common across engineering domains, provide a formalism for dynamical systems subject to discrete, possibly stochastic, state jumps and multi-modal continuous-time flows. Despite the versatility and importance of SHSs across applications, a general procedure for the explicit learning of both discrete events and multi-mode continuous dynamics remains an open problem. This work introduces Neural Hybrid Automata (NHAs), a recipe for learning SHS dynamics without a priori knowledge on the number, mode parameters, and inter-modal transition dynamics. NHAs provide a systematic inference method based on normalizing flows, neural differential equations, and self-supervision. We showcase NHAs on several tasks, including mode recovery and flow learning in systems with stochastic transitions, and end-to-end learning of hierarchical robot controllers.

We showcase NHAs on several tasks, including mode recovery and flow learning in systems with stochastic transitions, and end-to-end learning of hierarchical robot controllers.

paragraphs: Some dynamical systems evolve continuously within a mode but also undergo discrete events that change their state or operating mode. Those events may be stochastic. Stochastic hybrid systems provide a formal language for this combination, but learning both the continuous behavior and the event mechanisms presents a broader challenge than learning either component alone.

Neural Hybrid Automata offer a procedure for learning these systems without prior knowledge of the number of modes, their parameters, or the dynamics of transitions between them. The inference method combines normalizing flows, neural differential equations, and self-supervision. Its purpose is to learn the different forms of behavior and the transitions connecting them within one systematic approach.

The authors demonstrate the method on recovering modes and learning continuous flows in systems with stochastic transitions. They also show end-to-end learning of hierarchical robot controllers. These examples illustrate the scope of the proposed recipe across dynamics inference and control, addressing situations in which a useful model must account for both continuous evolution and discrete changes.
summary.tldr: Neural Hybrid Automata learn continuous dynamics and stochastic mode transitions without requiring the modes or transition dynamics to be specified in advance.

title: Neural Hybrid Automata: Learning Dynamics With Multiple Modes and Stochastic Transitions

abstract: While deep learning reshaped the classical motion capture pipeline with feed-forward networks, generative models are required to recover fine alignment via iterative refinement. Unfortunately, the existing models are usually hand-crafted or learned in controlled conditions, only applicable to limited domains. We propose a method to learn a generative neural body model from unlabelled monocular videos by extending Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). We equip them with a skeleton to apply to time-varying and articulated motion. A key insight is that implicit models require the inverse of the forward kinematics used in explicit surface models. Our reparameterization defines spatial latent variables relative to the pose of body parts and thereby overcomes ill-posed inverse operations with an overparameterization. This enables learning volumetric body shape and appearance from scratch while jointly refining the articulated pose; all without ground truth labels for appearance, pose, or 3D shape on the input videos. When used for novel-view-synthesis and motion capture, our neural model improves accuracy on diverse datasets.

A-NeRF learns a generative body model from unlabeled, single-camera videos, extending neural radiance fields with a skeleton so that the representation can accommodate articulated motion over time.

The central technical issue is how spatial locations relate to moving body parts. Explicit surface models use forward kinematics to move a body with its skeleton; the implicit representation needs an inverse relationship. The paper introduces spatial latent variables relative to body-part poses, using an overparameterized representation to handle inverse operations that would otherwise be ill-posed.

This construction lets the method learn volumetric shape and appearance from scratch while jointly refining pose. The input videos require no ground-truth appearance, pose, or three-dimensional shape labels. Evaluations report improved accuracy on diverse datasets for rendering previously unseen viewpoints and capturing motion. The contribution connects image generation and pose refinement within a learned, articulated body representation.
summary.tldr: A-NeRF learns an articulated body representation from unlabeled monocular video while jointly refining shape, appearance, and pose.

title: A-NeRF: Articulated Neural Radiance Fields for Learning Human Shape, Appearance, and Pose

abstract: Communication requires having a common language, a lingua franca, between agents. This language could emerge via a consensus process, but it may require many generations of trial and error. Alternatively, the lingua franca can be given by the environment, where agents ground their language in representations of the observed world. We demonstrate a simple way to ground language in learned representations, which facilitates decentralized multi-agent communication and coordination. We find that a standard representation learning algorithm -- autoencoding -- is sufficient for arriving at a grounded common language. When agents broadcast these representations, they learn to understand and respond to each other's utterances and achieve surprisingly strong task performance across a variety of multi-agent communication environments.

paragraphs: This paper studies how cooperating agents can develop a shared basis for communication. A common language might emerge through repeated attempts to coordinate, but that consensus process can require many rounds of trial and error. The authors investigate another source of common meaning: representations grounded in what agents observe in their environment.

Their method uses autoencoding, a standard representation-learning approach, to construct those grounded representations. Agents broadcast the resulting representations and learn to interpret and respond to one another’s messages. This makes observation-based representation learning part of the communication mechanism, connecting what agents say to information about the world they are interacting with.

Across a variety of multi-agent communication environments, the authors find that this simple approach supports strong task performance. Their result establishes autoencoding as sufficient for obtaining a grounded common language in the settings evaluated. It highlights a practical connection between representation learning and decentralized coordination: useful communication can build on learned descriptions of observations rather than relying entirely on an unconstrained consensus process.
summary.tldr: Agents can use autoencoded observations as a grounded common language that supports strong decentralized coordination.

title: Learning to Ground Multi-Agent Communication with Autoencoders

abstract: Low-rank and nonsmooth matrix optimization problems capture many fundamental tasks in statistics and machine learning. While significant progress has been made in recent years in developing efficient methods for \textit{smooth} low-rank optimization problems that avoid maintaining high-rank matrices and computing expensive high-rank SVDs, advances for nonsmooth problems have been slow paced. In this paper we consider standard convex relaxations for such problems. Mainly, we prove that under a natural \textit{generalized strict complementarity} condition and under the relatively mild assumption that the nonsmooth objective can be written as a maximum of smooth functions, the \textit{extragradient method}, when initialized with a "warm-start'' point, converges to an optimal solution with rate $O(1/t)$ while requiring only two \textit{low-rank} SVDs per iteration. We give a precise trade-off between the rank of the SVDs required and the radius of the ball in which we need to initialize the method. We support our theoretical results with empirical experiments on several nonsmooth low-rank matrix recovery tasks, demonstrating that using simple initializations, the extragradient method produces exactly the same iterates when full-rank SVDs are replaced with SVDs of rank that matches the rank of the (low-rank) ground-truth matrix to be recovered.

paragraphs: Many matrix estimation problems seek low-rank solutions, but optimization can still require expensive decompositions of high-rank matrices. This paper addresses nonsmooth objectives, where progress on avoiding that expense has been slower than for smooth problems. It analyzes the extragradient method for standard convex relaxations of these tasks.

The main guarantee requires generalized strict complementarity, an objective expressible as a maximum of smooth functions, and initialization sufficiently close to an appropriate solution. Under these conditions, the method converges at a rate of O(1/t) using only two low-rank singular value decompositions per iteration. The analysis specifies a tradeoff between the decomposition rank and the radius of the permitted initialization region.

Experiments on nonsmooth low-rank matrix recovery tasks support the theory. With simple initializations, replacing full-rank decompositions by decompositions matching the ground-truth rank produces exactly the same iterates in the reported experiments. This links the computational savings to preservation of the optimization trajectory, while the formal convergence claim remains conditional on the stated structural and initialization requirements.
summary.tldr: Under structural and warm-start conditions, extragradient optimization achieves O(1/t) convergence using only low-rank matrix decompositions.

title: Low-Rank Extragradient Method for Nonsmooth and Low-Rank Matrix Optimization Problems

abstract: Distributionally robust learning (DRL) is increasingly seen as a viable method to train machine learning models for improved model generalization. These min-max formulations, however, are more difﬁcult to solve. We provide a new stochastic gradient descent algorithm to efﬁciently solve this DRL formulation. Our approach applies gradient descent to the outer minimization formulation and estimates the gradient of the inner maximization based on a sample average approximation. The latter uses a subset of the data sampled without replacement in each iteration, progressively increasing the subset size to ensure convergence. We rigorously establish convergence to a near-optimal solution under standard regularity assumptions and, for strongly convex losses, match the best known $O(\epsilon{ −1})$ rate of convergence up to a known threshold. Empirical results demonstrate the signiﬁcant beneﬁts of our approach over previous work in improving learning for model generalization.

paragraphs: Distributionally robust learning trains models through a min-max objective: the learning procedure minimizes a loss evaluated against an inner worst-case choice. This formulation is attractive for improving generalization, but the nested optimization makes training harder. The paper develops a stochastic gradient method intended to solve this problem efficiently.

The method applies gradient descent to the outer minimization and uses a sample average approximation to estimate the gradient associated with the inner maximization. At each iteration, it samples a subset of the data without replacement. The subset grows progressively, allowing the approximation to become more accurate as optimization proceeds and supporting the convergence argument.

Under standard regularity assumptions, the authors prove convergence to a near-optimal solution. For strongly convex losses, they match the best known O(1/epsilon) convergence rate up to a specified threshold. Those qualifications are part of the theoretical result. Empirical comparisons also report substantial benefits over previous work for generalization. Together, the analysis and experiments support growing data subsets as a practical way to reduce the difficulty of robust training.
summary.tldr: A stochastic optimization method uses progressively larger data subsets to solve distributionally robust learning problems with qualified convergence guarantees.

title: Efficient Generalization with Distributionally Robust Learning

abstract: Over the last several decades, software has been woven into the fabric of every aspect of our society. As software development surges and code infrastructure of enterprise applications ages, it is now more critical than ever to increase software development productivity and modernize legacy applications. Advances in deep learning and machine learning algorithms have enabled breakthroughs in computer vision, speech recognition, natural language processing and beyond, motivating researchers to leverage AI techniques to improve software development efficiency. Thus, the fast-emerging research area of “AI for Code” has garnered new interest and gathered momentum. In this paper, we present a large-scale dataset \textit{CodeNet}, consisting of over 14 million code samples and about 500 million lines of code in 55 different programming languages, which is aimed at teaching AI to code. In addition to its large scale, CodeNet has a rich set of high-quality annotations to benchmark and help accelerate research in AI techniques for a variety of critical coding tasks, including code similarity and classification, code translation between a large variety of programming languages, and code performance (runtime and memory) improvement techniques. Additionally, CodeNet provides sample input and output test sets for 98.5\% of the code samples, which can be used as an oracle for determining code correctness and potentially guide reinforcement learning for code quality improvements. As a usability feature, we provide several pre-processing tools in CodeNet to transform source code into representations that can be readily used as inputs into machine learning models. Results of code classification and code similarity experiments using the CodeNet dataset are provided as a reference. We hope that the scale, diversity and rich, high-quality annotations of CodeNet will offer unprecedented research opportunities at the intersection of AI and Software Engineering.

They provide a way to check program behavior and could potentially supply feedback for reinforcement learning aimed at improving code quality. The paper reports classification and similarity experiments as reference results. Its main contribution is the scale and organization of the research resource, with the other supported tasks representing opportunities for further work.
summary.tldr: CodeNet supplies millions of annotated programs across 55 languages to support research on code understanding, translation, and performance improvement.

title: CodeNet: A Large-Scale AI for Code Dataset for Learning a Diversity of Coding Tasks

abstract: Progress in deep reinforcement learning (RL) is heavily driven by the availability of challenging benchmarks used for training agents. However, benchmarks that are widely adopted by the community are not explicitly designed for evaluating specific capabilities of RL methods. While there exist environments for assessing particular open problems in RL (such as exploration, transfer learning, unsupervised environment design, or even language-assisted RL), it is generally difficult to extend these to richer, more complex environments once research goes beyond proof-of-concept results. We present MiniHack, a powerful sandbox framework for easily designing novel RL environments. MiniHack is a one-stop shop for RL experiments with environments ranging from small rooms to complex, procedurally generated worlds. By leveraging the full set of entities and environment dynamics from NetHack, one of the richest grid-based video games, MiniHack allows designing custom RL testbeds that are fast and convenient to use. With this sandbox framework, novel environments can be designed easily, either using a human-readable description language or a simple Python interface. In addition to a variety of RL tasks and baselines, MiniHack can wrap existing RL benchmarks and provide ways to seamlessly add additional complexity.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning benchmarks strongly shape which capabilities researchers can study. Widely used environments do not always isolate particular abilities, while specialized environments can be difficult to expand once a method moves beyond a small demonstration. MiniHack addresses this problem by providing a framework for creating and extending custom reinforcement learning environments.

The framework draws on the entities and dynamics of NetHack, a rich grid-based game. Researchers can construct environments ranging from small rooms to complex worlds generated procedurally. They can specify tasks through a human-readable description language or a simple Python interface, making environment design a direct part of the experimental workflow.

MiniHack also supplies tasks and baselines and can wrap existing benchmarks to add complexity. Its value lies in supporting a progression from focused tests of capabilities toward richer settings within one framework. The paper presents infrastructure for research on problems such as exploration, transfer, environment design, and language-assisted learning, rather than claiming that the framework itself solves those problems.
summary.tldr: MiniHack lets researchers build and extend reinforcement learning environments from simple rooms to complex procedurally generated worlds.

title: MiniHack the Planet: A Sandbox for Open-Ended Reinforcement Learning Research

abstract: In this paper, we study both multi-armed and contextual bandit problems in censored environments. Our goal is to estimate the performance loss due to censorship in the context of classical algorithms designed for uncensored environments. Our main contributions include the introduction of a broad class of censorship models and their analysis in terms of the effective dimension of the problem -- a natural measure of its underlying statistical complexity and main driver of the regret bound. In particular, the effective dimension allows us to maintain the structure of the original problem at first order, while embedding it in a bigger space, and thus naturally leads to results analogous to uncensored settings. Our analysis involves a continuous generalization of the Elliptical Potential Inequality, which we believe is of independent interest. We also discover an interesting property of decision-making under censorship: a transient phase during which initial misspecification of censorship is self-corrected at an extra cost; followed by a stationary phase that reflects the inherent slowdown of learning governed by the effective dimension. Our results are useful for applications of sequential decision-making models where the feedback received depends on strategic uncertainty (e.g., agents’ willingness to follow a recommendation) and/or random uncertainty (e.g., loss or delay in arrival of information).

paragraphs: Bandit algorithms learn which decisions work well from the feedback they receive. In censored environments, that feedback can be unavailable because people do not follow recommendations or information is lost or delayed. This paper studies how such censorship affects classical algorithms for both multi-armed and contextual bandits.

The authors introduce a broad family of censorship models and describe their statistical difficulty through an effective dimension. This quantity drives their bounds on regret, the performance lost through imperfect decisions during learning. Their formulation embeds the problem in a larger space while retaining its original structure at first order, allowing results analogous to those for uncensored feedback. The analysis uses a continuous generalization of the Elliptical Potential Inequality.

The results also distinguish two phases. An initial phase pays an extra cost while correcting misspecified censorship, followed by a stationary phase with a learning slowdown governed by effective dimension. This distinction helps separate the temporary cost of learning the feedback process from the continuing cost of receiving censored information.
summary.tldr: The paper uses effective dimension to quantify how censored feedback slows bandit learning and separates initial correction costs from the continuing slowdown.

title: Effective Dimension in Bandit Problems under Censorship

abstract: Recently, the accuracy of image-text matching has been greatly improved by multimodal pretrained models, all of which are trained on millions or billions of paired images and texts. Different from them, this paper studies a new scenario as unpaired image-text matching, in which paired images and texts are assumed to be unavailable during model training. To deal with this, we propose a simple yet effective method namely Multimodal Aligned Conceptual Knowledge (MACK), which is inspired by the knowledge use in human brain. It can be directly used as general knowledge to correlate images and texts even without model training, or further fine-tuned based on unpaired images and texts to better generalize to certain datasets. In addition, we extend it as a re-ranking method, which can be easily combined with existing image-text matching models to substantially improve their performance.

paragraphs: Image-text matching often benefits from models trained on enormous collections of paired images and descriptions. This paper studies a different training setting: paired images and texts are unavailable. The challenge is to establish useful connections between the two kinds of information without training examples that explicitly say which image belongs with which text.

The proposed method, Multimodal Aligned Conceptual Knowledge, or MACK, uses aligned conceptual knowledge to correlate images and language. Inspired by human knowledge use, it can serve directly as general knowledge without additional model training. It can also be fine-tuned using unpaired images and texts to better adapt to particular datasets.

The authors further extend MACK into a re-ranking method that can be combined with existing image-text matching models. They report substantial performance improvements from that combination. The contribution therefore offers several uses for the same conceptual knowledge: direct matching, adaptation without paired examples, and refinement of another model’s rankings. Its importance lies in broadening the available training setup for connecting visual and textual content.
summary.tldr: MACK uses aligned conceptual knowledge to match images and text without paired training examples and to improve existing models through re-ranking.

title: MACK: Multimodal Aligned Conceptual Knowledge for Unpaired Image-text Matching

abstract: Sliced Wasserstein distances preserve properties of classic Wasserstein distances while being more scalable for computation and estimation in high dimensions. The goal of this work is to quantify this scalability from three key aspects: (i) empirical convergence rates; (ii) robustness to data contamination; and (iii) efficient computational methods. For empirical convergence, we derive fast rates with explicit dependence of constants on dimension, subject to log-concavity of the population distributions. For robustness, we characterize minimax optimal, dimension-free robust estimation risks, and show an equivalence between robust sliced 1-Wasserstein estimation and robust mean estimation. This enables lifting statistical and algorithmic guarantees available for the latter to the sliced 1-Wasserstein setting. Moving on to computational aspects, we analyze the Monte Carlo estimator for the average-sliced distance, demonstrating that larger dimension can result in faster convergence of the numerical integration error. For the max-sliced distance, we focus on a subgradient-based local optimization algorithm that is frequently used in practice, albeit without formal guarantees, and establish an $O(\epsilon^{-4})$ computational complexity bound for it. Our theory is validated by numerical experiments, which altogether provide a comprehensive quantitative account of the scalability question.

paragraphs: Sliced Wasserstein distances offer a more scalable way to compare high-dimensional distributions while preserving properties of classical Wasserstein distances. This paper quantifies that scalability along three separate axes: estimation from samples, robustness to contaminated data, and the computational cost of evaluating the distances.

For empirical convergence, the authors obtain fast rates with explicit dimensional dependence in the constants, assuming log-concave population distributions. For robustness, they characterize minimax-optimal estimation risks that do not depend on dimension. They also establish an equivalence between robust sliced 1-Wasserstein estimation and robust mean estimation, allowing guarantees for the latter to transfer to the former.

On computation, they show that higher dimension can improve the numerical-integration convergence of a Monte Carlo estimator for average-sliced distance. For max-sliced distance, they establish an O(epsilon^-4) complexity bound for a commonly used subgradient local-optimization method. Numerical experiments validate the theory. These results clarify several distinct meanings of scalability without treating higher dimension as uniformly beneficial.
summary.tldr: The paper quantifies sliced Wasserstein scalability through convergence rates, dimension-free robustness results, and guarantees for numerical computation.

title: Statistical, Robustness, and Computational Guarantees for Sliced Wasserstein Distances

abstract: Foundational Models (FMs) have demonstrated unprecedented capabilities including zero-shot learning, high fidelity data synthesis, and out of domain generalization. However, the parameter capacity of FMs is still limited, leading to poor out-of-the-box performance of FMs on many expert tasks (e.g. retrieval of car manuals technical illustrations from language queries), data for which is either unseen or belonging to a long-tail part of the data distribution of the huge datasets used for FM pre-training. This underlines the necessity to explicitly evaluate and finetune FMs on such expert tasks, arguably ones that appear the most in practical real-world applications. In this paper, we propose a first of its kind FETA benchmark built around the task of teaching FMs to understand technical documentation, via learning to match their graphical illustrations to corresponding language descriptions. Our FETA benchmark focuses on text-to-image and image-to-text retrieval in public car manuals and sales catalogue brochures. FETA is equipped with a procedure for completely automatic annotation extraction (code would be released upon acceptance), allowing easy extension of FETA to more documentation types and application domains in the future. Our automatic annotation leads to an automated performance metric shown to be consistent with metrics computed on human-curated annotations (also released). We provide multiple baselines and analysis of popular FMs on FETA leading to several interesting findings that we believe would be very valuable to the FM community, paving the way towards real-world application of FMs for many practical expert tasks currently being `overlooked' by standard benchmarks focusing on common objects.

The contribution is an evaluation setting centered on technical documentation, together with a scalable way to construct its annotations. This makes specialized matching tasks available for explicit evaluation and fine-tuning, broadening attention beyond the common objects emphasized by standard benchmarks and toward the visual-language relationships encountered in expert documents.
summary.tldr: FETA benchmarks foundation models on matching technical illustrations and text, using automatically extracted annotations from automotive documents.

title: FETA: Towards Specializing Foundational Models for Expert Task Applications

abstract: The Santa Claus problem is a fundamental problem in {\em fair division}: the goal is to partition a set of {\em heterogeneous} items among {\em heterogeneous} agents so as to maximize the minimum value of items received by any agent. In this paper, we study the online version of this problem where the items are not known in advance and have to be assigned to agents as they arrive over time. If the arrival order of items is arbitrary, then no good assignment rule exists in the worst case. However, we show that, if the arrival order is random, then for $n$ agents and any $\varepsilon > 0$, we can obtain a competitive ratio of $1-\varepsilon$ when the optimal assignment gives value at least $\Omega(\log n / \varepsilon^2)$ to every agent (assuming each item has at most unit value). We also show that this result is almost tight: namely, if the optimal solution has value at most $C \ln n / \varepsilon$ for some constant $C$, then there is no $(1-\varepsilon)$-competitive algorithm even for random arrival order.

paragraphs: The Santa Claus problem allocates items among agents to maximize the value received by the least well-served agent. Both the items and the agents' valuations can differ. This paper studies the online version, in which each item must be assigned when it arrives, before the remaining items are known.

An arbitrary arrival order prevents a good worst-case guarantee. With a random arrival order, however, the authors obtain a competitive ratio of 1 minus epsilon under a size condition on the optimal allocation. Assuming each item has value at most one, every agent's value in that optimal allocation must be at least on the order of log(n) divided by epsilon squared.

The paper also proves a lower bound: when the optimal minimum value is at most C times ln(n) divided by epsilon for a constant C, no algorithm can achieve that competitive ratio, even with random ordering. The bounds are described as almost tight. Together, they show that random arrival helps, but near-optimal online fairness still depends on sufficiently large attainable value per agent.
summary.tldr: Random item order enables nearly optimal online fair allocation when every agent's optimal value is sufficiently large, with an almost matching impossibility bound.

title: Online Algorithms for the Santa Claus Problem

abstract: We present BYOL-Explore, a conceptually simple yet general approach for curiosity-driven exploration in visually complex environments. BYOL-Explore learns the world representation, the world dynamics and the exploration policy all-together by optimizing a single prediction loss in the latent space with no additional auxiliary objective. We show that BYOL-Explore is effective in DM-HARD-8, a challenging partially-observable continuous-action hard-exploration benchmark with visually rich 3-D environment. On this benchmark, we solve the majority of the tasks purely through augmenting the extrinsic reward with BYOL-Explore intrinsic reward, whereas prior work could only get off the ground with human demonstrations. As further evidence of the generality of BYOL-Explore, we show that it achieves superhuman performance on the ten hardest exploration games in Atari while having a much simpler design than other competitive agents.

paragraphs: BYOL-Explore addresses exploration in environments where visual observations are complex and useful progress can be difficult to discover. It uses curiosity-driven learning to help an agent seek experience, rather than depending only on rewards supplied by the task. The paper's central design choice is to connect representation learning, prediction of world dynamics, and exploration through one prediction loss.

That loss operates in a latent space, meaning the model predicts within a learned representation of its observations. The world representation, dynamics model, and exploration policy are learned together without an additional auxiliary objective. The resulting intrinsic reward is combined with the environment's extrinsic reward to guide behavior.

On DM-HARD-8, a visually rich benchmark with partial observability and continuous actions, this combination solves most tasks; the prior work described required human demonstrations to make progress. The method also achieves superhuman performance on the ten hardest Atari exploration games. These results provide evidence for the approach across two different settings while retaining a comparatively simple design.
summary.tldr: BYOL-Explore uses a single latent prediction loss to learn representations, dynamics, and curiosity-driven exploration with strong results on difficult exploration benchmarks.

title: BYOL-Explore: Exploration by Bootstrapped Prediction

abstract: Molecular Representation Learning (MRL) has emerged as a powerful tool for drug and materials discovery in a variety of tasks such as virtual screening and inverse design. While there has been a surge of interest in advancing model-centric techniques, the influence of both data quantity and quality on molecular representations is not yet clearly understood within this field. In this paper, we delve into the neural scaling behaviors of MRL from a data-centric viewpoint, examining four key dimensions: (1) data modalities, (2) dataset splitting, (3) the role of pre-training, and (4) model capacity.Our empirical studies confirm a consistent power-law relationship between data volume and MRL performance across these dimensions. Additionally, through detailed analysis, we identify potential avenues for improving learning efficiency.To challenge these scaling laws, we adapt seven popular data pruning strategies to molecular data and benchmark their performance. Our findings underline the importance of data-centric MRL and highlight possible directions for future research.

This paper examines how those representations improve as the available data change. Its emphasis is on data quantity and quality, complementing work centered on model design. The authors investigate scaling behavior to understand the relationship between the training data and measured learning performance.

The empirical study considers four dimensions: data modalities, dataset splitting, pretraining, and model capacity. Across those dimensions, the authors observe a consistent power-law relationship between data volume and performance. This is an empirical regularity in the studied settings, offering a way to characterize how performance changes with scale rather than establishing an unconditional rule for every molecular-learning problem.

The paper also analyzes potential ways to improve learning efficiency. To probe the scaling relationships, it adapts seven popular data-pruning strategies to molecular data and benchmarks them. Together, the scaling study and pruning evaluation position data selection and data organization as important research questions, alongside the choice of architecture, for improving molecular representation learning.
summary.tldr: An empirical study finds consistent power-law data scaling in molecular representation learning and benchmarks seven data-pruning strategies.

title: Uncovering Neural Scaling Laws in Molecular Representation Learning

abstract: This paper provides statistical sample complexity bounds for score-matching and its applications in causal discovery. We demonstrate that accurate estimation of the score function is achievable by training a standard deep ReLU neural network using stochastic gradient descent. We establish bounds on the error rate of recovering causal relationships using the score-matching-based causal discovery method of Rolland et al. [2022], assuming a sufficiently good estimation of the score function. Finally, we analyze the upper bound of score-matching estimation within the score-based generative modeling, which has been applied for causal discovery but is also of independent interest within the domain of generative models.

The contribution supplies theoretical bounds for an estimation procedure that also plays a role in generative modeling.

They then analyze a score-matching-based causal discovery method and bound its errors in recovering causal relationships. Together, the results connect neural score estimation to downstream statistical guarantees, with causal-recovery conclusions expressly conditioned on the quality of the score estimate.
summary.tldr: The paper bounds neural score-estimation accuracy and its implications for causal discovery and score-based generative modeling.

title: Sample Complexity Bounds for Score-Matching: Causal Discovery and Generative Modeling

abstract: A major challenge in monocular 3D object detection is the limited diversity and quantity of objects in real datasets. While augmenting real scenes with virtual objects holds promise to improve both the diversity and quantity of the objects, it remains elusive due to the lack of an effective 3D object insertion method in complex real captured scenes. In this work, we study augmenting complex real indoor scenes with virtual objects for monocular 3D object detection. The main challenge is to automatically identify plausible physical properties for virtual assets (e.g., locations, appearances, sizes, etc.) in cluttered real scenes. To address this challenge, we propose a physically plausible indoor 3D object insertion approach to automatically copy virtual objects and paste them into real scenes. The resulting objects in scenes have 3D bounding boxes with plausible physical locations and appearances. In particular, our method first identifies physically feasible locations and poses for the inserted objects to prevent collisions with the existing room layout. Subsequently, it estimates spatially-varying illumination for the insertion location, enabling the immersive blending of the virtual objects into the original scene with plausible appearances and cast shadows. We show that our augmentation method significantly improves existing monocular 3D object models and achieves state-of-the-art performance. For the first time, we demonstrate that a physically plausible 3D object insertion, serving as a generative data augmentation technique, can lead to significant improvements for discriminative downstream tasks such as monocular 3D object detection. Project website: https://gyhandy.github.io/3D-Copy-Paste/.

paragraphs: Detecting three-dimensional objects from a single image requires training examples with varied objects and reliable spatial labels. This paper increases that variety by inserting virtual objects into photographs of real indoor scenes. Its central concern is making the additions physically plausible within cluttered rooms, so the augmented images provide useful training examples.

The method first finds feasible positions and orientations for each inserted object, avoiding collisions with the existing room layout. It then estimates illumination at the chosen location. Accounting for lighting that varies across space helps the rendered object match its surroundings, including its appearance and cast shadows. The inserted objects also come with three-dimensional bounding boxes.

The authors report significant improvements to existing monocular 3D detection models and state-of-the-art performance using this augmentation. The finding connects the quality of generated training content to a downstream recognition task: plausible placement and rendering can make synthetic additions useful for learning from real scenes. The demonstrated application concerns complex indoor scenes and detection from individual images.
summary.tldr: Physically plausible virtual objects inserted into real indoor scenes improve training for monocular 3D object detection.

title: 3D Copy-Paste: Physically Plausible Object Insertion for Monocular 3D Detection

abstract: Prompting is the primary way to utilize the multitask capabilities of language models (LMs), but prompts occupy valuable space in the input context window, and repeatedly encoding the same prompt is computationally inefficient. Finetuning and distillation methods allow for specialization of LMs without prompting, but require retraining the model for each task. To avoid this trade-off entirely, we present gisting, which trains an LM to compress prompts into smaller sets of "gist" tokens which can be cached and reused for compute efficiency. Gist models can be trained with no additional cost over standard instruction finetuning by simply modifying Transformer attention masks to encourage prompt compression. On decoder (LLaMA-7B) and encoder-decoder (FLAN-T5-XXL) LMs, gisting enables up to 26x compression of prompts, resulting in up to 40% FLOPs reductions, 4.2% wall time speedups, and storage savings, all with minimal loss in output quality.

paragraphs: Prompts let a language model perform many tasks, but long instructions consume context space and cost computation each time they are encoded. Specializing a model through training can remove repeated prompting, yet typically requires separate retraining for each task. This paper introduces gisting as a way to retain reusable prompt information in a much smaller representation.

A gist model learns to compress a prompt into a small set of gist tokens that can be cached and reused. Training changes the Transformer's attention masks to encourage information to pass through this compressed representation. The authors state that this can be incorporated without additional cost beyond standard instruction finetuning, making compression part of the existing training process.

Experiments use both a decoder model, LLaMA-7B, and an encoder-decoder model, FLAN-T5-XXL. Reported results include up to 26-fold prompt compression, up to 40% fewer floating-point operations, 4.2% wall-time speedups, and storage savings with minimal output-quality loss. The difference between arithmetic savings and elapsed-time savings also shows why the two efficiency measures should be interpreted separately.
summary.tldr: Gisting trains language models to cache compressed prompt tokens, reducing computation and storage with minimal reported quality loss.

title: Learning to Compress Prompts with Gist Tokens

abstract: Studying conditional independence among many variables with few observations is a challenging task.Gaussian Graphical Models (GGMs) tackle this problem by encouraging sparsity in the precision matrix through $l_q$ regularization with $q\leq1$.However, most GMMs rely on the $l_1$ norm because the objective is highly non-convex for sub-$l_1$ pseudo-norms.In the frequentist formulation, the $l_1$ norm relaxation provides the solution path as a function of the shrinkage parameter $\lambda$.In the Bayesian formulation, sparsity is instead encouraged through a Laplace prior, but posterior inference for different $\lambda$ requires repeated runs of expensive Gibbs samplers.Here we propose a general framework for variational inference with matrix-variate Normalizing Flow in GGMs, which unifies the benefits of frequentist and Bayesian frameworks.As a key improvement on previous work, we train with one flow a continuum of sparse regression models jointly for all regularization parameters $\lambda$ and all $l_q$ norms, including non-convex sub-$l_1$ pseudo-norms.Within one model we thus have access to (i) the evolution of the posterior for any $\lambda$ and any $l_q$ (pseudo-) norm, (ii) the marginal log-likelihood for model selection, and (iii) the frequentist solution paths through simulated annealing in the MAP limit.

paragraphs: Gaussian graphical models study conditional independence among variables, a difficult task when observations are scarce. They encourage sparse precision matrices through regularization. The commonly used l1 penalty is easier to handle than sub-l1 alternatives, whose objectives are highly nonconvex. Bayesian approaches also face expensive repeated inference when the regularization strength changes.

The paper proposes variational inference using a matrix-valued normalizing flow. A single flow is trained jointly across a continuum of regularization strengths and lq penalties, including the nonconvex sub-l1 cases. This makes the regularization choices part of one conditional model instead of requiring a separate inference procedure for every choice.

The resulting framework provides access to how the posterior changes with the penalty and its strength, as well as marginal log-likelihoods for model selection. Through simulated annealing toward the maximum-a-posteriori limit, it also yields frequentist solution paths. The contribution connects uncertainty-aware Bayesian inference with the ability to trace regularized solutions, bringing both capabilities into one model.
summary.tldr: A conditional matrix flow models Gaussian graphical model posteriors across regularization strengths and penalties within one trained system.

title: Conditional Matrix Flows for Gaussian Graphical Models

abstract: While contextual bandit has a mature theory, effectively leveraging different feedback patterns to enhance the pace of learning remains unclear. Bandits with feedback graphs, which interpolates between the full information and bandit regimes, provides a promising framework to mitigate the statistical complexity of learning. In this paper, we propose and analyze an approach to contextual bandits with feedback graphs based upon reduction to regression. The resulting algorithms are computationally practical and achieve established minimax rates, thereby reducing the statistical complexity in real-world applications.

paragraphs: A contextual bandit chooses an action using information about the current situation and learns from the resulting feedback. The information revealed by a choice can vary: it may concern only that action or provide information about others as well. This paper studies how to use such feedback patterns to make learning more statistically efficient.

Feedback graphs describe the available information and cover settings between ordinary bandit feedback and full information. The authors propose an approach that reduces contextual-bandit learning with these graphs to regression. This reduction gives the decision problem a computational form built around predictive estimation, while retaining an explicit role for which feedback is available.

The paper analyzes the resulting algorithms and shows that they achieve established minimax rates, meaning their worst-case statistical performance matches the relevant known rates. It also describes the algorithms as computationally practical. The contribution connects these two requirements: using richer feedback to reduce the statistical difficulty of learning, while supplying a regression-based approach intended to make those benefits usable in applications.
summary.tldr: A regression-based approach makes contextual bandits with feedback graphs computationally practical while achieving established minimax rates.

title: Practical Contextual Bandits with Feedback Graphs

abstract: In many unpaired image domain translation problems, e.g., style transfer or super-resolution, it is important to keep the translated image similar to its respective input image. We propose the extremal transport (ET) which is a mathematical formalization of the theoretically best possible unpaired translation between a pair of domains w.r.t. the given similarity function. Inspired by the recent advances in neural optimal transport (OT), we propose a scalable algorithm to approximate ET maps as a limit of partial OT maps. We test our algorithm on toy examples and on the unpaired image-to-image translation task. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/milenagazdieva/ExtremalNeuralOptimalTransport

paragraphs: Unpaired image translation learns a relationship between two image domains without matched input-output examples. In tasks such as style transfer and super-resolution, the translated result should also remain similar to its particular input. This paper studies how to formalize the best possible translation with respect to a chosen measure of similarity.

The authors introduce extremal transport, a mathematical formulation of that objective. Its notion of optimality is explicitly tied to the supplied similarity function. This matters because preserving similarity is part of the translation problem itself: the formulation provides a precise target for how input and output should remain related across domains.

To make the formulation computationally usable, the paper proposes a scalable algorithm inspired by neural optimal transport. It approximates extremal transport maps through a limit of partial optimal transport maps. The authors test the algorithm on toy examples and unpaired image-to-image translation. The contribution connects a theoretically defined similarity objective with a neural approximation procedure; the abstract reports these evaluations without claiming a particular performance margin.
summary.tldr: Extremal transport formalizes similarity-preserving unpaired translation and is approximated with a scalable neural optimal transport algorithm.

title: Extremal Domain Translation with Neural Optimal Transport

abstract: Many approaches in machine learning rely on a weighted graph to encode thesimilarities between samples in a dataset. Entropic affinities (EAs), which are notably used in the popular Dimensionality Reduction (DR) algorithm t-SNE, are particular instances of such graphs. To ensure robustness to heterogeneous sampling densities, EAs assign a kernel bandwidth parameter to every sample in such a way that the entropy of each row in the affinity matrix is kept constant at a specific value, whose exponential is known as perplexity. EAs are inherently asymmetric and row-wise stochastic, but they are used in DR approaches after undergoing heuristic symmetrization methods that violate both the row-wise constant entropy and stochasticity properties. In this work, we uncover a novel characterization of EA as an optimal transport problem, allowing a natural symmetrization that can be computed efficiently using dual ascent. The corresponding novel affinity matrix derives advantages from symmetric doubly stochastic normalization in terms of clustering performance, while also effectively controlling the entropy of each row thus making it particularly robust to varying noise levels. Following, we present a new DR algorithm, SNEkhorn, that leverages this new affinity matrix. We show its clear superiority to state-of-the-art approaches with several indicators on both synthetic and real-world datasets.
