paragraphs: Many dimensionality-reduction methods start with a weighted graph describing similarities between samples. Entropic affinities adapt each sample's neighborhood scale to control row entropy, helping accommodate uneven sampling density. However, these affinities are asymmetric, and heuristic symmetrization can disrupt both their entropy control and row normalization.

This paper characterizes entropic affinities as an optimal transport problem. That formulation enables a natural symmetric construction computed through dual ascent. The resulting affinity matrix combines symmetric, doubly stochastic normalization with effective control over each row's entropy. These properties bring clustering advantages and robustness to varying noise levels, addressing weaknesses introduced by conventional symmetrization.

The authors build SNEkhorn, a dimensionality-reduction algorithm using the new affinity matrix. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report clear superiority over the compared state-of-the-art approaches across several indicators. The contribution links the construction of sample similarities to the quality of the resulting reduced representation, showing how a more principled normalization can improve the evaluated outcomes.
summary.tldr: SNEkhorn uses optimal transport to construct symmetric, entropy-controlled similarities that improve dimensionality reduction in the reported evaluations.

title: SNEkhorn: Dimension Reduction with Symmetric Entropic Affinities

abstract: In disentangled representation learning, a model is asked to tease apart a dataset's underlying sources of variation and represent them independently of one another. Since the model is provided with no ground truth information about these sources, inductive biases take a paramount role in enabling disentanglement. In this work, we construct an inductive bias towards encoding to and decoding from an organized latent space. Concretely, we do this by (i) quantizing the latent space into discrete code vectors with a separate learnable scalar codebook per dimension and (ii) applying strong model regularization via an unusually high weight decay. Intuitively, the latent space design forces the encoder to combinatorially construct codes from a small number of distinct scalar values, which in turn enables the decoder to assign a consistent meaning to each value. Regularization then serves to drive the model towards this parsimonious strategy. We demonstrate the broad applicability of this approach by adding it to both basic data-reconstructing (vanilla autoencoder) and latent-reconstructing (InfoGAN) generative models. For reliable evaluation, we also propose InfoMEC, a new set of metrics for disentanglement that is cohesively grounded in information theory and fixes well-established shortcomings in previous metrics. Together with regularization, latent quantization dramatically improves the modularity and explicitness of learned representations on a representative suite of benchmark datasets. In particular, our quantized-latent autoencoder (QLAE) consistently outperforms strong methods from prior work in these key disentanglement properties without compromising data reconstruction.

paragraphs: Disentangled representations aim to encode different sources of variation separately, even when training data does not identify those sources. This paper builds that preference into the latent space itself. Each dimension has its own learned collection of discrete scalar values, so an encoder constructs a representation by combining choices from these small codebooks.

The intended benefit is consistent meaning: reusing a limited set of values gives the decoder an opportunity to interpret each value consistently. Unusually strong weight decay encourages the model to adopt this economical strategy. The authors apply the combination to both a standard autoencoder, which reconstructs data, and InfoGAN, which reconstructs latent information.

The paper also introduces InfoMEC, information-theoretic evaluation metrics designed to address established problems in earlier disentanglement measures. Across representative benchmarks, quantization together with regularization substantially improves modularity and explicitness, properties concerning separation and accessibility of represented factors. The quantized-latent autoencoder consistently surpasses strong prior methods on these properties while preserving reconstruction quality in the reported evaluations.
summary.tldr: Discrete per-dimension latent codebooks and strong regularization improve disentanglement without sacrificing reconstruction in the reported autoencoder evaluations.

title: Disentanglement via Latent Quantization

abstract: Learning from visual observation (LfVO), aiming at recovering policies from only visual observation data, is promising yet a challenging problem. Existing LfVO approaches either only adopt inefficient online learning schemes or require additional task-specific information like goal states, making them not suited for open-ended tasks. To address these issues, we propose a two-stage framework for learning from visual observation. In the first stage, we introduce and pretrain State-to-Go (STG) Transformer offline to predict and differentiate latent transitions of demonstrations. Subsequently, in the second stage, the STG Transformer provides intrinsic rewards for downstream reinforcement learning tasks where an agent learns merely from intrinsic rewards. Empirical results on Atari and Minecraft show that our proposed method outperforms baselines and in some tasks even achieves performance comparable to the policy learned from environmental rewards. These results shed light on the potential of utilizing video-only data to solve difficult visual reinforcement learning tasks rather than relying on complete offline datasets containing states, actions, and rewards. The project’s website and code can befound at https://sites.google.com/view/stgtransformer.

paragraphs: Learning a policy from visual demonstrations is appealing because the demonstrations need not include recorded actions or rewards. The challenge is turning what an agent sees into a useful learning signal. The paper addresses approaches that rely on inefficient online learning or additional task-specific information such as goal states, which can make them unsuitable for open-ended tasks.

Its two-stage framework first pretrains a State-to-Go Transformer offline. The transformer learns to predict and distinguish transitions in the latent representations of demonstrations. In the second stage, it supplies intrinsic rewards for a reinforcement learning agent. The downstream agent learns solely from those intrinsic rewards, connecting visual demonstration structure to action learning.

Experiments on Atari and Minecraft show better performance than the evaluated baselines. On some tasks, performance is comparable to policies trained with environmental rewards. These findings suggest that video-only demonstrations can support difficult visual control tasks without requiring complete offline records of states, actions, and rewards. The comparable-performance result applies to some tasks rather than the entire evaluation.
summary.tldr: An offline-pretrained State-to-Go Transformer turns visual demonstrations into intrinsic rewards that support downstream reinforcement learning.

title: Learning from Visual Observation via Offline Pretrained State-to-Go Transformer

abstract: Vision-language models, such as contrastive language-image pre-training (CLIP), have demonstrated impressive results in natural image domains. However, these models often struggle when applied to specialized domains like remote sensing, and adapting to such domains is challenging due to the limited number of image-text pairs available for training. To address this, we propose S-CLIP, a semi-supervised learning method for training CLIP that utilizes additional unpaired images. S-CLIP employs two pseudo-labeling strategies specifically designed for contrastive learning and the language modality. The caption-level pseudo-label is given by a combination of captions of paired images, obtained by solving an optimal transport problem between unpaired and paired images. The keyword-level pseudo-label is given by a keyword in the caption of the nearest paired image, trained through partial label learning that assumes a candidate set of labels for supervision instead of the exact one. By combining these objectives, S-CLIP significantly enhances the training of CLIP using only a few image-text pairs, as demonstrated in various specialist domains, including remote sensing, fashion, scientific figures, and comics. For instance, S-CLIP improves CLIP by 10% for zero-shot classification and 4% for image-text retrieval on the remote sensing benchmark, matching the performance of supervised CLIP while using three times fewer image-text pairs.

paragraphs: CLIP can struggle when moved from natural images into specialist domains where paired images and captions are scarce. S-CLIP adapts the model using a small paired collection together with additional images that have no captions. Its central contribution is to turn those unpaired images into useful training examples through two complementary forms of pseudo-labeling.

At the caption level, an optimal transport problem connects unpaired and paired images, producing supervision from combinations of existing captions. At the keyword level, supervision comes from keywords in the caption of the nearest paired image. Partial-label learning handles this second signal through candidate labels, rather than requiring one exact label to be known.

Combining the two objectives improves training across remote sensing, fashion, scientific figures, and comics. On the remote-sensing benchmark, the authors report a 10% improvement in zero-shot classification and a 4% improvement in image-text retrieval over CLIP. S-CLIP also matches supervised CLIP there with three times fewer image-text pairs, demonstrating the value of exploiting images that lack specialist captions.
summary.tldr: S-CLIP uses caption- and keyword-level pseudo-labels to adapt CLIP to specialist domains with few paired captions and additional unpaired images.

title: S-CLIP: Semi-supervised Vision-Language Learning using Few Specialist Captions

abstract: In this paper, we systematically evaluate the robustness of multi-exit language models against adversarial slowdown. To audit their robustness, we design a slowdown attack that generates natural adversarial text bypassing early-exit points. We use the resulting WAFFLE attack as a vehicle to conduct a comprehensive evaluation of three multi-exit mechanisms with the GLUE benchmark against adversarial slowdown. We then show our attack significantly reduces the computational savings provided by the three methods in both white-box and black-box settings. The more complex a mechanism is, the more vulnerable it is to adversarial slowdown. We also perform a linguistic analysis of the perturbed text inputs, identifying common perturbation patterns that our attack generates, and comparing them with standard adversarial text attacks. Moreover, we show that adversarial training is ineffective in defeating our slowdown attack, but input sanitization with a conversational model, e.g., ChatGPT, can remove perturbations effectively. This result suggests that future work is needed for developing efficient yet robust multi-exit models. Our code is available at: https://github.com/ztcoalson/WAFFLE

paragraphs: Multi-exit language models save computation by allowing processing to stop before every layer has run. This paper studies whether deliberately modified text can undermine those savings. Its focus is adversarial slowdown: making inputs bypass early exits so that the model must perform more computation.

The authors develop WAFFLE, an attack that produces natural adversarial text, and use it to evaluate three exit mechanisms on GLUE. Across both white-box and black-box settings, the attack substantially reduces their computational savings. Among the mechanisms studied, greater complexity is associated with greater vulnerability. The paper also analyzes recurring linguistic perturbations and compares them with patterns from standard adversarial text attacks.

The defense experiments find that adversarial training does not defeat WAFFLE, while sanitizing inputs with a conversational model can effectively remove its perturbations. These results identify a weakness in the tested efficiency mechanisms and a possible direction for defense. They also motivate evaluating whether early-exit savings survive deliberately difficult inputs.
summary.tldr: WAFFLE generates text that bypasses early exits and substantially erodes the computational savings of three tested language-model exit mechanisms.

title: BERT Lost Patience Won't Be Robust to Adversarial Slowdown

abstract: Human Motion Prediction (HMP) aims to predict future poses at different moments according to past motion sequences. Previous approaches have treated the prediction of various moments equally, resulting in two main limitations: the learning of short-term predictions is hindered by the focus on long-term predictions, and the incorporation of prior information from past predictions into subsequent predictions is limited. In this paper, we introduce a novel multi-stage training framework called Temporal Continual Learning (TCL) to address the above challenges. To better preserve prior information, we introduce the Prior Compensation Factor (PCF). We incorporate it into the model training to compensate for the lost prior information. Furthermore, we derive a more reasonable optimization objective through theoretical derivation. It is important to note that our TCL framework can be easily integrated with different HMP backbone models and adapted to various datasets and applications. Extensive experiments on four HMP benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and flexibility of TCL. The code is available at https://github.com/hyqlat/TCL.

paragraphs: Human motion prediction uses past movement to forecast poses at future moments. The paper identifies two problems with treating all prediction times equally: attention to longer-term forecasts can hinder learning shorter-term forecasts, and information from earlier predictions is not fully carried into subsequent ones. Both problems concern how learning is organized across time.

Temporal Continual Learning, or TCL, addresses these issues through a multi-stage training framework. The authors introduce a Prior Compensation Factor to compensate during training for prior information that would otherwise be lost. They also theoretically derive a revised optimization objective, connecting the training strategy to an explicit treatment of information preservation.

The framework can be integrated with different motion-prediction backbones and adapted across datasets and applications. Experiments on four human-motion prediction benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness and flexibility. The contribution is therefore a training framework that can accompany different prediction models. It highlights the value of organizing learning across forecast times and compensating for lost prior information when building later predictions.
summary.tldr: TCL uses multi-stage training and prior compensation to improve human motion prediction across different forecast times and model backbones.

title: Temporal Continual Learning with Prior Compensation for Human Motion Prediction

abstract: Normal estimation for 3D point clouds is a fundamental task in 3D geometry processing. The state-of-the-art methods rely on priors of fitting local surfaces learned from normal supervision. However, normal supervision in benchmarks comes from synthetic shapes and is usually not available from real scans, thereby limiting the learned priors of these methods. In addition, normal orientation consistency across shapes remains difficult to achieve without a separate post-processing procedure. To resolve these issues, we propose a novel method for estimating oriented normals directly from point clouds without using ground truth normals as supervision. We achieve this by introducing a new paradigm for learning neural gradient functions, which encourages the neural network to fit the input point clouds and yield unit-norm gradients at the points. Specifically, we introduce loss functions to facilitate query points to iteratively reach the moving targets and aggregate onto the approximated surface, thereby learning a global surface representation of the data. Meanwhile, we incorporate gradients into the surface approximation to measure the minimum signed deviation of queries, resulting in a consistent gradient field associated with the surface. These techniques lead to our deep unsupervised oriented normal estimator that is robust to noise, outliers and density variations. Our excellent results on widely used benchmarks demonstrate that our method can learn more accurate normals for both unoriented and oriented normal estimation tasks than the latest methods. The source code and pre-trained model are publicly available.

paragraphs: Estimating surface normals from a 3D point cloud means recovering directions associated with the underlying surface. Existing learned methods often depend on normal labels from synthetic shapes, while real scans usually lack those labels. Making the normal directions consistently oriented also presents a challenge.

NeuralGF learns oriented normals directly from point clouds without ground-truth normal supervision. It trains a neural function to fit the cloud while producing unit-length gradients at its points. Its losses guide query points toward an approximated surface, building a global surface representation. Incorporating gradients into signed surface-deviation measurements helps produce a consistent gradient field from which normals can be estimated.

The reported estimator is robust to noise, outliers, and variations in point density. On widely used benchmarks, it produces more accurate results than the latest compared methods for both oriented and unoriented normal estimation. The approach connects surface reconstruction and normal estimation within one learned representation, reducing dependence on supervised normal labels and a separate orientation-fixing stage.
summary.tldr: NeuralGF learns a global surface and consistent gradient field to estimate accurate oriented point-cloud normals without normal supervision.

title: NeuralGF: Unsupervised Point Normal Estimation by Learning Neural Gradient Function

abstract: Task planning in language agents is emerging as an important research topic alongside the development of large language models (LLMs). It aims to break down complex user requests in natural language into solvable sub-tasks, thereby fulfilling the original requests. In this context, the sub-tasks can be naturally viewed as a graph, where the nodes represent the sub-tasks, and the edges denote the dependencies among them. Consequently, task planning is a decision-making problem that involves selecting a connected path or subgraph within the corresponding graph and invoking it. In this paper, we explore graph learning-based methods for task planning, a direction that is orthogonal to the prevalent focus on prompt design. Our interest in graph learning stems from a theoretical discovery: the biases of attention and auto-regressive loss impede LLMs' ability to effectively navigate decision-making on graphs, which is adeptly addressed by graph neural networks (GNNs). This theoretical insight led us to integrate GNNs with LLMs to enhance overall performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that GNN-based methods surpass existing solutions even without training, and minimal training can further enhance their performance. The performance gain increases with a larger task graph size.

paragraphs: A language agent must often turn a complex request into smaller tasks whose order depends on one another. This paper represents that structure as a graph: nodes are subtasks, and edges describe dependencies. Planning then becomes the problem of selecting and executing a connected path or subgraph that fulfills the request.

The authors investigate whether graph learning can improve this process. Their theoretical analysis identifies biases in attention and the autoregressive training loss that hinder LLM decision-making on graphs. This motivates combining an LLM with a graph neural network, whose handling of graph structure addresses the identified difficulties. The proposed direction changes how the planning structure is processed, alongside the separate question of how prompts are written.

In the reported experiments, GNN-based methods outperform existing solutions even without training, and a small amount of training improves them further. Their advantage grows as the task graph becomes larger. The findings suggest that explicitly processing dependencies can be particularly useful when an agent must navigate more extensive collections of interdependent subtasks.
summary.tldr: Combining graph neural networks with LLMs improves task planning in experiments, with larger gains on larger task graphs.

title: Can Graph Learning Improve Planning in LLM-based Agents?

abstract: We provide a technique for OLO that obtains regret $G\|w_\star\|\sqrt{T\log(\|w_\star\|G\sqrt{T})} + \|w_\star\|^2 + G^2$ on $G$-Lipschitz losses for any comparison point $w_\star$ without knowing either $G$ or $\|w_\star\|$. Importantly, this matches the optimal bound $G\|w_\star\|\sqrt{T}$ available with such knowledge (up to logarithmic factors), unless either $\|w_\star\|$ or $G$ is so large that even $G\|w_\star\|\sqrt{T}$ is roughly linear in $T$. Thus, at a high level it matches the optimal bound in all cases in which one can achieve sublinear regret.

Importantly, this matches the optimal bound $G\|w_\star\|\sqrt{T}$ available with such knowledge (up to logarithmic factors), unless either $\|w_\star\|$ or $G$ is so large that even $G\|w_\star\|\sqrt{T}$ is roughly linear in $T$. paragraphs: Online linear optimization evaluates a sequence of decisions through regret: the accumulated loss relative to a fixed comparison point. Strong guarantees often depend on knowing the scale of the losses and the size of that comparison point. This paper provides a technique that does not require either quantity in advance.

For G-Lipschitz losses and any comparison point w*, the bound contains a leading term proportional to G times the norm of w* times the square root of T, with an additional logarithmic factor. It also includes additive terms equal to the squared norm of w* and G squared. Those extra terms matter when assessing how closely the result matches a method with prior scale knowledge.

The authors show that the bound matches the known-scale optimum up to logarithmic factors unless one of the unknown scales is so large that the optimum is already roughly linear in T. At a high level, the technique therefore retains the optimal behavior in the regimes where sublinear regret is achievable.
summary.tldr: An online optimization technique adapts to unknown loss and comparator scales while matching optimal regret up to logarithmic factors in the stated sublinear regimes.

title: Fully Unconstrained Online Learning

abstract: We consider the problem of online fair division of indivisible goods to players when there are a finite number of types of goods and player values are drawn from distributions with unknown means. Our goal is to maximize social welfare subject to allocating the goods fairly in expectation. When a player's value for an item is unknown at the time of allocation, we show that this problem reduces to a variant of (stochastic) multi-armed bandits, where there exists an arm for each player's value for each type of good. At each time step, we choose a distribution over arms which determines how the next item is allocated. We consider two sets of fairness constraints for this problem: envy-freeness in expectation and proportionality in expectation. Our main result is the design of an explore-then-commit algorithm that achieves $\tilde{O}(T^{2/3})$ regret while maintaining either fairness constraint. This result relies on unique properties fundamental to fair-division constraints that allow faster rates of learning, despite the restricted action space.

paragraphs: This paper studies allocating indivisible goods over time when the allocator does not know how much each player values an arriving item. There are finitely many types of goods, and players' values follow distributions with unknown means. The objective is to maximize total welfare while preserving fairness in expectation.

The authors translate the problem into a stochastic bandit setting, with an arm for each player and type of good. At each step, a probability distribution over arms determines allocation. They consider two fairness requirements: envy-freeness in expectation and proportionality in expectation. These requirements concern expected allocations and values, rather than guaranteeing fairness for every individual realized item.

Their explore-then-commit algorithm first gathers information and then uses what it has learned for subsequent allocations. It achieves regret of order T to the two-thirds power, up to logarithmic factors, while maintaining either fairness constraint. The proof exploits particular properties of fair-division constraints, showing how meaningful learning guarantees remain possible despite restrictions on the available allocation decisions.
summary.tldr: An explore-then-commit algorithm learns valuable allocations while maintaining envy-freeness or proportionality in expectation.

title: Honor Among Bandits: No-Regret Learning for Online Fair Division

abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become the dominant solution for learning on graphs, the typical non-Euclidean structures. Conventional GNNs, constructed with the Artificial Neuron Network (ANN), have achieved impressive performance at the cost of high computation and energy consumption. In parallel, spiking GNNs with brain-like spiking neurons are drawing increasing research attention owing to the energy efficiency. So far, existing spiking GNNs consider graphs in Euclidean space, ignoring the structural geometry, and suffer from the high latency issue due to Back-Propagation-Through-Time (BPTT) with the surrogate gradient. In light of the aforementioned issues, we are devoted to exploring spiking GNN on Riemannian manifolds, and present a Manifold-valued Spiking GNN (MSG). In particular, we design a new spiking neuron on geodesically complete manifolds with the diffeomorphism, so that BPTT regarding the spikes is replaced by the proposed differentiation via manifold. Theoretically, we show that MSG approximates a solver of the manifold ordinary differential equation. Extensive experiments on common graphs show the proposed MSG achieves superior performance to previous spiking GNNs and energy efficiency to conventional GNNs.

paragraphs: Spiking graph neural networks offer an energy-efficient alternative to conventional graph models, but existing versions represent graphs in Euclidean space and can suffer high latency from backpropagation through time. This paper introduces a Manifold-valued Spiking GNN to incorporate structural geometry while changing how gradients through spikes are computed.

The authors design a spiking neuron on geodesically complete Riemannian manifolds using a diffeomorphism, a smooth invertible transformation. Their proposed differentiation through the manifold replaces backpropagation through time for the spikes. They also establish a theoretical interpretation: the resulting model approximates a solver for an ordinary differential equation defined on the manifold.

Experiments on common graphs show superior performance over previous spiking graph networks and better energy efficiency than conventional graph networks. These are distinct comparisons: the reported predictive advantage concerns earlier spiking models, while the energy advantage concerns conventional ones. The contribution brings geometry, spiking computation, and an alternative differentiation mechanism together, with theory connecting the architecture to continuous dynamics and experiments supporting its practical promise.
summary.tldr: MSG brings spiking graph networks onto Riemannian manifolds, replacing spike backpropagation through time and improving reported performance and energy efficiency.

title: Spiking Graph Neural Network on Riemannian Manifolds

abstract: The omnipresence of NP-hard combinatorial optimization problems (COPs) compels domain experts to engage in trial-and-error heuristic design. The long-standing endeavor of design automation has gained new momentum with the rise of large language models (LLMs). This paper introduces Language Hyper-Heuristics (LHHs), an emerging variant of Hyper-Heuristics that leverages LLMs for heuristic generation, featuring minimal manual intervention and open-ended heuristic spaces. To empower LHHs, we present Reflective Evolution (ReEvo), a novel integration of evolutionary search for efficiently exploring the heuristic space, and LLM reflections to provide verbal gradients within the space. Across five heterogeneous algorithmic types, six different COPs, and both white-box and black-box views of COPs, ReEvo yields state-of-the-art and competitive meta-heuristics, evolutionary algorithms, heuristics, and neural solvers, while being more sample-efficient than prior LHHs.

paragraphs: Designing heuristics for difficult combinatorial optimization problems often involves substantial expert trial and error. This paper introduces Language Hyper-Heuristics, which use large language models to generate heuristics with little manual intervention. Their search space is open-ended, allowing generated solutions to extend beyond a narrowly predefined collection of heuristic choices.

The proposed ReEvo method combines evolutionary search with language-model reflection. Evolution provides a way to explore candidate heuristics, while reflections offer verbal guidance about how that search might improve. The authors describe this guidance as verbal gradients: language feedback that helps direct exploration through the heuristic space.

Evaluation spans five algorithmic types and six combinatorial optimization problems, with both white-box and black-box views of the problems. ReEvo produces state-of-the-art or competitive methods across metaheuristics, evolutionary algorithms, heuristics, and neural solvers, while using samples more efficiently than earlier Language Hyper-Heuristics. The results support combining candidate search with reflective feedback as a broadly useful approach to automated algorithm design across the tested problem and algorithm families.
summary.tldr: ReEvo combines evolutionary search with language-model reflections to generate competitive optimization heuristics more sample-efficiently.

title: ReEvo: Large Language Models as Hyper-Heuristics with Reflective Evolution

abstract: Sparse training stands as a landmark approach in addressing the considerable training resource demands imposed by the continuously expanding size of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). However, the training of a sparse DNN encounters great challenges in achieving optimal generalization ability despite the efforts from the state-of-the-art sparse training methodologies. To unravel the mysterious reason behind the difficulty of sparse training, we connect the network sparsity with neural loss functions structure, and identify the cause of such difficulty lies in chaotic loss surface. In light of such revelation, we propose $S^{2} - SAM$, characterized by a **S**ingle-step **S**harpness_**A**ware **M**inimization that is tailored for **S**parse training. For the first time, $S^{2} - SAM$ innovates the traditional SAM-style optimization by approximating sharpness perturbation through prior gradient information, incurring *zero extra cost*. Therefore, $S^{2} - SAM$ not only exhibits the capacity to improve generalization but also aligns with the efficiency goal of sparse training. Additionally, we study the generalization result of $S^{2} - SAM$ and provide theoretical proof for convergence. Through extensive experiments, $S^{2} - SAM$ demonstrates its universally applicable plug-and-play functionality, enhancing accuracy across various sparse training methods. Code available at https://github.com/jjsrf/SSAM-NEURIPS2024.

For the first time, $S^{2} - SAM$ innovates the traditional SAM-style optimization by approximating sharpness perturbation through prior gradient information, incurring *zero extra cost*. Therefore, $S^{2} - SAM$ not only exhibits the capacity to improve generalization but also aligns with the efficiency goal of sparse training. Additionally, we study the generalization result of $S^{2} - SAM$ and provide theoretical proof for convergence. Through extensive experiments, $S^{2} - SAM$ demonstrates its universally applicable plug-and-play functionality, enhancing accuracy across various sparse training methods. Code available at https://github.com/jjsrf/SSAM-NEURIPS2024.

paragraphs: Sparse training aims to reduce the resources needed to train large neural networks, but retaining good performance on unseen data remains difficult. This paper connects that difficulty to the structure of the training loss. The authors identify a chaotic loss surface associated with network sparsity, motivating an optimization method designed specifically for sparse networks.

Their method, S²-SAM, adapts sharpness-aware minimization into a single-step procedure. Its central move is to approximate the sharpness perturbation using gradient information already available from earlier updates. The authors report that this approximation adds no extra cost, allowing the method to pursue better generalization while preserving the efficiency motivation behind sparse training.

The paper studies generalization and provides a convergence proof, alongside experiments across several sparse training methods. Those experiments show accuracy improvements when S²-SAM is added to the tested methods. The contribution is therefore both an explanation of why sparse optimization can be difficult and a broadly applicable optimization modification supported by theoretical analysis and empirical results.
summary.tldr: S²-SAM reuses prior gradients to improve sparse training with a single-step sharpness-aware update that the authors report adds no extra cost.

title: A Single-Step, Sharpness-Aware Minimization is All You Need to Achieve Efficient and Accurate Sparse Training

abstract: While training models and labeling data are resource-intensive, a wealth of pre-trained models and unlabeled data exists. To effectively utilize these resources, we present an approach to actively select pre-trained models while minimizing labeling costs. We frame this as an online contextual active model selection problem: At each round, the learner receives an unlabeled data point as a context. The objective is to adaptively select the best model to make a prediction while limiting label requests. To tackle this problem, we propose CAMS, a contextual active model selection algorithm that relies on two novel components: (1) a contextual model selection mechanism, which leverages context information to make informed decisions about which model is likely to perform best for a given context, and (2)an active query component, which strategically chooses when to request labels for data points, minimizing the overall labeling cost. We provide rigorous theoretical analysis for the regret and query complexity under both adversarial and stochastic settings. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our algorithm on a diverse collection of benchmark classification tasks. Notably, CAMS requires substantially less labeling effort (less than 10%) compared to existing methods on CIFAR10 and DRIFT benchmarks, while achieving similar or better accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to use available pretrained models without spending heavily on labels. Data arrives one example at a time, and the learner must decide which model should predict that example. Because different models may suit different inputs, the choice depends on the example’s context. The learner must also decide when obtaining the true label is worth the labeling cost.

CAMS combines these two decisions. Its contextual selection component estimates which model is likely to work best for the current input, while its active querying component strategically requests labels. Labels therefore serve as selectively acquired feedback for future choices, rather than a requirement for every incoming example.

The authors analyze both regret and the number of label queries under adversarial and stochastic settings. Benchmark classification experiments support the approach’s practical value. On CIFAR10 and DRIFT, CAMS uses less than 10% of the labeling effort of existing methods while delivering similar or better accuracy. These findings show substantial labeling savings in those evaluations without a corresponding loss in predictive performance.
summary.tldr: CAMS selects pretrained models for individual inputs and requests labels selectively, substantially reducing labeling effort in the reported benchmarks.

title: Contextual Active Model Selection

abstract: Graph anomaly detection (GAD), which aims to identify abnormal nodes that differ from the majority within a graph, has garnered significant attention. However, current GAD methods necessitate training specific to each dataset, resulting in high training costs, substantial data requirements, and limited generalizability when being applied to new datasets and domains. To address these limitations, this paper proposes ARC, a generalist GAD approach that enables a ``one-for-all'' GAD model to detect anomalies across various graph datasets on-the-fly. Equipped with in-context learning, ARC can directly extract dataset-specific patterns from the target dataset using few-shot normal samples at the inference stage, without the need for retraining or fine-tuning on the target dataset. ARC comprises three components that are well-crafted for capturing universal graph anomaly patterns: 1) smoothness-based feature **A**lignment module that unifies the features of different datasets into a common and anomaly-sensitive space; 2) ego-neighbor **R**esidual graph encoder that learns abnormality-related node embeddings; and 3) cross-attentive in-**C**ontext anomaly scoring module that predicts node abnormality by leveraging few-shot normal samples. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets from various domains demonstrate the superior anomaly detection performance, efficiency, and generalizability of ARC.

paragraphs: Detecting unusual nodes in a graph usually requires training a model for that particular dataset. ARC investigates a more reusable approach: a single detector that can work across graph datasets. At prediction time, it uses a few examples of normal nodes to understand the target dataset, without retraining or fine-tuning its parameters.

The architecture separates this task into three parts. A feature-alignment module puts different datasets into a shared representation that remains sensitive to anomalies. A graph encoder then produces node representations using differences between a node and its neighbors. Finally, a cross-attention module compares the resulting information with the supplied normal examples to assign anomaly scores.

The normal examples provide context about what counts as ordinary in the new graph. This allows dataset-specific information to influence predictions without a new training run. Experiments across benchmarks from several domains report advantages in detection performance, efficiency, and generalization, supporting ARC as an approach to reusable graph anomaly detection.
summary.tldr: ARC uses a few normal examples to detect graph anomalies across datasets without target-specific retraining.

title: ARC: A Generalist Graph Anomaly Detector with In-Context Learning

abstract: Cinematographers adeptly capture the essence of the world, crafting compelling visual narratives through intricate camera movements. Witnessing the strides made by large language models in perceiving and interacting with the 3D world, this study explores their capability to control cameras with human language guidance. We introduce ChatCam, a system that navigates camera movements through conversations with users, mimicking a professional cinematographer's workflow. To achieve this, we propose CineGPT, a GPT-based autoregressive model for text-conditioned camera trajectory generation. We also develop an Anchor Determinator to ensure precise camera trajectory placement. ChatCam understands user requests and employs our proposed tools to generate trajectories, which can be used to render high-quality video footage on radiance field representations. Our experiments, including comparisons to state-of-the-art approaches and user studies, demonstrate our approach's ability to interpret and execute complex instructions for camera operation, showing promising applications in real-world production settings. Project page: https://xinhangliu.com/chatcam.

paragraphs: Camera movement is part of how cinematographers communicate a visual story, but translating a verbal request into a precise movement requires more than understanding the words. ChatCam explores an interface in which users discuss the desired shot and the system produces the corresponding camera trajectory within a represented scene.

The system combines conversational interpretation with specialized tools. CineGPT, an autoregressive model conditioned on text, generates camera trajectories. An additional component called the Anchor Determinator places those trajectories precisely. This separates the movement being requested from its placement, allowing the system to address both aspects of camera control.

The resulting trajectories can be used to render video from radiance field representations. Comparisons with state-of-the-art approaches and user studies support the system's ability to interpret and carry out complex camera instructions. The findings suggest potential for production workflows where creative intent is expressed through conversation. The demonstrated contribution is a connection between language, trajectory generation, and scene placement, with real-world production presented as a promising application.
summary.tldr: ChatCam turns conversational camera instructions into trajectories that can be placed in scenes and used to render video.

title: ChatCam: Empowering Camera Control through Conversational AI

abstract: Federated learning (FL) is a machine learning paradigm that allows multiple FL participants (FL-PTs) to collaborate on training models without sharing private data. Due to data heterogeneity, negative transfer may occur in the FL training process. This necessitates FL-PT selection based on their data complementarity. In cross-silo FL, organizations that engage in business activities are key sources of FL-PTs. The resulting FL ecosystem has two features: (i) self-interest, and (ii) competition among FL-PTs. This requires the desirable FL-PT selection strategy to simultaneously mitigate the problems of free riders and conflicts of interest among competitors. To this end, we propose an optimal FL collaboration formation strategy -FedEgoists- which ensures that: (1) a FL-PT can benefit from FL if and only if it benefits the FL ecosystem, and (2) a FL-PT will not contribute to its competitors or their supporters. It provides an efficient clustering solution to group FL-PTs into coalitions, ensuring that within each coalition, FL-PTs share the same interest. We theoretically prove that the FL-PT coalitions formed are optimal since no coalitions can collaborate together to improve the utility of any of their members. Extensive experiments on widely adopted benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of FedEgoists compared to nine state-of-the-art baseline methods, and its ability to establish efficient collaborative networks in cross-silos FL with FL-PTs that engage in business activities.

paragraphs: Organizations collaborating through federated learning may have different data, competing business interests, and incentives to benefit without contributing. Data differences can also cause negative transfer, where collaboration harms learning. This paper treats the choice of collaborators as a problem involving both data complementarity and participants' interests.

FedEgoists groups participants into coalitions with shared interests. Its formation strategy enforces two conditions: a participant benefits from federated learning if and only if it benefits the ecosystem, and it does not contribute to competitors or their supporters. These conditions address free riding and indirect support for competitors alongside the learning benefits of collaboration.

The authors prove optimality in a specific sense: no formed coalitions can collaborate together to improve the utility of any of their members. Experiments on established benchmark datasets compare the strategy with nine state-of-the-art methods and support its effectiveness. The contribution is a way to organize collaborative networks that accounts for organizational incentives as well as the usefulness of shared training.
summary.tldr: FedEgoists forms federated-learning coalitions that address free riding and competitive conflicts, with a specific coalition-optimality guarantee.

title: Free-Rider and Conflict Aware Collaboration Formation for Cross-Silo Federated Learning

abstract: Text-to-image models have shown surprising performance in high-quality image generation, while also raising intensified concerns about the unauthorized usage of personal dataset in training and personalized fine-tuning. Recent approaches, embedding watermarks, introducing perturbations, and inserting backdoors into datasets, rely on adding minor information vulnerable to adversarial training, limiting their ability to detect unauthorized data usage. In this paper, we introduce a novel implicit Zero-Watermarking scheme that first utilizes the disentangled style domain to detect unauthorized dataset usage in text-to-image models. Specifically, our approach generates the watermark from the disentangled style domain, enabling self-generalization and mutual exclusivity within the style domain anchored by protected units. The domain achieves the maximum concealed offset of probability distribution through both the injection of identifier $z$ and dynamic contrastive learning, facilitating the structured delineation of dataset copyright boundaries for multiple sources of styles and contents. Additionally, we introduce the concept of watermark distribution to establish a verification mechanism for copyright ownership of hybrid or partial infringements, addressing deficiencies in the traditional mechanism of dataset copyright ownership for AI mimicry. Notably, our method achieves one-sample verification for copyright ownership in AI mimic generations. The code is available at: [https://github.com/Hlufies/ZWatermarking](https://github.com/Hlufies/ZWatermarking)

paragraphs: The paper addresses detecting unauthorized use of personal image datasets in text-to-image training and personalized fine-tuning. Existing protection approaches add small signals through watermarks, perturbations, or backdoors. The authors identify vulnerability to adversarial training as a weakness of these signals and propose an implicit zero-watermarking scheme based on a disentangled representation of style.

The method derives its watermark from a style domain organized around protected units. It aims to make the watermark generalize within that domain while keeping protected style domains mutually exclusive. Injecting an identifier, z, and applying dynamic contrastive learning create a concealed shift in the probability distribution. This provides a way to delineate protected contributions across multiple sources of style and content.

The authors also introduce a watermark-distribution-based verification mechanism for cases involving mixed sources or only partial use of protected material. They report that ownership verification can be performed from one AI-generated mimic sample. The contribution therefore combines a style-based protection mechanism with a verification approach intended to handle more complicated reuse than a single intact dataset.
summary.tldr: An implicit watermark built in a disentangled style domain supports detecting protected dataset use, including reported verification from a single mimic generation.

title: Disentangled Style Domain for Implicit $z$-Watermark Towards Copyright Protection

abstract: Object tracking is a fundamental task in computer vision, requiring the localization of objects of interest across video frames. Diffusion models have shown remarkable capabilities in visual generation, making them well-suited for addressing several requirements of the tracking problem. This work proposes a novel diffusion-based methodology to formulate the tracking task. Firstly, their conditional process allows for injecting indications of the target object into the generation process. Secondly, diffusion mechanics can be developed to inherently model temporal correspondences, enabling the reconstruction of actual frames in video. However, existing diffusion models rely on extensive and unnecessary mapping to a Gaussian noise domain, which can be replaced by a more efficient and stable interpolation process. Our proposed interpolation mechanism draws inspiration from classic image-processing techniques, offering a more interpretable, stable, and faster approach tailored specifically for the object tracking task. By leveraging the strengths of diffusion models while circumventing their limitations, our Diffusion-based INterpolation TrackeR (DINTR) presents a promising new paradigm and achieves a superior multiplicity on seven benchmarks across five indicator representations.

paragraphs: Object tracking means following a specified target across successive video frames. This paper develops a diffusion-based formulation because diffusion models offer two useful capabilities: conditioning generation on information identifying the target, and modeling correspondences over time to reconstruct actual video frames. Together, these capabilities connect target identity with the way visual content changes.

The authors argue that conventional diffusion's extensive mapping into Gaussian noise is unnecessary for this tracking task. DINTR replaces that part of the process with an interpolation mechanism inspired by classical image processing. The approach retains the useful conditioning and temporal modeling aspects of diffusion while changing the route used to connect visual information.

The paper describes this interpolation process as more interpretable, stable, and faster for tracking. It evaluates DINTR on seven benchmarks using five representations of the indication specifying the target, reporting favorable performance across that range. The breadth of these evaluations supports the method's promise as a flexible tracking formulation. The main idea is to adapt diffusion mechanics to the structure of tracking instead of relying on a noise-based process designed around visual generation.
summary.tldr: DINTR adapts diffusion to object tracking through an interpolation process intended to improve speed, stability, and interpretability.

title: DINTR: Tracking via Diffusion-based Interpolation

abstract: Intracortical brain-computer interfaces (iBCIs) can restore movement and communication abilities to individuals with paralysis by decoding their intended behavior from neural activity recorded with an implanted device. While this activity yields high-performance decoding over short timescales, neural data is often nonstationary, which can lead to decoder failure if not accounted for. To maintain performance, users must frequently recalibrate decoders, which requires the arduous collection of new neural and behavioral data. Aiming to reduce this burden, several approaches have been developed that either limit recalibration data requirements (few-shot approaches) or eliminate explicit recalibration entirely (zero-shot approaches). However, progress is limited by a lack of standardized datasets and comparison metrics, causing methods to be compared in an ad hoc manner. Here we introduce the FALCON benchmark suite (Few-shot Algorithms for COnsistent Neural decoding) to standardize evaluation of iBCI robustness. FALCON curates five datasets of neural and behavioral data that span movement and communication tasks to focus on behaviors of interest to modern-day iBCIs. Each dataset includes calibration data, optional few-shot recalibration data, and private evaluation data. We implement a flexible evaluation platform which only requires user-submitted code to return behavioral predictions on unseen data. We also seed the benchmark by applying baseline methods spanning several classes of possible approaches. FALCON aims to provide rigorous selection criteria for robust iBCI decoders, easing their translation to real-world devices. https://snel-repo.github.io/falcon/

paragraphs: Implanted brain-computer interfaces decode intended behavior from neural recordings, potentially restoring movement and communication abilities. Neural signals can change over time, causing a previously effective decoder to fail. Recalibrating requires collecting new neural and behavioral data, creating a burden for users. Methods that need little or no explicit recalibration aim to reduce that burden.

FALCON provides a common benchmark for comparing these approaches. It brings together five datasets covering movement and communication behaviors relevant to intracortical interfaces. Each dataset includes initial calibration data, optional data for few-shot recalibration, and private evaluation data. This structure allows robustness to be assessed on unseen recordings while supporting approaches with different recalibration requirements.

The evaluation platform asks submitted code to return behavioral predictions, and the authors supply baseline methods from several approach families. The contribution is standardized evaluation infrastructure rather than a claim that decoder drift has been solved. By making comparisons more consistent, FALCON aims to provide stronger selection criteria for robust decoders and support their eventual translation into real-world devices.
summary.tldr: FALCON standardizes evaluation of neural decoders that aim to remain reliable as brain recordings change while requiring little or no recalibration.

title: Few-shot Algorithms for Consistent Neural Decoding (FALCON) Benchmark

abstract: Causal Temporal Representation Learning (Ctrl) methods aim to identify the temporal causal dynamics of complex nonstationary temporal sequences. Despite the success of existing Ctrl methods, they require either directly observing the domain variables or assuming a Markov prior on them. Such requirements limit the application of these methods in real-world scenarios when we do not have such prior knowledge of the domain variables. To address this problem, this work adopts a sparse transition assumption, aligned with intuitive human understanding, and presents identifiability results from a theoretical perspective. In particular, we explore under what conditions on the significance of the variability of the transitions we can build a model to identify the distribution shifts. Based on the theoretical result, we introduce a novel framework, *Causal Temporal Representation Learning with Nonstationary Sparse Transition* (CtrlNS), designed to leverage the constraints on transition sparsity and conditional independence to reliably identify both distribution shifts and latent factors. Our experimental evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets demonstrate significant improvements over existing baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to recover hidden causal factors and changing dynamics from temporal sequences whose statistical behavior varies over time. Existing approaches require either observing the variables that describe the domain or placing a Markov assumption on those variables. Such requirements become restrictive when the relevant domain information is unavailable.

The authors instead adopt a sparse transition assumption and investigate when changes in the transitions contain enough information to identify distribution shifts. Their theoretical contribution gives identifiability results under conditions on the significance of that variability. The guarantee therefore depends on the structure and informativeness of the transitions, rather than simply on having a sequence of observations.

Building on this analysis, the paper introduces CtrlNS, a framework that combines transition sparsity with conditional independence constraints to identify distribution changes and latent factors. Experiments using synthetic and real-world datasets report substantial improvements over existing baselines. The work offers a different set of assumptions for learning temporal causal representations, with theoretical conditions explaining when that alternative can support identification.
summary.tldr: CtrlNS uses sparse transitions and conditional independence to identify changing distributions and hidden temporal factors under stated identifiability conditions.

title: Causal Temporal Representation Learning with Nonstationary Sparse Transition

abstract: Facial parts swapping aims to selectively transfer regions of interest from the source image onto the target image while maintaining the rest of the target image unchanged.Most studies on face swapping designed specifically for full-face swapping, are either unable or significantly limited when it comes to swapping individual facial parts, which hinders fine-grained and customized character designs.However, designing such an approach specifically for facial parts swapping is challenged by a reasonable multiple reference feature fusion, which needs to be both efficient and effective.To overcome this challenge, FuseAnyPart is proposed to facilitate the seamless "fuse-any-part" customization of the face.In FuseAnyPart, facial parts from different people are assembled into a complete face in latent space within the Mask-based Fusion Module.Subsequently, the consolidated feature is dispatched to the Addition-based Injection Module forfusion within the UNet of the diffusion model to create novel characters.Extensive experiments qualitatively and quantitatively validate the superiority and robustness of FuseAnyPart.Source codes are available at https://github.com/Thomas-wyh/FuseAnyPart.

paragraphs: Facial-part swapping aims to transfer selected regions from reference faces while preserving the rest of a target image. Methods built for whole-face replacement often offer limited control over individual parts. FuseAnyPart addresses this finer-grained task, allowing facial regions from multiple people to contribute to a customized character.

Its central challenge is combining several references efficiently and coherently. A Mask-based Fusion Module assembles the selected facial parts into a complete face representation in latent space, where the model works with encoded features. An Addition-based Injection Module then introduces this combined representation into the diffusion model's UNet, allowing the generation process to use the assembled facial information.

The authors report qualitative and quantitative experiments supporting the method's superiority and robustness. The design matters because it gives the model an explicit stage for assembling reference parts before injecting them into generation. This provides a mechanism for the selective, multi-reference customization that whole-face swapping approaches handle poorly.
summary.tldr: FuseAnyPart assembles facial regions from multiple references in latent space and injects them into a diffusion model for selective customization.

title: FuseAnyPart: Diffusion-Driven Facial Parts Swapping via Multiple Reference Images

abstract: Existing human rendering methods require every part of the human to be fully visible throughout the input video. However, this assumption does not hold in real-life settings where obstructions are common, resulting in only partial visibility of the human. Considering this, we present OccFusion, an approach that utilizes efficient 3D Gaussian splatting supervised by pretrained 2D diffusion models for efficient and high-fidelity human rendering. We propose a pipeline consisting of three stages. In the Initialization stage, complete human masks are generated from partial visibility masks. In the Optimization stage, 3D human Gaussians are optimized with additional supervisions by Score-Distillation Sampling (SDS) to create a complete geometry of the human. Finally, in the Refinement stage, in-context inpainting is designed to further improve rendering quality on the less observed human body parts. We evaluate OccFusion on ZJU-MoCap and challenging OcMotion sequences and found that it achieves state-of-the-art performance in the rendering of occluded humans.
originalAbstract: Existing human rendering methods require every part of the human to be fully visible throughout the input video. We propose a pipeline consisting of three stages. In the Initialization stage, complete human masks are generated from partial visibility masks. In the Optimization stage, 3D human Gaussians are optimized with additional supervisions by Score-Distillation Sampling (SDS) to create a complete geometry of the human. Finally, in the Refinement stage, in-context inpainting is designed to further improve rendering quality on the less observed human body parts. We evaluate OccFusion on ZJU-MoCap and challenging OcMotion sequences and found that it achieves state-of-the-art performance in the rendering of occluded humans.

paragraphs: OccFusion tackles human rendering from videos in which obstructions hide parts of the body. The paper identifies full visibility as a restrictive assumption in existing approaches, because real scenes often provide only partial observations. Its method combines a 3D Gaussian representation with guidance from pretrained 2D diffusion models to complete and render the person.

Optimization then adjusts the 3D human Gaussians, using additional guidance from Score-Distillation Sampling to build complete geometry. Refinement applies in-context inpainting to improve the appearance of body regions that have been observed less.

Each stage addresses a different part of incomplete observation: the person's extent, their geometry, and the visual quality of less-seen regions. Evaluations on ZJU-MoCap and challenging OcMotion sequences show state-of-the-art results for rendering occluded people. The findings support combining efficient 3D Gaussian splatting with generative guidance when the input video cannot directly supply a complete view of the body.
summary.tldr: OccFusion combines 3D Gaussian splatting and diffusion guidance to reconstruct and render people despite partial visibility.

title: OccFusion: Rendering Occluded Humans with Generative Diffusion Priors

abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) encode the state of the world, including the status of entities and their relations, as described by a text? While existing work directly probes for a complete state of the world, our research explores whether and how LLMs abstract this world state in their internal representations. We propose a new framework for probing for world representations through the lens of state abstraction theory from reinforcement learning, which emphasizes different levels of abstraction, distinguishing between general abstractions that facilitate predicting future states and goal-oriented abstractions that guide the subsequent actions to accomplish tasks. To instantiate this framework, we design a text-based planning task, where an LLM acts as an agent in an environment and interacts with objects in containers to achieve a specified goal state. Our experiments reveal that fine-tuning as well as advanced pre-training strengthens LLM-built representations' tendency of maintaining goal-oriented abstractions during decoding, prioritizing task completion over recovery of the world's state and dynamics.

paragraphs: This paper asks how language models internally represent a world described in text, including entities and their relationships. Instead of checking only whether a complete world state can be recovered, it examines whether models retain useful abstractions. Such abstractions may preserve information needed for a task without representing every aspect of the world equally.

The proposed framework draws on state abstraction theory from reinforcement learning. It distinguishes general abstractions that support prediction of future states from goal-oriented abstractions that support actions toward a task's objective. To investigate this distinction, the authors design a text-based planning task in which a language-model agent interacts with objects in containers to reach a specified goal state.

The experiments find that fine-tuning and advanced pretraining strengthen a tendency to maintain goal-oriented abstractions during decoding. Representations increasingly favor task completion over recovery of the world's full state and dynamics. This finding changes how probing results can be interpreted: the relevant question includes what an internal representation supports, alongside how completely it describes the environment.
summary.tldr: A state-abstraction probing framework finds that fine-tuning and advanced pretraining strengthen goal-oriented world representations in a text-based planning task.

title: Do LLMs Build World Representations? Probing Through the Lens of State Abstraction

abstract: We introduce Buffer of Thoughts (BoT), a novel and versatile thought-augmented reasoning approach for enhancing accuracy, efficiency and robustness of large language models (LLMs). Specifically, we propose meta-buffer to store a series of informative high-level thoughts, namely thought-template, distilled from the problem-solving processes across various tasks. Then for each problem, we retrieve a relevant thought-template and adaptively instantiate it with specific reasoning structures to conduct efficient reasoning. To guarantee the scalability and stability, we further propose buffer-manager to dynamically update the meta-buffer, thus enhancing the capacity of meta-buffer as more tasks are solved. We conduct extensive experiments on 10 challenging reasoning-intensive tasks, and achieve significant performance improvements over previous SOTA methods: 11\% on Game of 24, 20\% on Geometric Shapes and 51\% on Checkmate-in-One. Further analysis demonstrate the superior generalization ability and model robustness of our BoT, while requiring only 12\% of the cost of multi-query prompting methods (e.g., tree/graph of thoughts) on average. Code is available at: https://github.com/YangLing0818/buffer-of-thought-llm

paragraphs: Buffer of Thoughts aims to improve language-model reasoning by retaining useful patterns from earlier problem solving. Its central resource is a collection of high-level thought templates distilled across different tasks. These templates describe reusable approaches that can be adapted to the specific structure of a new problem.

For each problem, the method retrieves a relevant template and instantiates it with an appropriate reasoning structure. A separate buffer manager updates the collection as more tasks are solved. This combines reuse at the level of general strategy with adaptation at the level of the current task, while allowing the stored collection to develop over time.

Across ten reasoning-intensive tasks, the authors report improvements over previous leading methods, including 11% on Game of 24, 20% on Geometric Shapes, and 51% on Checkmate-in-One. Additional analysis supports stronger generalization and robustness. Average cost is reported as 12% of that of multi-query prompting approaches such as tree or graph of thoughts. The findings suggest that reusable reasoning structure can improve both performance and efficiency in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Buffer of Thoughts reuses and updates reasoning templates, improving tested reasoning performance at a fraction of the average cost of multi-query prompting.

title: Buffer of Thoughts: Thought-Augmented Reasoning with Large Language Models

abstract: We introduce a lightweight, real-time motion recognition system that enables synergic human-machine performance through wearable IMU sensor data, MiniRocket time-series classification, and responsive multimedia control. By mapping dancer-specific movement to sound through somatic memory and association, we propose an alternative approach to human-machine collaboration, one that preserves the expressive depth of the performing body while leveraging machine learning for attentive observation and responsiveness. We demonstrate that this human-centered design reliably supports high accuracy classification (<50 ms latency), offering a replicable framework to integrate dance-literate machines into creative, educational, and live performance contexts.

paragraphs: Human-Machine Ritual presents a motion-recognition system for performance in which a machine responds to a dancer’s movements. It combines wearable inertial sensors, a time-series classifier called MiniRocket, and multimedia control. The goal is a responsive creative relationship that preserves the expressive role of the performer’s body.

Movement-to-sound mappings are specific to the dancer and draw on bodily memory and association. This makes recognition part of an individual expressive practice: the system observes movement patterns and connects them to responsive sound. The technical components support this relationship by translating a stream of sensor measurements into recognized movements that can drive multimedia responses.

The authors report high classification accuracy with latency below fifty milliseconds. They present the lightweight design as a replicable framework for creative, educational, and live performance settings. The contribution brings together responsive recognition and a human-centered mapping process, showing how machine learning can support attentive interaction with a performer while keeping embodied expression central to the experience.
summary.tldr: Wearable sensors and fast movement classification enable dancer-specific sound responses for collaborative human–machine performance.

title: Human-Machine Ritual: Synergic Performance through Real-Time Motion Recognition

abstract: In recent years, the alignment between artificial neural network (ANN) embeddings and blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) responses in functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) via neural encoding models has significantly advanced research on neural representation mechanisms and interpretability in the brain. However, these approaches remain limited in characterizing the brain’s inherently nonlinear response properties. To address this, we propose the Jacobian-based Nonlinearity Evaluation (JNE), an interpretability metric for nonlinear neural encoding models. JNE quantifies nonlinearity by statistically measuring the dispersion of local linear mappings (Jacobians) from model representations to predicted BOLD responses, thereby approximating the nonlinearity of BOLD signals. Centered on proposing JNE as a novel interpretability metric, we validated its effectiveness through controlled simulation experiments on various activation functions and network architectures, and further verified it on real fMRI data, demonstrating a hierarchical progression of nonlinear characteristics from primary to higher-order visual cortices, consistent with established cortical organization. We further extended JNE with Sample-Specificity (JNE-SS), revealing stimulus-selective nonlinear response patterns in functionally specialized brain regions. As the first interpretability metric for quantifying nonlinear responses, JNE provides new insights into brain information processing. Code available at https://github.com/Gaitxh/JNE.

paragraphs: Neural encoding models connect artificial neural network representations to fMRI blood-oxygenation responses. This paper asks how to characterize the nonlinear behavior captured by those models. The authors introduce Jacobian-based Nonlinearity Evaluation, or JNE, to quantify how the mapping from model representations to predicted brain responses changes across inputs.

A Jacobian describes a model’s local linear response to small changes in its input. JNE statistically measures how dispersed these local mappings are. Variation among them provides an approximation of nonlinearity in the BOLD responses through the fitted encoding model. The authors validate the metric with controlled simulations covering different activation functions and network architectures.

On real fMRI data, JNE reveals a progression of nonlinear characteristics from primary to higher-order visual cortex, consistent with established cortical organization. A sample-specific extension, JNE-SS, identifies stimulus-selective nonlinear patterns in specialized regions. Together, these results offer a way to examine both regional differences and stimulus-dependent behavior, using changes in local model mappings to make nonlinear encoding more interpretable.
summary.tldr: JNE measures variation in local model mappings to characterize nonlinear brain-response patterns in neural encoding models.

title: Jacobian-Based Interpretation of Nonlinear Neural Encoding Model

abstract: We introduce a method based on Conformal Prediction (CP) to quantify the uncertainty of full ranking algorithms. We focus on a specific scenario where $n+m$ items are to be ranked by some ``black box'' algorithm. It is assumed that the relative (ground truth) ranking of $n$ of them is known. The objective is then to quantify the error made by the algorithm on the ranks of the $m$ new items among the total $(n+m)$. In such a setting, the true ranks of the $n$ original items in the total $(n+m)$ depend on the (unknown) true ranks of the $m$ new ones. Consequently, we have no direct access to a calibration set to apply a classical CP method. To address this challenge, we propose to construct distribution-free bounds of the unknown conformity scores using recent results on the distribution of conformal p-values. Using these scores upper bounds, we provide valid prediction sets for the rank of any item. We also control the false coverage proportion, a crucial quantity when dealing with multiple prediction sets. Finally, we empirically show on both synthetic and real data the efficiency of our CP method for state-of-the-art ranking algorithms such as RankNet or LambdaMart.

paragraphs: This paper quantifies uncertainty when a ranking algorithm orders a combined collection of known and new items. The true relative ordering of n original items is available, but the positions of m new items are unknown. The goal is to provide uncertainty sets for ranks within the full collection of n+m items.

The difficulty is that adding new items also changes the original items' absolute ranks. Their known relative ordering therefore does not directly provide the calibration information needed by ordinary conformal prediction. The authors address this by constructing distribution-free bounds on unknown conformity scores, drawing on results about the distribution of conformal p-values.

Upper bounds on those scores yield valid prediction sets for individual ranks. The method also controls the false coverage proportion, addressing errors across multiple prediction sets rather than only one at a time. Experiments on synthetic and real data demonstrate efficiency with ranking algorithms including RankNet and LambdaMart. The result adds uncertainty information around a black-box ranking without requiring its full ground-truth ordering.
summary.tldr: The method constructs conformal uncertainty sets for full rankings when only the relative ordering of a subset of items is known.

title: Transductive Conformal Inference for Full Ranking

abstract: We study weight-only post-training quantization (PTQ), which quantizes the weights of a large language model (LLM) without retraining, using little or no calibration data. Weight-only PTQ is crucial for reducing the memory footprint and latency of LLM inference, especially in memory-bound, small-batch inference scenarios, such as personalized inference on edge devices. Despite its importance, irregular weight distributions with heavy-tailed outliers in LLMs complicate quantization, recently motivating rotation-based methods that transform weights into near-Gaussian distributions, which are more regular with fewer outliers, thereby reducing quantization error. In this work, we first derive the information-theoretically optimal bit allocation for Gaussianized weights under given bit budgets, revealing that fine-grained fractional-bit quantizers approaching the Gaussian distortion-rate bound are essential to achieve near-optimal quantization performance. To bridge this theoretical insight and practical implementation, we introduce Q-Palette, a versatile collection of fractional-bit quantizers that range from trellis-coded quantizers offering near-optimal distortion to simpler vector and scalar quantizers optimized for faster inference, all efficiently implemented with optimized CUDA kernels across various bitwidths. Furthermore, leveraging Q-Palette as a foundational component, we propose a novel mixed-scheme quantization framework, jointly optimizing quantizer choices and layer fusion decisions given resource constraints. The code is available at https://github.com/snu-mllab/Q-Palette.

Irregular weight distributions and large outliers make accurate compression difficult. Rotation-based approaches make the weights more nearly Gaussian, and this paper studies how to allocate a limited bit budget under that distributional setting.

The authors derive an information-theoretically optimal allocation for Gaussianized weights. Their analysis identifies fine-grained fractional-bit quantizers approaching the Gaussian distortion-rate bound as essential for near-optimal performance.
