paragraphs: A prediction can be explained partly by examining which training examples most influenced it. This paper brings influence functions from robust statistics into that role, tracing a prediction backward through the learning procedure to the training data. The aim is to identify examples that bear the most responsibility for a particular model output.

To make the method practical for modern models, the authors develop an efficient implementation requiring access to gradients and Hessian-vector products. This connects the explanation to the model's training computations. They also investigate approximations on non-convex and non-differentiable models, where the supporting theory no longer applies, and find that these approximations can still provide useful information.

Experiments with linear models and convolutional neural networks demonstrate several uses: interpreting behavior, debugging models, finding dataset errors, and constructing visually indistinguishable training-set attacks. These applications show that influential examples can reveal both useful training signals and vulnerabilities. The empirical usefulness outside the theory's scope is an explicitly qualified result, rather than a general guarantee that every influence estimate is accurate.
summary.tldr: Influence functions trace predictions to influential training examples, supporting interpretation, debugging, dataset checks, and analysis of training-set attacks.

title: Understanding Black-box Predictions via Influence Functions

abstract: Understanding the representational power of Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) with multiple layers is an ill-understood problem and is an area of active research. Motivated from the approach of Inherent Structure formalism (Stillinger & Weber, 1982), extensively used in analysing Spin Glasses, we propose a novel measure called Inherent Structure Capacity (ISC), which characterizes the representation capacity of a fixed architecture RBM by the expected number of modes of distributions emanating from the RBM with parameters drawn from a prior distribution. Though ISC is intractable, we show that for a single layer RBM architecture ISC approaches a finite constant as number of hidden units are increased and to further improve the ISC, one needs to add a second layer. Furthermore, we introduce Lean RBMs, which are multi-layer RBMs where each layer can have at-most O(n) units with the number of visible units being n. We show that for every single layer RBM with Omega(n^{2+r}), r >= 0, hidden units there exists a two-layered lean RBM with Theta(n^2) parameters with the same ISC, establishing that 2 layer RBMs can achieve the same representational power as single-layer RBMs but using far fewer number of parameters. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first result which quantitatively establishes the need for layering.

summary.tldr: Under Inherent Structure Capacity, lean two-layer RBMs can match much wider single-layer models using substantially fewer parameters.

title: Using Inherent Structures to design Lean 2-layer RBMs

abstract: Ordinal Embedding is the problem of placing n objects into R^d to satisfy constraints like "object a is closer to b than to c." It can accommodate data that embeddings from features or distances cannot, but is a more difficult problem. We propose a novel landmark-based method as a partial solution. At small to medium scales, we present a novel combination of existing methods with some new theoretical justification. For very large values of n optimizing over an entire embedding breaks down, so we propose a novel method which first embeds a subset of m << n objects and then embeds the remaining objects independently and in parallel. We prove a distance error bound for our method in terms of m and that it has O(dn log m) time complexity, and show empirically that it is able to produce high quality embeddings in a fraction of the time needed for any published method.

paragraphs: Ordinal embedding places objects in a geometric space using relative comparisons, such as one object being closer to a second than to a third. This makes it applicable when ordinary feature vectors or numerical distances are unavailable. The difficulty is that jointly optimizing positions for a very large collection of objects becomes impractical.

The paper proposes a landmark-based approach as a partial solution. For small and medium problems, it combines existing methods and supplies new theoretical justification. For very large collections, it first embeds a much smaller subset of objects. It then places the remaining objects independently, allowing those computations to run in parallel.

The authors prove a distance-error bound expressed in terms of the number of landmarks. They also establish time complexity of O(dn log m), where d is the embedding dimension, n the total number of objects, and m the landmark count. Experiments produce high-quality embeddings in a fraction of the time required by previously published methods. The approach makes the smaller initial embedding central to both scalability and the error analysis.
summary.tldr: Embedding a small landmark set first enables parallel placement of remaining objects, with a distance-error bound and efficient scaling.

title: Scaling Up Ordinal Embedding: A Landmark Approach

abstract: Distributed data-parallel algorithms aim to accelerate the training of deep neural networks by parallelizing the computation of large mini-batch gradient updates across multiple nodes. Approaches that synchronize nodes using exact distributed averaging (e.g., via AllReduce) are sensitive to stragglers and communication delays. The PushSum gossip algorithm is robust to these issues, but only performs approximate distributed averaging. This paper studies Stochastic Gradient Push (SGP), which combines PushSum with stochastic gradient updates. We prove that SGP converges to a stationary point of smooth, non-convex objectives at the same sub-linear rate as SGD, and that all nodes achieve consensus. We empirically validate the performance of SGP on image classification (ResNet-50, ImageNet) and machine translation (Transformer, WMT’16 En-De) workloads.

paragraphs: Distributed training spreads gradient computations across several machines to accelerate learning. Methods that synchronize machines through exact averaging, such as AllReduce, are sensitive to slow workers and communication delays. PushSum gossip offers robustness to these issues, but its averaging is approximate, raising the question of whether optimization still converges appropriately.

Stochastic Gradient Push combines PushSum communication with stochastic gradient updates. The paper proves convergence to a stationary point for smooth, nonconvex objectives at the same sublinear rate as stochastic gradient descent. It also proves that the machines reach consensus, so approximate communication does not prevent eventual agreement among their models.

The authors empirically validate SGP on ResNet-50 image classification with ImageNet and Transformer machine translation with WMT’16 English–German data. The theoretical result explains why approximate averaging can be compatible with a familiar optimization rate, while the experiments examine the method on substantial deep-learning workloads. The guarantee is convergence to a stationary point, which is the specific target established for these nonconvex objectives rather than a guarantee of global optimality.
summary.tldr: Stochastic Gradient Push combines gossip averaging with gradient updates, matching SGD’s sublinear stationary-point convergence rate while ensuring agreement across workers.

title: Stochastic Gradient Push for Distributed Deep Learning

abstract: Two types of zeroth-order stochastic algorithms have recently been designed for nonconvex optimization respectively based on the first-order techniques SVRG and SARAH/SPIDER. This paper addresses several important issues that are still open in these methods. First, all existing SVRG-type zeroth-order algorithms suffer from worse function query complexities than either zeroth-order gradient descent (ZO-GD) or stochastic gradient descent (ZO-SGD). In this paper, we propose a new algorithm ZO-SVRG-Coord-Rand and develop a new analysis for an existing ZO-SVRG-Coord algorithm proposed in Liu et al. 2018b, and show that both ZO-SVRG-Coord-Rand and ZO-SVRG-Coord (under our new analysis) outperform other exiting SVRG-type zeroth-order methods as well as ZO-GD and ZO-SGD. Second, the existing SPIDER-type algorithm SPIDER-SZO (Fang et al., 2018) has superior theoretical performance, but suffers from the generation of a large number of Gaussian random variables as well as a $\sqrt{\epsilon}$-level stepsize in practice. In this paper, we develop a new algorithm ZO-SPIDER-Coord, which is free from Gaussian variable generation and allows a large constant stepsize while maintaining the same convergence rate and query complexity, and we further show that ZO-SPIDER-Coord automatically achieves a linear convergence rate as the iterate enters into a local PL region without restart and algorithmic modification.

paragraphs: Zeroth-order optimization uses function evaluations rather than directly supplied gradients. This paper improves variance-reduced methods for nonconvex problems, where reducing noisy update estimates does not automatically reduce the total number of function queries. It addresses both SVRG-based methods with disappointing query bounds and a SPIDER-based method with practical implementation costs.

For the SVRG family, the authors introduce ZO-SVRG-Coord-Rand and give a new analysis of the existing ZO-SVRG-Coord algorithm. Their results show better function-query complexity than earlier SVRG-type zeroth-order methods and zeroth-order gradient descent and stochastic gradient descent. Part of the advance therefore comes from a new algorithm, and part from a stronger understanding of an existing one.

For the SPIDER family, ZO-SPIDER-Coord avoids generating Gaussian random variables and permits a large constant step size while preserving the compared method's convergence rate and query complexity. It also automatically attains linear convergence once iterates enter a local Polyak–Łojasiewicz region. That faster rate depends on entering this region and requires neither restarting nor modifying the algorithm.
summary.tldr: New algorithms and sharper analysis improve zeroth-order query efficiency while enabling constant-step SPIDER updates and conditional local linear convergence.

title: Improved Zeroth-Order Variance Reduced Algorithms and Analysis for Nonconvex Optimization

abstract: We are concerned with obtaining well-calibrated output distributions from regression models. Such distributions allow us to quantify the uncertainty that the model has regarding the predicted target value. We introduce the novel concept of distribution calibration, and demonstrate its advantages over the existing definition of quantile calibration. We further propose a post-hoc approach to improving the predictions from previously trained regression models, using multi-output Gaussian Processes with a novel Beta link function. The proposed method is experimentally verified on a set of common regression models and shows improvements for both distribution-level and quantile-level calibration.

paragraphs: A regression model can predict a distribution over possible target values, giving a description of uncertainty alongside its prediction. For that description to be useful, the distribution must be well calibrated. This paper focuses on improving the reliability of these uncertainty outputs and introduces a concept called distribution calibration.

The authors demonstrate advantages of distribution calibration over an existing notion based on quantiles. This changes the object of evaluation: the goal is to assess calibration at the level of the predicted distribution, while also considering quantile-level behavior. The distinction matters because the paper treats distribution calibration as a separate target for making regression uncertainty more trustworthy.

To improve predictions, the authors propose a post-hoc method built from multi-output Gaussian processes and a new Beta link function. It operates on previously trained regression models, making calibration an additional adjustment to their outputs. Experiments across common regression models show improvements in both distribution-level and quantile-level calibration, supporting the method as a practical way to refine predicted uncertainty.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces distribution calibration and a post-hoc Gaussian-process method that improves regression uncertainty calibration.

title: Distribution calibration for regression

abstract: In this paper we derive new concentration inequalities for the conditional value at risk (CVaR) of a random variable, and compare them to the previous state of the art (Brown, 2007). We show analytically that our lower bound is strictly tighter than Brown’s, and empirically that this difference is significant. While our upper bound may be looser than Brown’s in some cases, we show empirically that in most cases our bound is significantly tighter. After discussing when each upper bound is superior, we conclude with empirical results which suggest that both of our bounds will often be significantly tighter than Brown’s.

While our upper bound may be looser than Brown’s in some cases, we show empirically that in most cases our bound is significantly tighter. After discussing when each upper bound is superior, we conclude with empirical results which suggest that both of our bounds will often be significantly tighter than Brown’s.

paragraphs: This paper develops new concentration inequalities for conditional value at risk, or CVaR. The contribution concerns how tightly this risk quantity can be bounded. The authors compare their lower and upper bounds with an established earlier result, assessing both mathematical improvement and its significance in empirical comparisons.

For the lower bound, the conclusion is especially strong: the authors analytically establish that their bound is strictly tighter than the earlier one. Their empirical results also indicate that the difference is significant. These two pieces of evidence serve different purposes. The analysis establishes the ordering of the bounds, while the experiments show that the improvement can be consequential in the cases examined.

The upper bound has a qualified result. It can be looser in some cases, although empirical comparisons show significantly tighter bounds in most cases studied. The paper discusses when each upper bound is preferable. Its overall empirical conclusion is that both new bounds will often be substantially tighter, without claiming uniform superiority for the upper bound.
summary.tldr: New CVaR concentration bounds include a provably tighter lower bound and an upper bound that is often, but not always, tighter empirically.

title: Concentration Inequalities for Conditional Value at Risk

abstract: Encoder-decoder networks using convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture have been extensively used in deep learning literatures thanks to its excellent performance for various inverse problems in computer vision, medical imaging, etc. However, it is still difficult to obtain coherent geometric view why such an architecture gives the desired performance. Inspired by recent theoretical understanding on generalizability, expressivity and optimization landscape of neural networks, as well as the theory of convolutional framelets, here we provide a unified theoretical framework that leads to a better understanding of geometry of encoder-decoder CNNs. Our unified mathematical framework shows that encoder-decoder CNN architecture is closely related to nonlinear basis representation using combinatorial convolution frames, whose expressibility increases exponentially with the network depth. We also demonstrate the importance of skipped connection in terms of expressibility, and optimization landscape.

We also demonstrate the importance of skipped connection in terms of expressibility, and optimization landscape.

paragraphs: Encoder-decoder convolutional networks perform well on inverse problems in areas such as computer vision and medical imaging, but their success is difficult to explain geometrically. This paper develops a unified mathematical framework for understanding these architectures, drawing on convolutional framelets and theoretical perspectives on expressivity, generalization, and optimization.

The framework connects encoder-decoder CNNs to nonlinear basis representations built from combinatorial convolution frames. In this view, the architecture supplies a structured way to represent signals, and its expressibility grows exponentially with network depth. This gives depth a mathematical interpretation in terms of representational capacity, rather than treating it solely as an architectural setting.

The authors also demonstrate the importance of skip connections for both expressibility and the optimization landscape. Their analysis therefore links two architectural choices, depth and skipped connections, to properties of representation and learning. The contribution is a coherent theoretical account of encoder-decoder geometry. Exponential growth in expressibility describes what the representation can express; it is not itself a claim of exponential improvement in task accuracy.
summary.tldr: A unified geometric framework connects encoder-decoder CNNs to nonlinear basis representations and explains how depth and skip connections affect expressibility.

title: Understanding Geometry of Encoder-Decoder CNNs

abstract: Composition is one of the most important properties of differential privacy (DP), as it allows algorithm designers to build complex private algorithms from DP primitives. We consider precise composition bounds of the overall privacy loss for exponential mechanisms, one of the fundamental classes of mechanisms in DP. Exponential mechanism has also become a fundamental building block in private machine learning, e.g. private PCA and hyper-parameter selection. We give explicit formulations of the optimal privacy loss for both the adaptive and non-adaptive composition of exponential mechanism. For the non-adaptive setting in which each mechanism has the same privacy parameter, we give an efficiently computable formulation of the optimal privacy loss. In the adaptive case, we derive a recursive formula and an efficiently computable upper bound. These precise understandings about the problem lead to a 40% saving of the privacy budget in a practical application. Furthermore, the algorithm-specific analysis shows a difference in privacy parameters of adaptive and non-adaptive composition, which was widely believed to not exist based on the evidence from general analysis.

paragraphs: Differential privacy composition determines the total privacy loss when private procedures are combined. This paper studies precise composition for exponential mechanisms, a class used in applications such as private principal component analysis and hyperparameter selection. Tighter accounting can make a meaningful difference to how much privacy budget an overall algorithm consumes.

The authors give explicit formulations of optimal privacy loss for adaptive and non-adaptive composition. In the non-adaptive case, when all mechanisms share the same privacy parameter, they provide an efficiently computable formulation. For adaptive composition, they derive a recursive formula and an efficiently computable upper bound.

The analysis yields a reported 40 percent privacy-budget saving in one practical application. It also reveals a difference between the privacy parameters of adaptive and non-adaptive composition for these mechanisms, contrary to a widespread belief based on general analyses. The contribution is therefore both practical and conceptual: accounting tailored to a mechanism class can sharpen privacy estimates and expose distinctions that broader composition results do not reveal.
summary.tldr: Precise composition analysis for exponential mechanisms sharpens privacy accounting and reveals differences between adaptive and non-adaptive use.

title: Optimal Differential Privacy Composition for Exponential Mechanisms

abstract: Significant work has been recently dedicated to the stochastic delayed bandits because of its relevance in applications. The applicability of existing algorithms is however restricted by the fact that strong assumptions are often made on the delay distributions, such as full observability, restrictive shape constraints, or uniformity over arms. In this work, we weaken them significantly and only assume that there is a bound on the tail of the delay. In particular, we cover the important case where the delay distributions vary across arms, and the case where the delays are heavy-tailed. Addressing these difficulties, we propose a simple but efficient UCB-based algorithm called the PatientBandits. We provide both problemsdependent and problems-independent bounds on the regret as well as performance lower bounds.

In particular, we cover the important case where the delay distributions vary across arms, and the case where the delays are heavy-tailed. paragraphs: In a stochastic bandit problem, a learner repeatedly chooses among actions and learns from their rewards. Delayed feedback complicates this process because information about earlier choices may arrive only after further decisions have been made. This paper focuses on cases where different actions have different delay distributions, including distributions with heavy tails.

The authors weaken several assumptions used in earlier delayed-bandit methods, such as uniform delays across actions or restrictive conditions on distribution shape. Their delay assumption requires only a bound on the tail. This still places a condition on how delays behave, while permitting a wider range of action-dependent and heavy-tailed feedback patterns.

To handle this setting, they propose PatientBandits, a simple algorithm based on upper confidence bounds. The analysis supplies both problem-dependent and problem-independent regret bounds, along with performance lower bounds. These results characterize the algorithm's performance from complementary perspectives and provide a theoretical reference for the difficulty of delayed learning. The contribution is to broaden the delay models covered by an efficient bandit approach.
summary.tldr: PatientBandits handles action-dependent and heavy-tailed feedback delays under a tail-bound assumption, with regret guarantees and performance lower bounds.

title: Stochastic bandits with arm-dependent delays

abstract: We present an approach for unsupervised domain adaptation{—}with a strong focus on practical considerations of within-domain class imbalance and between-domain class distribution shift{—}from a class-conditioned domain alignment perspective. Current methods for class-conditioned domain alignment aim to explicitly minimize a loss function based on pseudo-label estimations of the target domain. However, these methods suffer from pseudo-label bias in the form of error accumulation. We propose a method that removes the need for explicit optimization of model parameters from pseudo-labels. Instead, we present a sampling-based implicit alignment approach, where the sample selection is implicitly guided by the pseudo-labels. Theoretical analysis reveals the existence of a domain-discriminator shortcut in misaligned classes, which is addressed by the proposed approach to facilitate domain-adversarial learning. Empirical results and ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the proposed approach, especially in the presence of within-domain class imbalance and between-domain class distribution shift.

However, these methods suffer from pseudo-label bias in the form of error accumulation. We propose a method that removes the need for explicit optimization of model parameters from pseudo-labels. Instead, we present a sampling-based implicit alignment approach, where the sample selection is implicitly guided by the pseudo-labels. Theoretical analysis reveals the existence of a domain-discriminator shortcut in misaligned classes, which is addressed by the proposed approach to facilitate domain-adversarial learning. Empirical results and ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of the proposed approach, especially in the presence of within-domain class imbalance and between-domain class distribution shift.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation must transfer a model to a target domain without target labels. Class-conditioned alignment tries to match corresponding classes across domains, often using estimated target labels called pseudo-labels. The paper focuses on practical difficulties when classes are imbalanced within a domain or their relative frequencies differ between domains.

Directly optimizing a loss built from pseudo-labels can accumulate errors when those labels are wrong. The authors instead use pseudo-labels to guide which samples are selected, producing alignment implicitly through sampling. Pseudo-labels still influence training, but the method removes the need to optimize model parameters explicitly against them as target labels.

The theoretical analysis identifies a shortcut available to a domain discriminator when classes are misaligned, and the proposed approach addresses that shortcut to support adversarial domain learning. Experiments and ablations confirm effectiveness, particularly under class imbalance and shifts in class distributions. The result highlights sample selection as an alternative way to use uncertain class information when aligning domains.
summary.tldr: The method uses pseudo-label-guided sampling for implicit class alignment, improving domain adaptation especially under class imbalance and distribution shifts.

title: Implicit Class-Conditioned Domain Alignment for Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

abstract: We introduce a new measure to evaluate the transferability of representations learned by classifiers. Our measure, the Log Expected Empirical Prediction (LEEP), is simple and easy to compute: when given a classifier trained on a source data set, it only requires running the target data set through this classifier once. We analyze the properties of LEEP theoretically and demonstrate its effectiveness empirically. Our analysis shows that LEEP can predict the performance and convergence speed of both transfer and meta-transfer learning methods, even for small or imbalanced data. Moreover, LEEP outperforms recently proposed transferability measures such as negative conditional entropy and H scores. Notably, when transferring from ImageNet to CIFAR100, LEEP can achieve up to 30% improvement compared to the best competing method in terms of the correlations with actual transfer accuracy.
originalAbstract: We introduce a new measure to evaluate the transferability of representations learned by classifiers. Our measure, the Log Expected Empirical Prediction (LEEP), is simple and easy to compute: when given a classifier trained on a source data set, it only requires running the target data set through this classifier once. We analyze the properties of LEEP theoretically and demonstrate its effectiveness empirically. Our analysis shows that LEEP can predict the performance and convergence speed of both transfer and meta-transfer learning methods, even for small or imbalanced data. Moreover, LEEP outperforms recently proposed transferability measures such as negative conditional entropy and H scores. Notably, when transferring from ImageNet to CIFAR100, LEEP can achieve up to 30% improvement compared to the best competing method in terms of the correlations with actual transfer accuracy.

paragraphs: LEEP measures how well representations learned by a classifier are likely to transfer to a target dataset. The practical question is whether a model trained on one dataset provides a useful starting point for another. A useful score can inform that decision without requiring the full transfer-learning process for every candidate.

The proposed Log Expected Empirical Prediction score requires only one pass of the target dataset through the source classifier. The authors analyze its properties theoretically and evaluate it empirically. They report that it can predict both performance and convergence speed for transfer and meta-transfer learning, including situations with small or imbalanced datasets.

LEEP outperforms the compared negative conditional entropy and H-score measures in the reported evaluation. For transfer from ImageNet to CIFAR100, the authors report up to a 30% improvement over the best competing measure in correlation with actual transfer accuracy. That figure describes how well the score tracks transfer outcomes; it is not a claimed 30% increase in the transferred classifier’s accuracy.
summary.tldr: LEEP estimates representation transferability with one target-data pass and correlates well with reported transfer performance and convergence speed.

title: LEEP: A New Measure to Evaluate Transferability of Learned Representations

abstract: Many computer vision applications require solving multiple tasks in real-time. A neural network can be trained to solve multiple tasks simultaneously using multi-task learning. This can save computation at inference time as only a single network needs to be evaluated. Unfortunately, this often leads to inferior overall performance as task objectives can compete, which consequently poses the question: which tasks should and should not be learned together in one network when employing multi-task learning? We study task cooperation and competition in several different learning settings and propose a framework for assigning tasks to a few neural networks such that cooperating tasks are computed by the same neural network, while competing tasks are computed by different networks. Our framework offers a time-accuracy trade-off and can produce better accuracy using less inference time than not only a single large multi-task neural network but also many single-task networks.
originalAbstract: Many computer vision applications require solving multiple tasks in real-time. A neural network can be trained to solve multiple tasks simultaneously using multi-task learning. This can save computation at inference time as only a single network needs to be evaluated. We study task cooperation and competition in several different learning settings and propose a framework for assigning tasks to a few neural networks such that cooperating tasks are computed by the same neural network, while competing tasks are computed by different networks. Our framework offers a time-accuracy trade-off and can produce better accuracy using less inference time than not only a single large multi-task neural network but also many single-task networks.

paragraphs: A single network can solve several vision tasks at once, potentially reducing the computation needed at inference time. However, sharing a network can also hurt overall performance when task objectives compete. This paper studies which tasks cooperate and which interfere, treating the choice of task grouping as a central part of building an efficient multi-task system.

The authors examine task cooperation and competition across several learning settings. They then propose a framework that assigns tasks to a small number of networks. Cooperating tasks share a network, while competing tasks are assigned to different networks. This creates intermediate arrangements between one network handling every task and a separate network for each task.

The framework offers a tradeoff between inference time and accuracy. The authors report that it can achieve higher accuracy with less inference time than both a single large multi-task network and a collection of single-task networks. The result shows that selective sharing can improve both objectives in the studied settings. The useful design decision is therefore not only how much to share, but which tasks should share their computation.
summary.tldr: Grouping cooperating tasks into shared networks can improve both accuracy and inference time compared with fully shared or fully separate models.

title: Which Tasks Should Be Learned Together in Multi-task Learning?

abstract: Label distribution covers a certain number of labels, representing the degree to which each label describes the instance. When dealing with label ambiguity, label distribution could describe the supervised information in a fine-grained way. Unfortunately, many training sets only contain simple logical labels rather than label distributions due to the difficulty of obtaining label distributions directly. To solve this problem, we consider the label distributions as the latent vectors and infer them from the logical labels in the training datasets by using variational inference. After that, we induce a predictive model to train the label distribution data by employing the multi-output regression technique. The recovery experiment on thirteen real-world LDL datasets and the predictive experiment on ten multi-label learning datasets validate the advantage of our approach over the state-of-the-art approaches.

paragraphs: A logical label records whether a label applies, whereas a label distribution expresses how strongly each label describes an example. Those degrees can represent ambiguity more precisely, but they are difficult to obtain directly. This paper proposes recovering such richer supervision from training datasets that contain only simpler logical labels.

The method treats each unknown label distribution as a latent vector and infers it through variational inference. It then uses multi-output regression to learn a predictive model from the resulting distribution-valued data. This creates a two-stage connection between the available annotations and the desired predictions: first infer degrees of relevance, then learn to predict those degrees from examples.

The authors evaluate distribution recovery on thirteen real-world label-distribution-learning datasets and predictive performance on ten multi-label datasets. Both sets of experiments support an advantage over the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The results matter because they assess both parts of the proposal: whether richer labels can be recovered and whether learning from the enhanced labels helps with prediction.
summary.tldr: Variational Label Enhancement infers graded label relevance from logical labels and uses the recovered distributions to train a predictor.

title: Variational Label Enhancement

abstract: In this work we develop a quantum field theory formalism for deep learning, where input signals are encoded in Gaussian states, a generalization of Gaussian processes which encode the agent’s uncertainty about the input signal. We show how to represent linear and non-linear layers as unitary quantum gates, and interpret the fundamental excitations of the quantum model as particles, dubbed “Hintons”. On top of opening a new perspective and techniques for studying neural networks, the quantum formulation is well suited for optical quantum computing, and provides quantum deformations of neural networks that can be run efficiently on those devices. Finally, we discuss a semi-classical limit of the quantum deformed models which is amenable to classical simulation.

We show how to represent linear and non-linear layers as unitary quantum gates, and interpret the fundamental excitations of the quantum model as particles, dubbed “Hintons”. On top of opening a new perspective and techniques for studying neural networks, the quantum formulation is well suited for optical quantum computing, and provides quantum deformations of neural networks that can be run efficiently on those devices. Finally, we discuss a semi-classical limit of the quantum deformed models which is amenable to classical simulation.

paragraphs: This paper develops a quantum field theory formulation of deep learning. Input signals are represented using Gaussian states, which generalize Gaussian processes and encode uncertainty about the signal. The framework therefore gives uncertainty in the input a place within the mathematical representation of the network, rather than treating the input only as fixed numerical values.

The authors show how both linear and nonlinear layers can be represented as unitary quantum gates. They interpret the quantum model's elementary excitations as particles, which they name Hintons. This construction provides a different mathematical perspective on neural networks and opens access to techniques associated with the quantum formulation.

The work also connects that perspective to computation. The formulation is suited to optical quantum computing and yields quantum-deformed neural networks that can run efficiently on those devices. The authors additionally discuss a semiclassical limit that permits classical simulation. These contributions establish a framework for representing and studying networks across quantum and classically simulable regimes, with the practical connection centered on the proposed model constructions.
summary.tldr: A quantum field theory formulation represents neural-network layers as quantum gates and connects them to optical quantum computation.

title: The Hintons in your Neural Network: a Quantum Field Theory View of Deep Learning

abstract: A graph generative model defines a distribution over graphs. Typically, the model consists of a sequential process that creates and adds nodes and edges. Such sequential process defines an ordering of the nodes in the graph. The computation of the model’s likelihood requires to marginalize the node orderings; this makes maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) challenging due to the (factorial) number of possible permutations. In this work, we provide an expression for the likelihood of a graph generative model and show that its calculation is closely related to the problem of graph automorphism. In addition, we derive a variational inference (VI) algorithm for fitting a graph generative model that is based on the maximization of a variational bound of the log-likelihood. This allows the model to be trained with node orderings from the approximate posterior instead of ad-hoc orderings. Our experiments show that our log-likelihood bound is significantly tighter than the bound of previous schemes. The models fitted with the VI algorithm are able to generate high-quality graphs that match the structures of target graphs not seen during training.

paragraphs: Many graph generators construct a graph by adding nodes and edges in sequence. That process assigns an order to nodes, even though a graph can admit many such orders. Computing the graph's likelihood requires accounting for those possibilities, and their factorial growth makes direct maximum-likelihood training difficult.

The paper derives an expression for graph likelihood and connects its calculation to graph automorphism. It then develops a variational inference algorithm that maximizes a lower bound on log-likelihood. This lets training use node orderings drawn from an approximate posterior, giving the choice of ordering a probabilistic basis rather than relying on an ad hoc sequence.

Experiments find that the resulting log-likelihood bound is significantly tighter than bounds from previous schemes. Models trained this way also generate high-quality graphs whose structures match target graphs absent from training. The findings connect more careful treatment of node order to both improved likelihood approximation and useful graph generation, while retaining an approximate inference procedure.
summary.tldr: Variational inference learns probabilistically grounded node orderings for graph generation and produces tighter likelihood bounds.

title: Order Matters: Probabilistic Modeling of Node Sequence for Graph Generation

abstract: We give a dimensionality reduction procedure to approximate the sum of distances of a given set of $n$ points in $R^d$ to any “shape” that lies in a $k$-dimensional subspace. Here, by “shape” we mean any set of points in $R^d$. Our algorithm takes an input in the form of an $n \times d$ matrix $A$, where each row of $A$ denotes a data point, and outputs a subspace $P$ of dimension $O(k^{3}/\epsilon^6)$ such that the projections of each of the $n$ points onto the subspace $P$ and the distances of each of the points to the subspace $P$ are sufficient to obtain an $\epsilon$-approximation to the sum of distances to any arbitrary shape that lies in a $k$-dimensional subspace of $R^d$. These include important problems such as $k$-median, $k$-subspace approximation, and $(j,l)$ subspace clustering with $j \cdot l \leq k$. Dimensionality reduction reduces the data storage requirement to $(n+d)k^{3}/\epsilon^6$ from nnz$(A)$. Here nnz$(A)$ could potentially be as large as $nd$. Our algorithm runs in time nnz$(A)/\epsilon^2 + (n+d)$poly$(k/\epsilon)$, up to logarithmic factors. For dense matrices, where nnz$(A) \approx nd$, we give a faster algorithm, that runs in time $nd + (n+d)$poly$(k/\epsilon)$ up to logarithmic factors. Our dimensionality reduction algorithm can also be used to obtain poly$(k/\epsilon)$ size coresets for $k$-median and $(k,1)$-subspace approximation problems in polynomial time.

paragraphs: This paper compresses high-dimensional data while preserving the information needed to approximate an aggregate geometric objective: the sum of distances from data points to a target shape. Here, a shape can be any set of points, provided it lies within a k-dimensional subspace. The guarantee covers a family of possible shapes rather than one predetermined target.

The procedure constructs a subspace whose dimension is O(k³/ε⁶). For each input point, it keeps both the projection onto that subspace and the distance to it. Together, these quantities suffice for the stated ε-approximation. Keeping the distance alongside the projection is part of the guarantee; the compressed representation contains more than the projected coordinates alone.

The result applies to k-median, subspace approximation, and specified subspace-clustering problems. Storage scales with (n+d)k³/ε⁶ rather than the original number of nonzero matrix entries, which can reach nd. The paper provides running-time guarantees, including a faster dense-matrix variant, and uses the reduction to construct small coresets for two of the covered objectives.
summary.tldr: A projection plus each point’s distance to the projection subspace preserves approximate sums of distances to any shape contained in a k-dimensional subspace.

title: Dimensionality Reduction for the Sum-of-Distances Metric

abstract: Motivated by emerging applications such as live-streaming e-commerce, promotions and recommendations, we introduce a general class of multi-armed bandit problems that have the following two features: (i) the decision maker can pull and collect rewards from at most $K$ out of $N$ different arms in each time period; (ii) the expected reward of an arm immediately drops after it is pulled, and then non-parametrically recovers as the idle time increases. With the objective of maximizing expected cumulative rewards over $T$ time periods, we propose, construct and prove performance guarantees for a class of “Purely Periodic Policies”. For the offline problem when all model parameters are known, our proposed policy obtains an approximation ratio that is at the order of $1-\mathcal O(1/\sqrt{K})$, which is asymptotically optimal when $K$ grows to infinity. For the online problem when the model parameters are unknown and need to be learned, we design an Upper Confidence Bound (UCB) based policy that approximately has $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(N\sqrt{T})$ regret against the offline benchmark. Our framework and policy design may have the potential to be adapted into other offline planning and online learning applications with non-stationary and recovering rewards.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated decisions in which using an option reduces its immediate value, while leaving it idle allows its expected reward to recover. At each time step, the decision maker may choose at most K of N options. Recovery is nonparametric, allowing the problem to describe reward patterns without prescribing a particular recovery formula.

The authors construct purely periodic policies for maximizing cumulative expected reward. When the model is known, their policy achieves an approximation ratio of order 1 minus a term proportional to 1 divided by the square root of K. This guarantee approaches optimality as the number of options that can be selected per period grows.

When the model must also be learned, an upper-confidence-bound policy has approximately N times the square root of the time horizon in regret against the offline benchmark, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The framework connects scheduling and learning: actions must balance current reward against future recovery. The authors suggest that this design may also adapt to other problems with recovering, nonstationary rewards.
summary.tldr: Periodic scheduling and confidence-based learning provide guarantees for bandits whose rewards recover while options remain unused.

title: Dynamic Planning and Learning under Recovering Rewards

abstract: Can models with particular structure avoid being biased towards spurious correlation in out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization? Peters et al. (2016) provides a positive answer for linear cases. In this paper, we use a functional modular probing method to analyze deep model structures under OOD setting. We demonstrate that even in biased models (which focus on spurious correlation) there still exist unbiased functional subnetworks. Furthermore, we articulate and confirm the functional lottery ticket hypothesis: the full network contains a subnetwork with proper structure that can achieve better OOD performance. We then propose Modular Risk Minimization to solve the subnetwork selection problem. Our algorithm learns the functional structure from a given dataset, and can be combined with any other OOD regularization methods. Experiments on various OOD generalization tasks corroborate the effectiveness of our method.

paragraphs: The paper asks whether the internal structure of a deep network can help it generalize when the data distribution changes. Its concern is spurious correlation: a model may rely on associations present in its training data that do not remain useful elsewhere. The authors examine whether better behavior is already present within parts of such a model.

Using functional modular probing, they analyze subnetworks under out-of-distribution conditions. They demonstrate that models biased toward spurious correlations can still contain unbiased functional subnetworks. This motivates their functional lottery ticket hypothesis: a full network contains a suitably structured subnetwork capable of better out-of-distribution performance. The emphasis is on which functional structure is selected within the larger model.

To make that observation actionable, the authors propose Modular Risk Minimization, which learns a functional structure from a supplied dataset and addresses subnetwork selection. The method can be combined with other out-of-distribution regularization approaches. Experiments across several generalization tasks support its effectiveness, connecting the structural analysis to a practical learning procedure.
summary.tldr: Modular Risk Minimization selects functional subnetworks that can generalize better beyond the training distribution, even within models biased toward spurious correlations.

title: Can Subnetwork Structure Be the Key to Out-of-Distribution Generalization?

abstract: Polythetic classifications, based on shared patterns of features that need neither be universal nor constant among members of a class, are common in the natural world and greatly outnumber monothetic classifications over a set of features. We show that threshold meta-learners, such as Prototypical Networks, require an embedding dimension that is exponential in the number of task-relevant features to emulate these functions. In contrast, attentional classifiers, such as Matching Networks, are polythetic by default and able to solve these problems with a linear embedding dimension. However, we find that in the presence of task-irrelevant features, inherent to meta-learning problems, attentional models are susceptible to misclassification. To address this challenge, we propose a self-attention feature-selection mechanism that adaptively dilutes non-discriminative features. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in meta-learning Boolean functions, and synthetic and real-world few-shot learning tasks.

paragraphs: Many categories depend on combinations of features without requiring every member to share one fixed defining feature. The paper studies these polythetic categories in few-shot learning, where a model must infer a classification task from limited examples. It asks how the classifier's structure affects its ability to represent these patterns.

The authors show that threshold-based meta-learners, including Prototypical Networks, need embedding dimensions that grow exponentially with the number of relevant features to emulate these classification functions. The proposed self-attention feature-selection mechanism adaptively reduces the influence of features that do not distinguish classes. Results on Boolean-function learning and synthetic and real-world few-shot tasks demonstrate the approach's effectiveness, connecting representational capacity with the separate challenge of selecting useful information.
summary.tldr: Attention represents polythetic categories efficiently, and adaptive feature selection helps it handle irrelevant features in few-shot tasks.

title: Attentional Meta-learners for Few-shot Polythetic Classification

abstract: In this work, we pursue a unified paradigm for multimodal pretraining to break the shackles of complex task/modality-specific customization. We propose OFA, a Task-Agnostic and Modality-Agnostic framework that supports Task Comprehensiveness. OFA unifies a diverse set of cross-modal and unimodal tasks, including image generation, visual grounding, image captioning, image classification, language modeling, etc., in a simple sequence-to-sequence learning framework. OFA follows the instruction-based learning in both pretraining and finetuning stages, requiring no extra task-specific layers for downstream tasks. In comparison with the recent state-of-the-art vision & language models that rely on extremely large cross-modal datasets, OFA is pretrained on only 20M publicly available image-text pairs. Despite its simplicity and relatively small-scale training data, OFA achieves new SOTAs in a series of cross-modal tasks while attaining highly competitive performances on uni-modal tasks. Our further analysis indicates that OFA can also effectively transfer to unseen tasks and unseen domains. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/OFA-Sys/OFA.

paragraphs: Multimodal learning often uses customized architectures or output components for different tasks and data types. OFA investigates how much of this variety can fit into one sequence-to-sequence framework. It brings tasks including image generation, visual grounding, captioning, image classification, and language modeling into a shared formulation.

The framework uses instructions during both pretraining and finetuning, without requiring additional task-specific layers for downstream tasks. This gives task descriptions a common role throughout learning. OFA is pretrained on 20 million publicly available image-text pairs, a scale the authors describe as relatively small compared with contemporary vision-and-language models relying on much larger cross-modal datasets.

Despite its unified design, OFA achieves reported state-of-the-art results on several cross-modal tasks and highly competitive results on unimodal tasks. Further analysis indicates effective transfer to tasks and domains absent from training. These findings provide evidence that architectural unification can coexist with strong performance across diverse objectives. The transfer result is an observed capability in the analysis, rather than a guarantee for every unfamiliar task or domain.
summary.tldr: OFA uses instruction-based sequence-to-sequence learning to unify diverse vision and language tasks with strong reported performance.

title: OFA: Unifying Architectures, Tasks, and Modalities Through a Simple Sequence-to-Sequence Learning Framework

abstract: Stochastic high-order methods for finding first-order stationary points in nonconvex finite-sum optimization have witnessed increasing interest in recent years, and various upper and lower bounds of the oracle complexity have been proved. However, under standard regularity assumptions, existing complexity bounds are all dimension-dependent (e.g., polylogarithmic dependence), which contrasts with the dimension-free complexity bounds for stochastic first-order methods and deterministic high-order methods. In this paper, we show that the polylogarithmic dimension dependence gap is not essential and can be closed. More specifically, we propose stochastic high-order algorithms with novel first-order and high-order derivative estimators, which can achieve dimension-free complexity bounds. With the access to $p$-th order derivatives of the objective function, we prove that our algorithm finds $\epsilon$-stationary points with $O(n^{(2p-1)/(2p)}/\epsilon^{(p+1)/p})$ high-order oracle complexities, where $n$ is the number of individual functions. Our result strictly improves the complexity bounds of existing high-order deterministic methods with respect to the dependence on $n$, and it is dimension-free compared with existing stochastic high-order methods.

paragraphs: The paper studies nonconvex optimization problems whose objective is a sum of individual functions. Its goal is to find a first-order stationary point, where the gradient is sufficiently small. Existing stochastic methods using higher-order derivatives had complexity bounds that depended on the number of dimensions, even when that dependence was only polylogarithmic.

The authors show that this dimension dependence is avoidable under the standard regularity setting considered. They introduce stochastic algorithms with new estimators for both first-order and higher-order derivatives. Given access to derivatives of order p, their method reaches an epsilon-stationary point using O(n^((2p-1)/(2p))/epsilon^((p+1)/p)) high-order oracle calls, where n counts the component functions.

The result improves two aspects of previous guarantees: dependence on n compared with existing deterministic higher-order methods, and dependence on dimension compared with stochastic higher-order methods. The contribution concerns the number of derivative-oracle calls required to meet a stationarity target. It establishes that the dimension factor in earlier bounds is not an essential obstacle for this class of algorithms.
summary.tldr: New stochastic derivative estimators yield dimension-free oracle complexity bounds for finding stationary points in nonconvex finite-sum optimization.

title: Dimension-free Complexity Bounds for High-order Nonconvex Finite-sum Optimization

abstract: Deep neural networks have been demonstrated to be vulnerable to adversarial noise, promoting the development of defense against adversarial attacks. Motivated by the fact that adversarial noise contains well-generalizing features and that the relationship between adversarial data and natural data can help infer natural data and make reliable predictions, in this paper, we study to model adversarial noise by learning the transition relationship between adversarial labels (i.e. the flipped labels used to generate adversarial data) and natural labels (i.e. the ground truth labels of the natural data). Specifically, we introduce an instance-dependent transition matrix to relate adversarial labels and natural labels, which can be seamlessly embedded with the target model (enabling us to model stronger adaptive adversarial noise). Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our method could effectively improve adversarial accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper studies adversarial noise through the relationship between the labels used to generate attacks and the correct labels of the original data. Its motivation is that adversarial noise contains features that generalize, and relationships between adversarial and natural data can help infer the natural data and support reliable predictions.

The method introduces an instance-dependent transition matrix. Here, adversarial labels are the flipped labels used when generating adversarial examples, while natural labels are the original ground truth. The matrix relates these two label types separately for each instance, allowing the modeled relationship to vary across examples instead of treating it as a single shared transition.

The transition matrix can be embedded in the target model, which the authors describe as enabling the modeling of stronger adaptive adversarial noise. Empirical evaluations show that the method can improve adversarial accuracy. The contribution is therefore an explicit model of the attack-label relationship, with experimental support for using that relationship to improve predictions under adversarial perturbations.
summary.tldr: An instance-dependent transition matrix models relationships between adversarial and natural labels to improve adversarial accuracy.

title: Modeling Adversarial Noise for Adversarial Training

abstract: Federated learning (FL) aims to perform privacy-preserving machine learning on distributed data held by multiple data owners. To this end, FL requires the data owners to perform training locally and share the gradients or weight updates (instead of the private inputs) with the central server, which are then securely aggregated over multiple data owners. Although aggregation by itself does not offer provable privacy protection, prior work suggested that if the batch size is sufficiently large the aggregation may be secure enough. In this paper, we propose the Cocktail Party Attack (CPA) that, contrary to prior belief, is able to recover the private inputs from gradients/weight updates aggregated over as many as 1024 samples. CPA leverages the crucial insight that aggregate gradients from a fully connected (FC) layer is a linear combination of its inputs, which allows us to frame gradient inversion as a blind source separation (BSS) problem. We adapt independent component analysis (ICA)—a classic solution to the BSS problem—to recover private inputs for FC and convolutional networks, and show that CPA significantly outperforms prior gradient inversion attacks, scales to ImageNet-sized inputs, and works on large batch sizes of up to 1024.

paragraphs: Federated learning keeps training inputs with their owners while sharing gradients or model updates with a server. Aggregating those updates has been viewed as a practical obstacle to reconstructing individual inputs, especially with large batches. This paper examines that belief while emphasizing that aggregation alone does not provide a formal privacy guarantee.

The Cocktail Party Attack treats aggregated gradients as mixtures whose components can be separated. Its key observation is that gradients from a fully connected layer contain linear combinations of the layer's inputs. The authors turn reconstruction into a blind source separation problem and adapt independent component analysis to recover private inputs for fully connected and convolutional networks.

The reported attack recovers inputs from aggregates containing as many as 1,024 samples, handles ImageNet-sized inputs, and substantially outperforms earlier gradient inversion attacks. These findings show that increasing aggregation size can leave recoverable information in shared updates. They specifically challenge confidence in large-batch aggregation as sufficient practical protection for the settings studied.
summary.tldr: The Cocktail Party Attack reconstructs private inputs from federated learning updates aggregated over up to 1,024 samples.

title: Cocktail Party Attack: Breaking Aggregation-Based Privacy in Federated Learning Using Independent Component Analysis

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) problems can be challenging without well-shaped rewards. Prior work on provably efficient RL methods generally proposes to address this issue with dedicated exploration strategies. However, another way to tackle this challenge is to reformulate it as a multi-task RL problem, where the task space contains not only the challenging task of interest but also easier tasks that implicitly function as a curriculum. Such a reformulation opens up the possibility of running existing multi-task RL methods as a more efficient alternative to solving a single challenging task from scratch. In this work, we provide a theoretical framework that reformulates a single-task RL problem as a multi-task RL problem defined by a curriculum. Under mild regularity conditions on the curriculum, we show that sequentially solving each task in the multi-task RL problem is more computationally efficient than solving the original single-task problem, without any explicit exploration bonuses or other exploration strategies. We also show that our theoretical insights can be translated into an effective practical learning algorithm that can accelerate curriculum learning on simulated robotic tasks.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can be difficult when rewards provide little guidance toward successful behavior. A common response is to design explicit exploration strategies. This paper studies another possibility: introduce easier related tasks so that solving them in sequence provides a curriculum for the original difficult task.

The authors give a theoretical framework that reformulates a single-task problem as a multitask problem defined by such a curriculum. Under mild regularity conditions on the curriculum, sequentially solving its tasks is more computationally efficient than solving the original task from scratch. This advantage does not require explicit exploration bonuses or other exploration strategies.

The conditions on the curriculum are central to the claim: the result identifies a setting where a structured sequence of tasks provides a computational benefit. The authors also translate their theoretical insights into a practical algorithm that accelerates curriculum learning on simulated robotic tasks. Together, the analysis and experiments explain how reformulating the learning problem can improve efficiency without adding a dedicated exploration mechanism.
summary.tldr: Under curriculum regularity conditions, solving easier tasks sequentially reduces the computational cost of learning a difficult reinforcement learning task.

title: Understanding the Complexity Gains of Single-Task RL with a Curriculum

abstract: Generative flow networks (GFlowNets) are a family of algorithms for training a sequential sampler of discrete objects under an unnormalized target density and have been successfully used for various probabilistic modeling tasks. Existing training objectives for GFlowNets are either local to states or transitions, or propagate a reward signal over an entire sampling trajectory. We argue that these alternatives represent opposite ends of a gradient bias-variance tradeoff and propose a way to exploit this tradeoff to mitigate its harmful effects. Inspired by the TD($\lambda$) algorithm in reinforcement learning, we introduce subtrajectory balance or SubTB($\lambda$), a GFlowNet training objective that can learn from partial action subsequences of varying lengths. We show that SubTB($\lambda$) accelerates sampler convergence in previously studied and new environments and enables training GFlowNets in environments with longer action sequences and sparser reward landscapes than what was possible before. We also perform a comparative analysis of stochastic gradient dynamics, shedding light on the bias-variance tradeoff in GFlowNet training and the advantages of subtrajectory balance.

paragraphs: GFlowNets learn to construct discrete objects through sequences of actions, aiming to sample according to a target density that need not be normalized. Existing training objectives either focus on individual states or transitions, or pass reward information across a complete construction sequence. This paper treats those choices as endpoints of a gradient bias–variance tradeoff.

The authors introduce subtrajectory balance, called SubTB(λ), inspired by TD(λ) in reinforcement learning. Its objective learns from partial action sequences of different lengths. This provides intermediate training signals between purely local updates and updates covering an entire episode, creating a way to manage the tradeoff identified by the authors.

Experiments show faster sampler convergence in both previously studied and new environments. The method also enables training with longer action sequences and sparser rewards than was previously possible in the studied settings. A comparative analysis of stochastic gradient dynamics helps explain these advantages. The contribution is a training objective that makes partial episodes useful for learning, connecting improved empirical behavior with an analysis of the updates driving that behavior.
summary.tldr: Subtrajectory balance trains GFlowNets on partial action sequences, improving convergence and supporting longer sequences with sparser rewards.

title: Learning GFlowNets From Partial Episodes For Improved Convergence And Stability

abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning has shown significant progress in extracting useful representations from high-dimensional inputs albeit using hand-crafted auxiliary tasks and pseudo rewards. Automatically learning such representations in an object-centric manner geared towards control and fast adaptation remains an open research problem. In this paper, we introduce a method that tries to discover meaningful features from objects, translating them to temporally coherent ‘question’ functions and leveraging the subsequent learned general value functions for control. We compare our approach with state-of-the-art techniques alongside other ablations and show competitive performance in both stationary and non-stationary settings. Finally, we also investigate the discovered general value functions and through qualitative analysis show that the learned representations are not only interpretable but also, centered around objects that are invariant to changes across tasks facilitating fast adaptation.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from images requires finding useful information within large pixel inputs. Existing approaches often guide that process with manually designed auxiliary tasks or pseudo rewards. This paper investigates automatically discovering representations organized around objects, with the aim of making them useful both for controlling behavior and for adapting when tasks change.

The method seeks meaningful object features and turns them into question functions that remain coherent over time. It then learns general value functions associated with those questions and uses them for control. The central idea is to connect object-based observations with temporally extended predictions, so representation learning produces information relevant to an agent's behavior.

Comparisons with state-of-the-art methods and ablations show competitive performance in both stationary and non-stationary settings. Qualitative analysis finds that the learned representations are interpretable and centered on objects that remain invariant across task changes, facilitating fast adaptation. These findings suggest that automatically discovered object-focused predictions can provide useful structure for control, with interpretability supported by the authors' qualitative investigation.
summary.tldr: The method discovers object-focused predictive questions from pixels and uses their learned value functions for control and adaptation.

title: Discovering Object-Centric Generalized Value Functions From Pixels

abstract: In data poisoning attacks, an adversary tries to change a model’s prediction by adding, modifying, or removing samples in the training data. Recently, ensemble-based approaches for obtaining provable defenses against data poisoning have been proposed where predictions are done by taking a majority vote across multiple base models. In this work, we show that merely considering the majority vote in ensemble defenses is wasteful as it does not effectively utilize available information in the logits layers of the base models. Instead, we propose Run-Off Election (ROE) , a novel aggregation method based on a two-round election across the base models: In the first round, models vote for their preferred class and then a second, Run-Off election is held between the top two classes in the first round. Based on this approach, we propose DPA+ROE and FA+ROE defense methods based on Deep Partition Aggregation (DPA) and Finite Aggregation (FA) approaches from prior work. We evaluate our methods on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and GTSRB and obtain improvements in certified accuracy by up to $3%$-$4%$. Also, by applying ROE on a boosted version of DPA, we gain improvements around $12%$-$27%$ comparing to the current state-of-the-art, establishing a new state-of-the-art in (pointwise) certified robustness against data poisoning. In many cases, our approach outperforms the state-of-the-art, even when using 32 times less computational power.

paragraphs: Data poisoning changes training examples to influence a model's predictions. Some certified defenses train multiple base models and combine their predictions by majority vote. This paper argues that such voting leaves useful information unused: a model's output scores contain more than just the identity of its highest-scoring class.

Run-Off Election uses two voting rounds. Base models first vote for their preferred class, and the two leading classes advance to a second election. This gives the ensemble another opportunity to use the base models' preferences when deciding between the finalists. The authors integrate the aggregation rule with Deep Partition Aggregation and Finite Aggregation, producing two modified defenses.

Evaluations on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and GTSRB report certified-accuracy improvements of up to 3–4%. Combining the rule with a boosted version of Deep Partition Aggregation yields reported improvements of roughly 12–27% over the existing state of the art. In many evaluated cases, it also outperforms that reference using 32 times less computation. The results show that aggregation design can materially affect pointwise poisoning certificates.
summary.tldr: A two-round ensemble vote uses more of the base models' output information to improve certified robustness against training-data poisoning.

title: Run-off Election: Improved Provable Defense against Data Poisoning Attacks

abstract: Designing protein sequences with desired biological function is crucial in biology and chemistry. Recent machine learning methods use a surrogate sequence-function model to replace the expensive wet-lab validation. How can we efficiently generate diverse and novel protein sequences with high fitness? In this paper, we propose IsEM-Pro, an approach to generate protein sequences towards a given fitness criterion. At its core, IsEM-Pro is a latent generative model, augmented by combinatorial structure features from a separately learned Markov random fields (MRFs). We develop an Monte Carlo Expectation-Maximization method (MCEM) to learn the model. During inference, sampling from its latent space enhances diversity while its MRFs features guide the exploration in high fitness regions. Experiments on eight protein sequence design tasks show that our IsEM-Pro outperforms the previous best methods by at least 55% on average fitness score and generates more diverse and novel protein sequences.

summary.tldr: IsEM-Pro combines latent generation with Markov random field features to produce more diverse, novel protein sequences with higher evaluated fitness.

title: Importance Weighted Expectation-Maximization for Protein Sequence Design

abstract: Offline model selection (OMS), that is, choosing the best policy from a set of many policies given only logged data, is crucial for applying offline RL in real-world settings. One idea that has been extensively explored is to select policies based on the mean squared Bellman error (MSBE) of the associated Q-functions. However, previous work has struggled to obtain adequate OMS performance with Bellman errors, leading many researchers to abandon the idea. To this end, we elucidate why previous work has seen pessimistic results with Bellman errors and identify conditions under which OMS algorithms based on Bellman errors will perform well. Moreover, we develop a new estimator of the MSBE that is more accurate than prior methods. Our estimator obtains impressive OMS performance on diverse discrete control tasks, including Atari games.

paragraphs: Offline model selection asks which policy to choose when only previously logged interactions are available. This is an important part of offline reinforcement learning because developing many candidate policies does not itself identify the best one. One proposed selection signal is the mean squared Bellman error of a policy’s associated Q-function, which measures a form of inconsistency in its value predictions.

Earlier attempts to use this signal produced disappointing selection results. This paper revisits those outcomes, explaining why Bellman-error approaches performed poorly and identifying conditions under which they can work well. The distinction matters: poor results from previous methods do not by themselves establish that the underlying selection criterion is unusable.

The authors also introduce an estimator of mean squared Bellman error that is more accurate than earlier methods. It delivers strong policy-selection performance across diverse discrete control tasks, including Atari games. Together, the analysis and experiments support reconsidering Bellman errors for offline selection, with attention to the conditions for success and the quality of the error estimate.
summary.tldr: A more accurate Bellman-error estimator and an analysis of success conditions revive its use for offline policy selection.

title: Revisiting Bellman Errors for Offline Model Selection

abstract: Some neural language models (LMs) exhibit a remarkable capacity for in-context learning (ICL): they can fit predictors to datasets provided as input. While the mechanisms underlying ICL are well-studied in the context of synthetic problems like in-context linear regression, there is still some divergence between these model problems and the “real” ICL exhibited by LMs trained on large text corpora. In this paper, we study ICL through the lens of a new family of model problems we term in context language learning (ICLL). In ICLL, LMs are presented with a set of strings from a formal language, and must generate additional strings from the same language. We focus on in- context learning of regular languages generated by random finite automata. We evaluate a diverse set of neural sequence models on regular ICLL tasks. We first show that Transformers significantly outperform neural sequence models with recurrent or convolutional representations on ICLL tasks. Next, we provide evidence that they do so by computing in-context n-gram statistics using specialized attention heads. Finally, we show that hard-wiring these heads into neural models improves performance not just on synthetic ICLL, but natural language modeling, reducing the perplexity of 340M-parameter Transformers by up to 1.14 points (6.7%) on the SlimPajama dataset. Our results highlight the usefulness of in-context formal language learning as a tool for understanding ICL in models of natural text.

The result shows how a controlled formal-language task can generate architectural insights that also prove useful in a natural-text setting.
summary.tldr: Formal-language learning tasks reveal evidence for n-gram attention mechanisms whose explicit inclusion also improves natural language modeling.

title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms

abstract: Determining the optimal configuration of adsorbates on a slab (adslab) is pivotal in the exploration of novel catalysts across diverse applications. Traditionally, the quest for the lowest energy adslab configuration involves placing the adsorbate onto the slab followed by an optimization process. Prior methodologies have relied on heuristics, problem-specific intuitions, or brute-force approaches to guide adsorbate placement. In this work, we propose a novel framework for adsorbate placement using denoising diffusion. The model is designed to predict the optimal adsorbate site and orientation corresponding to the lowest energy configuration. Further, we have an end-to-end evaluation framework where diffusion-predicted adslab configuration is optimized with a pretrained machine learning force field and finally evaluated with Density Functional Theory (DFT). Our findings demonstrate an acceleration of up to 5x or 3.5x improvement in accuracy compared to the previous best approach. Given the novelty of this framework and application, we provide insights into the impact of pretraining, model architectures, and conduct extensive experiments to underscore the significance of this approach.
