A typical workflow first places the molecule and then optimizes the resulting configuration toward lower energy. The initial placement therefore matters to the search. Earlier approaches have used heuristics, specialized intuition, or brute force to choose where the molecule goes and how it is oriented.

AdsorbDiff uses denoising diffusion to predict a site and orientation intended to lead to the lowest-energy configuration. The authors evaluate this placement model within a complete pipeline: a pretrained machine-learning force field optimizes the predicted configuration, and Density Functional Theory provides the final evaluation. This tests placement in conjunction with the subsequent optimization process.

The reported results show up to fivefold acceleration or a 3.5-fold improvement in accuracy relative to the previous best approach. These are qualified outcomes, rather than a claim that both gains occur together in every case. The study also examines pretraining and architecture choices, helping explain how this diffusion-based placement framework behaves.
summary.tldr: AdsorbDiff predicts molecular placements on catalyst surfaces, reporting up to fivefold acceleration or 3.5-fold better accuracy than the previous best approach.

title: AdsorbDiff: Adsorbate Placement via Conditional Denoising Diffusion

abstract: We approach designing a state-space model for deep learning applications through its dual representation, the transfer function, and uncover a highly efficient sequence parallel inference algorithm that is state-free: unlike other proposed algorithms, state-free inference does not incur any significant memory or computational cost with an increase in state size. We achieve this using properties of the proposed frequency domain transfer function parametrization, which enables direct computation of its corresponding convolutional kernel’s spectrum via a single Fast Fourier Transform. Our experimental results across multiple sequence lengths and state sizes illustrates, on average, a 35% training speed improvement over S4 layers – parametrized in time-domain – on the Long Range Arena benchmark, while delivering state-of-the-art downstream performances over other attention-free approaches. Moreover, we report improved perplexity in language modeling over a long convolutional Hyena baseline, by simply introducing our transfer function parametrization. Our code is available at https://github.com/ruke1ire/RTF.

paragraphs: This paper designs state-space models through their transfer functions, an alternative representation in the frequency domain. That formulation yields a sequence-parallel inference algorithm described as state-free. Increasing the state size does not impose significant additional memory or computational cost on this inference procedure, addressing a key scaling concern.

The proposed parameterization allows the spectrum of the corresponding convolutional kernel to be computed directly with a single Fast Fourier Transform. This connects the model’s mathematical representation to an efficient computational path. The efficiency comes from properties of the transfer-function formulation used to carry out sequence processing.

Across multiple sequence lengths and state sizes on Long Range Arena, experiments report an average training-speed improvement of 35% over time-domain S4 layers. The method also achieves state-of-the-art downstream performance among compared attention-free approaches. In language modeling, introducing the transfer-function parameterization improves perplexity over a long-convolution Hyena baseline. These findings link the representation change to both computational gains and stronger predictive results in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: A transfer-function parameterization enables state-free sequence processing and reports faster training and improved performance on sequence-modeling benchmarks.

title: State-Free Inference of State-Space Models: The *Transfer Function* Approach

abstract: We study the generic identifiability of causal effects in linear non-Gaussian acyclic models (LiNGAM) with latent variables. We consider the problem in two main settings: When the causal graph is known a priori, and when it is unknown. In both settings, we provide a complete graphical characterization of the identifiable direct or total causal effects among observed variables. Moreover, we propose efficient algorithms to certify the graphical conditions. Finally, we propose an adaptation of the reconstruction independent component analysis (RICA) algorithm that estimates the causal effects from the observational data given the causal graph. Experimental results show the effectiveness of the proposed method in estimating the causal effects.

paragraphs: Hidden variables can complicate attempts to determine causal effects from observational data. This paper studies that problem within linear non-Gaussian acyclic models, or LiNGAMs, allowing some variables to remain unobserved. Its focus is generic identifiability: determining which causal effects can be recovered in this model setting, rather than simply proposing an estimator for every possible effect.

The authors consider two distinct situations: one where the causal graph is already known and another where it is unknown. For both, they provide a complete graphical characterization of identifiable direct or total effects among observed variables. Direct effects concern an immediate causal connection, while total effects include influence transmitted through intervening variables. Efficient algorithms check the corresponding graphical conditions.

The paper also adapts reconstruction independent component analysis to estimate causal effects from observational data when the causal graph is given. Experiments support the effectiveness of this estimator. Together, the results connect a structural question—whether an effect is identifiable—to a practical estimation procedure. The guarantees belong to the stated linear, non-Gaussian, acyclic model setting with latent variables.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes identifiable causal effects in LiNGAMs with hidden variables and provides algorithms for checking and estimating them.

title: Causal Effect Identification in LiNGAM Models with Latent Confounders

abstract: Transformers have achieved great success in numerous NLP tasks but continue to exhibit notable gaps in multi-step factual reasoning, especially when real-world knowledge is sparse. Recent advances in grokking have demonstrated that neural networks can transition from memorizing to perfectly generalizing once they detect underlying logical patterns – yet these studies have primarily used small, synthetic tasks. In this paper, for the first time, we extend grokking to real-world factual data and address the challenge of dataset sparsity by augmenting existing knowledge graphs with carefully designed synthetic data to raise the ratio $\phi_r$ of inferred facts to atomic facts above the threshold required for grokking. Surprisingly, we find that even factually incorrect synthetic data can strengthen emergent reasoning circuits rather than degrade accuracy, as it forces the model to rely on relational structure rather than memorization. When evaluated on multi-hop reasoning benchmarks, our approach achieves up to 95–100% accuracy on 2WikiMultiHopQA – substantially improving over strong baselines and matching or exceeding current state-of-the-art results. We further provide an in-depth analysis of how increasing $\phi_r$ drives the formation of generalizing circuits inside Transformers. Our findings suggest that grokking-based data augmentation can unlock implicit multi-hop reasoning capabilities, opening the door to more robust and interpretable factual reasoning in large-scale language models.

paragraphs: Grokking describes a transition from memorizing training examples to generalizing their underlying logical structure. Earlier studies largely examined small synthetic tasks. This paper extends the idea to factual reasoning with real-world knowledge graphs, where sparse knowledge can make it difficult for transformers to learn how to combine facts across multiple steps.

The authors add carefully designed synthetic data to increase the ratio of inferred facts to atomic facts beyond the threshold required for grokking. They find that even factually incorrect synthetic examples can improve the emerging reasoning circuits in their setting. Their explanation is that these examples encourage reliance on relationships and structure rather than memorization. On 2WikiMultiHopQA, the approach reaches reported accuracies of up to 95–100%, substantially improving on strong baselines and matching or exceeding reported state-of-the-art results. These findings suggest that structured augmentation can help unlock implicit multi-hop reasoning. The observation about incorrect examples is tied to this designed augmentation process; the contribution is evidence about learning relational structure from the constructed data.
summary.tldr: Structured synthetic augmentation promotes grokking on real-world factual data and yields strong reported multi-hop reasoning accuracy.

title: Grokking in the Wild: Data Augmentation for Real-World Multi-Hop Reasoning with Transformers

abstract: State-space models (SSMs) offer efficient alternatives to Transformers for long sequences, but their fixed-size recurrent state limits capability on algorithmic tasks, such as retrieving past context. In this work, we examine how in-context retrieval operates in Transformer- and SSM-based language models and find that both rely on a Gather-and-Aggregate (G&A) mechanism: a Gather Head extracts relevant information from context, which an Aggregate Head integrates into representation. In both architectures, G&A concentrates in a few heads, forming bottlenecks even for simple retrieval. For example, disabling a single Gather or Aggregate Head in a pruned Llama-3.1-8B impairs retrieving the correct answer letter in MMLU, reducing its accuracy from 66% to 25%. Moreover, this retrieval bottleneck can obscure knowledge demands of tasks as the pruned model succeeds on MMLU with functioning G&A heads yet fails on other knowledge benchmarks. The bottleneck similarly extends to tasks where SSMs typically underperform, like GSM8K, BBH, and dialogue. We show that SSMs’ retrieval challenges manifest in these heads, creating smoother attention patterns instead of the sharp transitions effective G&A requires. Thus, the Transformer-SSM retrieval gap exists in just a few heads, rather than the entire language model. % Result 3: Analyzing Hybrid models This suggests a unified explanation for Transformer vs. SSM performance gap while showing how to merge their strengths. We find that pretrained hybrid models, where SSMs are combined with attention layers, delegate the role of Aggregate Heads to attention. Similarly, replacing a single G&A head in a pretrained SSM with an attention variant boosts retrieval and benchmark scores.

This work concentrates in a small number of heads.

Hybrid models assign aggregation to attention layers, and replacing a single relevant head in a pretrained state-space model with an attention variant improves retrieval and benchmark scores. These findings locate a consequential architectural difference in a few specific components.
summary.tldr: A few Gather-and-Aggregate heads explain important retrieval bottlenecks and offer targeted ways to improve state-space language models.

title: Understanding the Skill Gap in Recurrent Language Models: The Role of the Gather-and-Aggregate Mechanism

abstract: Artificial intelligence will play a significant role in decision making in numerous aspects of society. Numerous fairness criteria have been proposed in the machine learning community, but there remains limited investigation into fairness as defined through specified attributes in a sequential decision-making framework. In this paper, we focus on causal logistic bandit problems where the learner seeks to make fair decisions, under a notion of fairness that accounts for counterfactual reasoning. We propose and analyze an algorithm by leveraging primal-dual optimization for constrained causal logistic bandits where the non-linear constraints are a priori unknown and must be learned in time. We obtain sub-linear regret guarantees with leading term similar to that for unconstrained logistic bandits (Lee et al., 2024) while guaranteeing sub-linear constraint violations. We show how to achieve zero cumulative constraint violations with a small increase in the regret bound.

paragraphs: This paper studies decision making in which a learner repeatedly chooses actions, learns from outcomes, and must respect fairness requirements. Its setting is causal logistic bandits, with fairness defined through counterfactual reasoning about specified attributes. A central difficulty is that the nonlinear fairness constraints are initially unknown, so the learner must discover them while making decisions.

The proposed algorithm uses primal-dual optimization to handle the performance objective and fairness constraints together. The analysis evaluates both regret, which tracks accumulated performance loss, and accumulated constraint violations. This makes the cost of learning to act fairly part of the mathematical problem rather than assuming the fairness requirements are already fully known.

The authors prove sublinear regret with a leading term similar to that of unconstrained logistic bandits, alongside sublinear constraint violations. Sublinear growth means these accumulated quantities grow more slowly than the number of decisions. They also show how to obtain zero cumulative constraint violations with a small increase in the regret bound. The results describe a theoretical trade-off between decision quality and constraint satisfaction.
summary.tldr: A primal-dual algorithm learns unknown counterfactual fairness constraints while providing regret and constraint-violation guarantees for causal logistic bandits.

title: Causal Logistic Bandits with Counterfactual Fairness Constraints

abstract: Group fairness based on adversarial training has gained significant attention on graph data, which was implemented by masking sensitive attributes to generate fair feature views. However, existing models suffer from training instability due to uncertainty of the generated masks and the trade-off between fairness and utility. In this work, we propose a stable fair Graph Neural Network (SFG) to maintain training stability while preserving accuracy and fairness performance. Specifically, we first theoretically derive a tight upper Lipschitz bound to control the stability of existing adversarial-based models and employ a stochastic projected subgradient algorithm to constrain the bound, which operates in a block-coordinate manner. Additionally, we construct the uncertainty set to train the model, which can prevent unstable training by dropping some overfitting nodes caused by chasing fairness. Extensive experiments conducted on three real-world datasets demonstrate that SFG is stable and outperforms other state-of-the-art adversarial-based methods in terms of both fairness and utility performance. Codes are available at https://github.com/sh-qiangchen/SFG.

paragraphs: Some graph fairness methods use adversarial training and mask sensitive attributes to create fair feature views. Their training can become unstable because the generated masks are uncertain and fairness must be balanced against predictive usefulness. This paper introduces a stable fair Graph Neural Network, SFG, to improve stability while preserving accuracy and fairness.

The authors derive a tight upper Lipschitz bound to control stability in existing adversarial approaches. They constrain this bound with a stochastic projected subgradient algorithm operating in a block-coordinate manner. They also construct an uncertainty set that allows training to drop some nodes whose overfitting, caused by pursuing fairness, contributes to instability.

Experiments on three real-world datasets show stable training and better fairness and utility than other state-of-the-art adversarial methods. The contribution combines a theoretical stability bound with concrete training procedures. Its findings support the idea that controlling instability can improve fairness and predictive usefulness together in these evaluated graph-learning settings, rather than treating unstable optimization as an unavoidable consequence of pursuing fairness.
summary.tldr: SFG combines a Lipschitz constraint and uncertainty-aware training to improve stability, fairness, and utility in adversarial graph learning.

title: Stable Fair Graph Representation Learning with Lipschitz Constraint

abstract: The Bradley-Terry (BT) model is widely practiced in reward modeling for reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF). Despite its effectiveness, reward models (RMs) trained with BT model loss as one-way classifiers are prone to over-optimization, losing generalizability to unseen inputs. In this paper, we study the cause of over-optimization and its downstream effects on the RLHF procedure, highlighting the importance of robustness in RMs. First, we show that the excessive dispersion of hidden state norms is the main source of over-optimization. Correspondingly, we propose batch-wise sum-to-zero regularization (BSR) that enforces reward sum for each batch to be zero-centered, constraining the rewards with abnormally large magnitudes. We assess the impact of BSR in improving robustness in RMs through four scenarios of over-optimization, where BSR consistently manifests better robustness on unseen inputs. Then, we compare the plain BT model and BSR on RLHF training and empirically show that robust RMs better align the policy to the gold preference model. Finally, we apply BSR to high-quality data and models, which surpasses state-of-the-art RMs in the 8B scale by adding more than 5% in complex preference prediction tasks. By conducting RLOO training with 8B RMs, AlpacaEval 2.0, with reducing generation length by 40% while adding a 7% increase in win rate, further highlights that robustness in RMs induces robustness in RLHF training.
originalAbstract: The Bradley-Terry (BT) model is widely practiced in reward modeling for reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF). Despite its effectiveness, reward models (RMs) trained with BT model loss as one-way classifiers are prone to over-optimization, losing generalizability to unseen inputs. In this paper, we study the cause of over-optimization and its downstream effects on the RLHF procedure, highlighting the importance of robustness in RMs. First, we show that the excessive dispersion of hidden state norms is the main source of over-optimization. Correspondingly, we propose batch-wise sum-to-zero regularization (BSR) that enforces reward sum for each batch to be zero-centered, constraining the rewards with abnormally large magnitudes. We assess the impact of BSR in improving robustness in RMs through four scenarios of over-optimization, where BSR consistently manifests better robustness on unseen inputs. Then, we compare the plain BT model and BSR on RLHF training and empirically show that robust RMs better align the policy to the gold preference model. Finally, we apply BSR to high-quality data and models, which surpasses state-of-the-art RMs in the 8B scale by adding more than 5% in complex preference prediction tasks. By conducting RLOO training with 8B RMs, AlpacaEval 2.0, with reducing generation length by 40% while adding a 7% increase in win rate, further highlights that robustness in RMs induces robustness in RLHF training.

paragraphs: Reward models guide language-model alignment by scoring outputs according to learned preferences. The paper studies how models trained with Bradley-Terry loss can become over-optimized and lose their ability to generalize to unseen inputs. The authors identify excessive variation in hidden-state norms as the main source of this behavior in their analysis.

They propose batch-wise sum-to-zero regularization, or BSR, which centers the sum of rewards within each batch at zero. This constrains unusually large reward magnitudes. Across four over-optimization scenarios, BSR improves robustness on unseen inputs. In downstream reinforcement learning, the more robust reward models also produce policies that align better with the gold preference model.

With high-quality data and models, BSR surpasses state-of-the-art reward models at the 8-billion-parameter scale, reporting an improvement of more than 5% on complex preference prediction tasks. RLOO training with these reward models also yields a reported 7% win-rate increase on AlpacaEval 2.0 while reducing generation length by 40%. These results connect reward-model robustness with practical changes in aligned policy behavior.
summary.tldr: Centering batch rewards reduces reward-model over-optimization and improves robustness and downstream alignment in the reported experiments.

title: On the Robustness of Reward Models for Language Model Alignment

abstract: Interpretability research now offers a variety of techniques for identifying abstract internal mechanisms in neural networks. Can such techniques be used to predict how models will behave on out-of-distribution examples? In this work, we provide a positive answer to this question. Through a diverse set of language modeling tasks—including symbol manipulation, knowledge retrieval, and instruction following—we show that the most robust features for correctness prediction are those that play a distinctive causal role in the model’s behavior. Specifically, we propose two methods that leverage causal mechanisms to predict the correctness of model outputs: counterfactual simulation (checking whether key causal variables are realized) and value probing (using the values of those variables to make predictions). Both achieve high AUC-ROC in distribution and outperform methods that rely on causal-agnostic features in out-of-distribution settings, where predicting model behaviors is more crucial. Our work thus highlights a novel and significant application for internal causal analysis of language models.

paragraphs: Interpretability methods can identify internal mechanisms involved in a language model’s behavior. This paper asks whether those mechanisms also help predict when its answers will be correct, especially on examples outside the familiar distribution. The authors investigate this across symbol manipulation, knowledge retrieval, and instruction following.

They introduce two approaches that use variables with a distinctive causal role in the model’s behavior. Counterfactual simulation checks whether key causal variables are realized, while value probing predicts correctness from the values of those variables. Both methods use information selected for its role in producing behavior, giving internal causal analysis a practical use in assessing model outputs.

Both approaches achieve high AUC-ROC on in-distribution examples and outperform methods based on causal-agnostic features under distribution shifts. Across the studied tasks, causally distinctive features provide the most robust correctness predictions. These findings support using mechanistic understanding to anticipate model reliability on unfamiliar inputs, extending interpretability from explaining behavior to predicting where that behavior will succeed.
summary.tldr: Features tied to internal causal mechanisms predict language model correctness more robustly under distribution shifts in the studied tasks.

title: Internal Causal Mechanisms Robustly Predict Language Model Out-of-Distribution Behaviors

abstract: LLM-to-NAS is a promising field at the intersection of Large Language Models (LLMs) and Neural Architecture Search (NAS), as recent research has explored the potential of architecture generation leveraging LLMs on multiple search spaces. However, the existing LLM-to-NAS methods face the challenges of limited search spaces, time-cost search efficiency, and uncompetitive performance across standard NAS benchmarks and multiple downstream tasks. In this work, we propose the Reflective Zero-cost NAS (RZ-NAS) method that can search NAS architectures with humanoid reflections and training-free metrics to elicit the power of LLMs. We rethink LLMs’ roles in NAS in current work and design a structured, prompt-based to comprehensively understand the search tasks and architectures from both text and code levels. By integrating LLM reflection modules, we use LLM-generated feedback to provide linguistic guidance within architecture optimization. RZ-NAS enables effective search within both micro and macro search spaces without extensive time cost, achieving SOTA performance across multiple downstream tasks.

paragraphs: RZ-NAS uses a language model to help search for neural network architectures. The paper targets three problems in existing approaches: restricted search spaces, expensive searches, and weak results across benchmarks and downstream tasks. Its proposal combines language-model reflection with metrics that evaluate candidate architectures without training them.

Structured prompts help the language model interpret both the search task and candidate architectures through their text and code. Reflection modules then produce feedback in natural language to guide architecture optimization. The training-free metrics provide another source of guidance, allowing the search to assess candidates without the extensive training costs associated with direct performance evaluation.

The authors report effective searches in both micro and macro search spaces, covering choices at different architectural scales. They also report state-of-the-art performance across multiple downstream tasks without extensive search time. The contribution is a coordinated search strategy in which generated feedback and inexpensive evaluation support architecture refinement. Here, zero-cost refers to the training-free metrics; the framework still performs a search involving prompts, candidate architectures, and feedback.
summary.tldr: RZ-NAS combines language-model reflection with training-free metrics to guide efficient architecture searches across multiple search spaces.

title: RZ-NAS: Enhancing LLM-guided Neural Architecture Search via Reflective Zero-Cost Strategy

abstract: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is a widely used parameter-efficient fine-tuning method. In standard LoRA layers, one of the matrices, $A$ or $B$, is initialized to zero, ensuring that fine-tuning starts from the pretrained model. However, there is no theoretical support for this practice. In this paper, we investigate the impact of non-zero initialization on LoRA’s fine-tuning dynamics from an infinite-width perspective. Our analysis reveals that, compared to zero initialization, simultaneously initializing $A$ and $B$ to non-zero values improves LoRA’s robustness to suboptimal learning rates, particularly smaller ones. Further analysis indicates that although the non-zero initialization of $AB$ introduces random noise into the pretrained weight, it generally does not affect fine-tuning performance. In other words, fine-tuning does not need to strictly start from the pretrained model. The validity of our findings is confirmed through extensive experiments across various models and datasets. The code is available at https://github.com/Leopold1423/non_zero_lora-icml25.

Our analysis reveals that, compared to zero initialization, simultaneously initializing $A$ and $B$ to non-zero values improves LoRA’s robustness to suboptimal learning rates, particularly smaller ones. paragraphs: LoRA adapts a pretrained model through a low-rank weight update represented by two matrices. Standard practice initializes one matrix to zero, making their initial product zero and preserving the pretrained model at the start of fine-tuning. This paper questions whether that exact starting point is necessary and investigates what happens when both matrices begin with nonzero values.

The authors analyze training dynamics in the infinite-width setting. They find that nonzero initialization makes LoRA more robust to poorly chosen learning rates, especially rates that are too small. Initializing both matrices this way adds random noise to the pretrained weights through their product, but the analysis indicates that this generally does not damage fine-tuning performance.

Experiments across multiple models and datasets support these findings. The result challenges the practical need to begin fine-tuning at exactly the pretrained weights. Its significance concerns sensitivity to learning-rate choices and the tolerance of initial perturbations; the stated findings do not imply that nonzero initialization improves every training configuration.
summary.tldr: Initializing both LoRA matrices to nonzero values can improve robustness to suboptimal learning rates without generally harming fine-tuning performance.

title: Beyond Zero Initialization: Investigating the Impact of Non-Zero Initialization on LoRA Fine-Tuning Dynamics

abstract: Recent advances in molecular generative models have demonstrated great promise for accelerating scientific discovery, particularly in drug design. However, these models often struggle to generate high-quality molecules, especially in conditional scenarios where specific molecular properties must be satisfied. In this work, we introduce GeoRCG, a general framework to improve molecular generative models by integrating geometric representation conditions with provable theoretical guarantees. We decompose the generation process into two stages: first, generating an informative geometric representation; second, generating a molecule conditioned on the representation. Compared with single-stage generation, the easy-to-generate representation in the first stage guides the second stage generation toward a high-quality molecule in a goal-oriented way. Leveraging EDM and SemlaFlow as base generators, we observe significant quality improvements in unconditional molecule generation on the widely used QM9 and GEOM-DRUG datasets. More notably, in the challenging conditional molecular generation task, our framework achieves an average 50% performance improvement over state-of-the-art approaches, highlighting the superiority of conditioning on semantically rich geometric representations. Furthermore, with such representation guidance, the number of diffusion steps can be reduced to as small as 100 while largely preserving the generation quality achieved with 1,000 steps, thereby significantly reducing the generation iterations needed.

paragraphs: Generating a high-quality molecule is especially challenging when it must satisfy specified properties. GeoRCG divides this task into two stages. It first generates an informative geometric representation, then generates a molecule conditioned on that representation. The intermediate representation is easier to generate and provides structured guidance for the more demanding molecular generation step.

The framework comes with theoretical guarantees and is applied to EDM and SemlaFlow as base generators. Its central contribution is the use of semantically informative geometry as a conditioning signal. This gives the molecule generator a goal-oriented intermediate target rather than requiring the complete generation process to happen in one stage.

The authors report significant improvements in unconditional generation on QM9 and GEOM-DRUG, and an average 50% performance improvement over state-of-the-art approaches in conditional generation. Representation guidance also permits reducing diffusion from 1,000 steps to as few as 100 while largely preserving generation quality. These findings connect the intermediate representation to both better outputs and fewer generation iterations in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: GeoRCG generates a geometric representation before a molecule, improving reported generation quality and reducing required diffusion iterations.

title: Geometric Representation Condition Improves Equivariant Molecule Generation

abstract: Detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) examples is an important task for deploying reliable machine learning models in safety-critial applications. While post-hoc methods based on the Mahalanobis distance applied to pre-logit features are among the most effective for ImageNet-scale OOD detection, their performance varies significantly across models. We connect this inconsistency to strong variations in feature norms, indicating severe violations of the Gaussian assumption underlying the Mahalanobis distance estimation. We show that simple $\ell_2$-normalization of the features mitigates this problem effectively, aligning better with the premise of normally distributed data with shared covariance matrix. Extensive experiments on 44 models across diverse architectures and pretraining schemes show that $\ell_2$-normalization improves the conventional Mahalanobis distance-based approaches significantly and consistently, and outperforms other recently proposed OOD detection methods.

paragraphs: Mahalanobis-based detectors identify unfamiliar inputs using features from just before a neural network’s output layer. These post-hoc methods can perform well at ImageNet scale, yet their effectiveness varies considerably between models. This paper links that inconsistency to large differences in the lengths, or norms, of feature vectors.

The distance estimation relies on a Gaussian modeling assumption with a shared covariance matrix. Strong norm variation can severely violate that assumption. The authors show that applying l2 normalization to features mitigates the problem and makes the representation better aligned with the modeling premise. The proposed change is therefore a simple transformation of the features used by the detector.

Experiments across 44 models, covering diverse architectures and pretraining schemes, show substantial and consistent improvements over conventional Mahalanobis approaches. The normalized method also outperforms other recently proposed OOD detectors in the reported evaluations. The findings connect a practical performance issue to a mismatch in feature geometry and show that a small preprocessing change can improve this family of detectors.
summary.tldr: Normalizing feature vectors substantially improves Mahalanobis OOD detection across 44 evaluated models by mitigating problematic feature-norm variation.

title: Mahalanobis++: Improving OOD Detection via Feature Normalization

abstract: Dataset distillation has emerged as an effective strategy, significantly reducing training costs and facilitating more efficient model deployment. Recent advances have leveraged generative models to distill datasets by capturing the underlying data distribution. Unfortunately, existing methods require model fine-tuning with distillation losses to encourage diversity and representativeness. However, these methods do not guarantee sample diversity, limiting their performance. We propose a mode-guided diffusion model leveraging a pre-trained diffusion model without the need to fine-tune with distillation losses. Our approach addresses dataset diversity in three stages: Mode Discovery to identify distinct data modes, Mode Guidance to enhance intra-class diversity, and Stop Guidance to mitigate artifacts in synthetic samples that affect performance. We evaluate our approach on ImageNette, ImageIDC, ImageNet-100, and ImageNet-1K, achieving accuracy improvements of 4.4%, 2.9%, 1.6%, and 1.6%, respectively, over state-of-the-art methods. Our method eliminates the need for fine-tuning diffusion models with distillation losses, significantly reducing computational costs.

Our method eliminates the need for fine-tuning diffusion models with distillation losses, significantly reducing computational costs.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation aims to reduce training costs by replacing a dataset with a compact set of useful examples. Generative models can help create these examples, but existing approaches often fine-tune them with distillation losses and still do not guarantee diversity. This paper proposes guiding a pretrained diffusion model without that additional distillation-specific fine-tuning.

The method addresses diversity through three stages. Mode Discovery identifies distinct patterns in the data. Mode Guidance uses those patterns to increase variation among examples within the same class. Stop Guidance then mitigates artifacts in synthetic samples that can hurt performance. Together, the stages address both coverage of the data and the usefulness of generated examples.

Evaluations report accuracy improvements of 4.4%, 2.9%, 1.6%, and 1.6% over state-of-the-art methods on ImageNette, ImageIDC, ImageNet-100, and ImageNet-1K, respectively. The method also significantly reduces computational costs by removing fine-tuning with distillation losses. The findings support explicit guidance toward data modes as a practical way to improve synthetic distilled datasets.
summary.tldr: MGD³ guides a pretrained diffusion model toward diverse data modes, improving dataset distillation without distillation-loss fine-tuning.

title: MGD$^3$ : Mode-Guided Dataset Distillation using Diffusion Models

abstract: Any well-behaved generative model over a variable $\mathbf{x}$ can be expressed as a deterministic transformation of an exogenous (outsourced’) Gaussian noise variable $\mathbf{z}$: $\mathbf{x}=f_\theta(\mathbf{z})$. In such a model (eg, a VAE, GAN, or continuous-time flow-based model), sampling of the target variable $\mathbf{x} \sim p_\theta(\mathbf{x})$ is straightforward, but sampling from a posterior distribution of the form $p(\mathbf{x}\mid\mathbf{y}) \propto p_\theta(\mathbf{x})r(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})$, where $r$ is a constraint function depending on an auxiliary variable $\mathbf{y}$, is generally intractable. We propose to amortize the cost of sampling from such posterior distributions with diffusion models that sample a distribution in the noise space ($\mathbf{z}$). These diffusion samplers are trained by reinforcement learning algorithms to enforce that the transformed samples $f_\theta(\mathbf{z})$ are distributed according to the posterior in the data space ($\mathbf{x}$). For many models and constraints, the posterior in noise space is smoother than in data space, making it more suitable for amortized inference. Our method enables conditional sampling under unconditional GAN, (H)VAE, and flow-based priors, comparing favorably with other inference methods. We demonstrate the proposed outsourced diffusion sampling in several experiments with large pretrained prior models: conditional image generation, reinforcement learning with human feedback, and protein structure generation.

paragraphs: A well-behaved generative model can be represented as a deterministic transformation of Gaussian noise into data. Drawing ordinary samples is then straightforward, but drawing samples that also satisfy an additional constraint is generally intractable. This paper moves that conditional sampling problem into the model's underlying noise space.

The authors train diffusion samplers over noise variables using reinforcement learning. Training aims to make the samples, after passing through the original generator, follow the desired posterior distribution in data space. Learning a sampler amortizes the inference cost, and the paper observes that the noise-space posterior is smoother for many models and constraints.

The method supports conditional sampling from unconditional GAN, VAE, hierarchical VAE, and flow-based priors. Experiments with large pretrained models cover conditional image generation, reinforcement learning with human feedback, and protein structure generation, with favorable comparisons to other inference methods. The central idea is to use a generator's noise representation as the place to learn constrained sampling, taking advantage of smoother posterior structure when it is present.
summary.tldr: Outsourced diffusion sampling learns posterior samplers in a generator's noise space, enabling conditional generation from existing unconditional models.

title: Outsourced Diffusion Sampling: Efficient Posterior Inference in Latent Spaces of Generative Models

abstract: We introduce Griffin, the first foundation model attemptation designed specifically for Relational Databases (RDBs). Unlike previous smaller models focused on single RDB tasks, Griffin unifies the data encoder and task decoder to handle diverse tasks. Additionally, we enhance the architecture by incorporating a cross-attention module and a novel aggregator. Griffin utilizes pretraining on both single-table and RDB datasets, employing advanced encoders for categorical, numerical, and metadata features, along with innovative components such as cross-attention modules and enhanced message-passing neural networks (MPNNs) to capture the complexities of relational data. Evaluated on large-scale, heterogeneous, and temporal graphs extracted from RDBs across various domains (spanning over 150 million nodes), Griffin demonstrates superior or comparable performance to individually trained models, excels in low-data scenarios, and shows strong transferability with similarity and diversity in pretraining across new datasets and tasks, highlighting its potential as a universally applicable foundation model for RDBs. Code available at https://github.com/yanxwb/Griffin.

paragraphs: Griffin explores a foundation-model approach to relational databases, aiming to support diverse prediction tasks through shared machinery. The paper contrasts this with smaller models trained for individual database tasks. Its design unifies data encoding and task decoding so that pretraining can contribute to multiple datasets and uses.

The model is pretrained on both single-table data and relational databases. It includes encoders for categorical, numerical, and metadata features, together with cross-attention, a new aggregation component, and enhanced message-passing networks. These components let the model process different feature types and the connections represented by graphs extracted from relational data.

Evaluation spans large, heterogeneous, and temporal database graphs across several domains, collectively exceeding 150 million nodes. Griffin performs better than or comparably to individually trained models and is particularly effective when data are limited. The authors also report strong transfer to new datasets and tasks, with similarity and diversity in pretraining contributing to transferability. These results support Griffin’s potential as a broadly reusable relational-database model.
summary.tldr: Griffin shares graph-based encoding and task decoding across relational databases, showing strong transfer and performance in low-data settings.

title: Griffin: Towards a Graph-Centric Relational Database Foundation Model

abstract: Building a virtual cell capable of accurately simulating cellular behaviors in silico has long been a dream in computational biology. We introduce CellFlux, an image-generative model that simulates cellular morphology changes induced by chemical and genetic perturbations using flow matching. Unlike prior methods, CellFlux models distribution-wise transformations from unperturbed to perturbed cell states, effectively distinguishing actual perturbation effects from experimental artifacts such as batch effects—a major challenge in biological data. Evaluated on chemical (BBBC021), genetic (RxRx1), and combined perturbation (JUMP) datasets, CellFlux generates biologically meaningful cell images that faithfully capture perturbation-specific morphological changes, achieving a 35% improvement in FID scores and a 12% increase in mode-of-action prediction accuracy over existing methods. Additionally, CellFlux enables continuous interpolation between cellular states, providing a potential tool for studying perturbation dynamics. These capabilities mark a significant step toward realizing virtual cell modeling for biomedical research. Project page: https://yuhui-zh15.github.io/CellFlux/.

paragraphs: CellFlux models how the appearance of cells changes after chemical or genetic perturbations. Its goal is to generate images that reflect those changes, contributing toward virtual models of cellular behavior. A central difficulty is separating the biological effect of a perturbation from experimental artifacts, including differences between batches of measurements.

The method uses flow matching to learn transformations between distributions of unperturbed and perturbed cell states. Modeling the change at the distribution level helps distinguish perturbation effects from these experimental artifacts. CellFlux also supports continuous interpolation between cellular states, providing a possible way to explore changes between the modeled conditions.

Evaluations cover chemical perturbations in BBBC021, genetic perturbations in RxRx1, and combined perturbations in JUMP. The authors report biologically meaningful images, a 35% improvement in FID scores, and a 12% increase in mode-of-action prediction accuracy over existing methods. These findings support the model’s ability to capture perturbation-specific morphology, while its proposed use for studying perturbation dynamics remains a potential application.
summary.tldr: CellFlux uses flow matching to generate perturbation-specific cell images while separating biological changes from experimental artifacts.

title: CellFlux: Simulating Cellular Morphology Changes via Flow Matching

abstract: Existing efforts to align multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with human preferences have only achieved progress in narrow areas, such as hallucination reduction, but remain limited in practical applicability and generalizability. To this end, we introduce MM-RLHF, a dataset containing 120k fine-grained, human-annotated preference comparison pairs. This dataset represents a substantial advancement over existing resources, offering superior size, diversity, annotation granularity, and quality. Leveraging this dataset, we propose several key innovations to improve both the quality of reward models and the efficiency of alignment algorithms. Notably, we introduce the Critique-Based Reward Model, which generates critiques of model outputs before assigning scores, offering enhanced interpretability and more informative feedback compared to traditional scalar reward mechanisms. Additionally, we propose Dynamic Reward Scaling, a method that adjusts the loss weight of each sample according to the reward signal, thereby optimizing the use of high-quality comparison pairs. Our approach is rigorously evaluated across 10 distinct dimensions, encompassing 27 benchmarks, with results demonstrating significant and consistent improvements in model performance (Figure.1).

Leveraging this dataset, we propose several key innovations to improve both the quality of reward models and the efficiency of alignment algorithms. Notably, we introduce the Critique-Based Reward Model, which generates critiques of model outputs before assigning scores, offering enhanced interpretability and more informative feedback compared to traditional scalar reward mechanisms. Additionally, we propose Dynamic Reward Scaling, a method that adjusts the loss weight of each sample according to the reward signal, thereby optimizing the use of high-quality comparison pairs. Our approach is rigorously evaluated across 10 distinct dimensions, encompassing 27 benchmarks, with results demonstrating significant and consistent improvements in model performance (Figure.1).

paragraphs: Aligning multimodal language models with human preferences requires feedback covering more than isolated problems such as hallucinations. MM-RLHF introduces 120,000 finely annotated human preference comparison pairs to support broader alignment. The authors describe the dataset as an improvement in scale, diversity, annotation detail, and quality over existing resources.

The paper also changes how preference feedback becomes a training signal. Its Critique-Based Reward Model first generates a critique of an output and then assigns a score. This provides an explanation alongside the numerical assessment and more informative feedback than a scalar alone. Dynamic Reward Scaling adjusts each sample’s loss weight according to its reward signal.

Together, these components aim to improve reward modeling and use high-quality comparisons more efficiently during alignment. Evaluation spans 10 dimensions and 27 benchmarks, with significant and consistent performance improvements reported across the assessment. The contribution therefore combines a substantial human-feedback resource with methods for interpreting and weighting that feedback, supported by broad multimodal evaluation.
summary.tldr: MM-RLHF combines 120,000 human preference pairs, critique-based rewards, and dynamic sample weighting to improve multimodal model alignment.

title: MM-RLHF: The Next Step Forward in Multimodal LLM Alignment

abstract: Existing training-time safety alignment techniques for large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreak attacks. Direct preference optimization (DPO), a widely deployed alignment method, exhibits limitations in both experimental and theoretical contexts as its loss function proves suboptimal for refusal learning. Through gradient-based analysis, we identify these shortcomings and propose an improved safety alignment that disentangles DPO objectives into two components: (1) robust refusal training, which encourages refusal even when partial unsafe generations are produced, and (2) targeted unlearning of harmful knowledge. This approach significantly increases LLM robustness against a wide range of jailbreak attacks, including prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn attacks across both in-distribution and out-of-distribution scenarios. Furthermore, we introduce a method to emphasize critical refusal tokens by incorporating a reward-based token-level weighting mechanism for refusal learning, which further improves the robustness against adversarial exploits. Our research also suggests that robustness to jailbreak attacks is correlated with token distribution shifts in the training process and internal representations of refusal and harmful tokens, offering valuable directions for future research in LLM safety alignment. The code is available at https://github.com/wicai24/DOOR-Alignment.

paragraphs: Safety training can leave language models vulnerable to prompts that induce harmful responses. This paper examines direct preference optimization, or DPO, and identifies limitations in its suitability for learning refusals through both experiments and gradient analysis. The authors use those findings to redesign the safety objective around two distinct training goals.

One goal strengthens refusal behavior even after a partial unsafe continuation has already been produced. The other targets unlearning of harmful knowledge. Separating these objectives lets training address both the ability to refuse and the harmful information being suppressed. A further reward-based weighting mechanism emphasizes individual tokens that are especially important for learning refusal.

The approach substantially improves robustness against prefilling, suffix, and multi-turn jailbreak attacks in both in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluations. Token weighting provides further gains. The study also suggests correlations between robustness, changes in token distributions during training, and internal representations of refusal and harmful tokens. Those associations offer research directions, while the reported robustness improvements concern the attacks and settings evaluated.
summary.tldr: Separating robust refusal training from harmful-knowledge unlearning, with extra weight on critical refusal tokens, improves resistance to evaluated jailbreak attacks.

title: Improving LLM Safety Alignment with Dual-Objective Optimization

abstract: Nonparametric contextual bandit is an important model of sequential decision making problems. Under $\alpha$-Tsybakov margin condition, existing research has established a regret bound of $\tilde{O}\left(T^{1-\frac{\alpha+1}{d+2}}\right)$ for bounded supports. However, the optimal regret with unbounded contexts has not been analyzed. The challenge of solving contextual bandit problems with unbounded support is to achieve both exploration-exploitation tradeoff and bias-variance tradeoff simultaneously. In this paper, we solve the nonparametric contextual bandit problem with unbounded contexts. We propose two nearest neighbor methods combined with UCB exploration. The first method uses a fixed $k$. Our analysis shows that this method achieves minimax optimal regret under a weak margin condition and relatively light-tailed context distributions. The second method uses adaptive $k$. By a proper data-driven selection of $k$, this method achieves an expected regret of $\tilde{O}\left(T^{1-\frac{(\alpha+1)\beta}{\alpha+(d+2)\beta}}+T^{1-\beta}\right)$, in which $\beta$ is a parameter describing the tail strength. This bound matches the minimax lower bound up to logarithm factors, indicating that the second method is approximately optimal.

paragraphs: Contextual bandits choose actions using observed context and learn from the rewards those actions produce. This paper studies the nonparametric setting when contexts can extend beyond any bounded region. Such distributions complicate learning because the method must balance action exploration with the accuracy of reward estimates in unevenly sampled parts of the context space.

The authors propose two methods that combine nearest-neighbor estimation with upper confidence bound exploration. One uses a fixed number of neighbors. The other selects that number adaptively from data. Choosing the neighborhood size controls a second tradeoff: using more observations can stabilize estimates, but incorporating less similar contexts can introduce bias.

The fixed-neighborhood method achieves minimax optimal regret under a weak margin condition and relatively light-tailed context distributions. The adaptive method has an expected regret bound depending on context dimension, the margin parameter, and tail strength. Its bound matches a minimax lower bound up to logarithmic factors. This establishes approximate optimality within the analyzed setting and clarifies how unbounded context distributions affect achievable learning performance.
summary.tldr: Nearest-neighbor bandit methods with confidence-based exploration achieve qualified optimality guarantees for context distributions with unbounded support.

title: Contextual Bandits for Unbounded Context Distributions

abstract: Current efforts in AI safety prioritize filtering harmful content, preventing manipulation of human behavior, and eliminating existential risks in cybersecurity or biosecurity. While pressing, this narrow focus overlooks critical human-centric considerations that shape the long-term trajectory of a society. In this position paper, we identify the risks of overlooking the impact of AI on the future of work and recommend comprehensive transition support towards the evolution of meaningful labor with human agency. Through the lens of economic theories, we highlight the intertemporal impacts of AI on human livelihood and the structural changes in labor markets that exacerbate income inequality. Additionally, the closed-source approach of major stakeholders in AI development resembles rent-seeking behavior through exploiting resources, breeding mediocrity in creative labor, and monopolizing innovation. To address this, we argue in favor of a robust international copyright anatomy supported by implementing collective licensing that ensures fair compensation mechanisms for using data to train AI models. We strongly recommend a pro-worker framework of global AI governance to enhance shared prosperity and economic justice while reducing technical debt.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that the future of work belongs within AI safety. The authors recognize concerns about harmful content, manipulation, and catastrophic misuse, but contend that these priorities leave important questions about livelihoods and human agency underexamined. They advocate transition support that helps meaningful work evolve as AI changes the economy.

Using economic theories, the paper considers how AI’s effects on livelihoods unfold over time and how changes in labor markets can worsen income inequality. It also criticizes the closed-source practices of major AI stakeholders as resembling rent seeking. In the authors’ account, these practices can exploit resources, weaken creative labor, and concentrate control over innovation.

The recommendations connect worker protection with the treatment of training data. The authors favor an international copyright framework and collective licensing to support fair compensation for data use. They also call for global AI governance oriented toward workers, shared prosperity, and economic justice. These are policy positions about how AI development should be governed, rather than evidence that a particular transition program has succeeded.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that AI safety should prioritize meaningful work, worker agency, and fair compensation for training-data use.

title: Position: AI Safety should prioritize the Future of Work

abstract: A digital twin (DT) is a virtual model of a real-world system that can assist decision-making by simulating scenarios induced by different policies. However, typical machine learning-based DTs do not optimise for this use case. We prove that, when model capacity is limited, training DTs to minimise one-step transition errors can produce suboptimal models for ranking sets of policies according to a reward function. We further show that this holds empirically, even with expressive model classes. To address this, we introduce DT$^2$, a decision-targeted DT training paradigm. Firstly, DT$^2$ uses fitted Q-evaluation to estimate values of candidate policies from offline data. A DT is then trained to generate rollouts that preserve pairwise policy rankings derived from these proxy ground-truth values with an architecture-agnostic loss function. We empirically demonstrate the efficacy of our method across a range of settings and architectures. DT$^2$ consistently improves policy ranking and reduces decision regret during policy selection relative to conventional DT training, both for policies used during training and for unseen policies, while maintaining a good level of raw simulation fidelity.

paragraphs: A digital twin can help choose policies by simulating their consequences, yet accurate prediction of individual transitions may not produce accurate policy rankings. This paper proves that mismatch can arise when model capacity is limited and observes it empirically even with expressive model classes. The training objective can therefore be poorly aligned with the decision the simulation is intended to support.

DT² trains digital twins directly to preserve policy rankings. It first uses fitted Q-evaluation on offline data to estimate candidate policy values. Those estimates serve as proxy ground truth, and an architecture-agnostic loss trains simulated rollouts to preserve the corresponding pairwise ordering of policies.

Across the evaluated settings and architectures, DT² improves policy ranking and reduces decision regret relative to conventional digital-twin training. The improvements hold for policies included during training and for unseen policies, while retaining good raw simulation fidelity. The approach makes the downstream choice explicit in training, using estimated policy comparisons to shape a simulator that is useful for selecting among alternatives.
summary.tldr: DT² trains digital twins to preserve estimated policy rankings, improving policy selection while maintaining good simulation fidelity.

title: $\textDT^\text2$: Decision-Targeted Digital Twins

abstract: Selective State Space Models (SSMs) such as Mamba have emerged as efficient alternatives to Transformers, achieving linear complexity through input-dependent parameterization. However, this selectivity transforms the system from linear time-invariant (LTI) to linear parameter-varying (LPV), where individually stable matrices can produce unbounded trajectories under switching. Existing work focuses on empirical performance, leaving global stability, robustness bounds, and practical certification unresolved. This paper develops a control-theoretic framework providing a comprehensive stability and robustness analysis for selective SSMs. We prove BIBO stability by viewing selective scans as continuous-time LTI sampling and establish two-term robustness bounds with linear growth in sequence length. For general LPV systems, we provide common quadratic Lyapunov function conditions and develop algorithms to extract certificate constants directly from network weights. These results bridge control theory and SSM architectures, providing verifiable certificates for individual selective-SSM layers as a step toward formal guarantees for deployment.

paragraphs: Mamba processes sequences efficiently by allowing its internal parameters to depend on the input. That flexibility complicates stability analysis: even when individual update matrices are stable, switching between them can produce an unbounded internal trajectory. The paper uses control theory to analyze the resulting system rather than inferring stability from successful empirical performance.

The authors interpret selective scans as samples of a continuous-time linear system and prove bounded-input, bounded-output stability. In plain language, bounded inputs lead to bounded outputs under the analyzed formulation. They also derive robustness bounds containing two terms that grow linearly with sequence length, quantifying how sensitivity can accumulate as sequences become longer.

For more general systems whose parameters vary, the paper supplies conditions based on a common quadratic Lyapunov function, a shared mathematical certificate of stability. Algorithms extract the relevant certificate constants directly from network weights. The resulting guarantees concern individual selective state-space layers, making them a concrete step toward verifiable deployment guarantees rather than a certification of an entire deployed model.
summary.tldr: A control-theoretic analysis provides stability proofs, robustness bounds, and weight-based certificates for individual selective state-space layers.

title: A Control-Theoretic View of Mamba on Stability and Robustness

abstract: Controlling the false discovery rate (FDR) under complex sparsity structures remains a fundamental challenge in large language model (LLM) analysis. Motivated by multiple comparison problems in LLMs, we consider a setting in which sparsity arises at the group level after a linear transformation of model parameters. We propose Split Group Knockoffs (SGKs), a general framework for group-wise variable selection under grouped transformational sparsity that extends the Split Knockoff procedure to grouped transformed variables. We establish theoretical guarantees for group-level FDR control and support recovery consistency, addressing challenges induced by group-wise penalties in transformed spaces. Applying SGK to LLM behavior auditing experiment reveals that model disagreement is not uniform across subjects, but instead concentrates in domains with greater semantic and reasoning complexity, where SGK effectively distinguishes genuine behavioral deviations from surface-level performance variation.

paragraphs: Split Group Knockoffs addresses variable selection when the relevant structure appears in groups after a linear transformation of model parameters. This setting arises in multiple-comparison problems motivated by language-model analysis. The statistical challenge is to identify meaningful groups while controlling how many selected groups are false discoveries.

The framework extends Split Knockoffs to grouped transformed variables. The authors establish theoretical guarantees for group-level false discovery rate control and support recovery consistency, addressing complications introduced by applying group penalties in transformed spaces. These results provide a formal basis for selecting structured groups in the setting studied.

An application to language-model behavior auditing finds that disagreement between models varies across subjects. It is concentrated in domains with greater semantic and reasoning complexity, where the method distinguishes genuine behavioral deviations from surface-level performance variation. The contribution connects a general structured-selection framework with an auditing task in which many apparent differences must be assessed together, making false discovery control central to interpreting the findings.
summary.tldr: Split Group Knockoffs provides theoretical false-discovery control for selecting transformed variable groups and applies it to language-model behavior auditing.

title: Split Group Knockoffs: Controlling False Discovery Rate in Transformational Group Sparsity

abstract: Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials (MLIPs) are becoming a central tool in simulation-based chemistry. However, like most deep learning models, MLIPs struggle to make accurate predictions on out-of-distribution data or when trained in a data-scarce regime, both common scenarios in simulation-based chemistry. Moreover, MLIPs do not provide uncertainty estimates by construction, which are fundamental to guide active learning pipelines and to ensure the accuracy of simulation results compared to quantum calculations. To address this shortcoming, we propose BLIPs: Bayesian Learned Interatomic Potentials. BLIP is a scalable, architecture-agnostic variational Bayesian framework for training or fine-tuning MLIPs, built on an adaptive version of Variational Dropout. BLIP delivers well-calibrated uncertainty estimates and minimal computational overhead for energy and forces prediction at inference time, while integrating seamlessly with (equivariant) message-passing architectures. Empirical results on simulation-based computational chemistry tasks demonstrate improved predictive accuracy with respect to standard MLIPs, and trustworthy uncertainty estimates, especially in data-scarse or heavy out-of-distribution regimes. Moreover, fine-tuning pretrained MLIPs with BLIP yields consistent performance gains and calibrated uncertainties.

paragraphs: Machine learning interatomic potentials predict energies and forces for chemistry simulations, but scarce training data and unfamiliar inputs can undermine their accuracy. Ordinary models also do not automatically provide uncertainty estimates. This matters because simulation workflows need to assess reliability and decide where additional quantum calculations would be useful.

BLIPs adds a scalable variational Bayesian framework to the training or fine-tuning of these potentials. Built around an adaptive version of variational dropout, the approach is designed to work across architectures, including equivariant message-passing networks. It supplies uncertainty estimates alongside energy and force predictions with minimal reported computational overhead at inference time.

Applying the framework to pretrained potentials also yields consistent performance gains and calibrated uncertainties. These findings make the contribution relevant both to building new potentials and to adding uncertainty-aware behavior to existing pretrained ones.
summary.tldr: BLIPs adds Bayesian training to interatomic potentials, improving reported accuracy and uncertainty calibration with little inference overhead.

title: BLIPs: Bayesian Learned Interatomic Potentials

abstract: Generations from large language models often fail to conform to desired constraints such as JSON schema. Existing locally constrained decoding (LCD) approaches enforce constraints by myopically masking out next tokens, resulting in biased sampling and degradation in performance. Recent work uses sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) methods to mitigate such biases, but designing effective proposal distributions or potential functions remains a key challenge. In this work, we propose a generic approach to construct proposals and potentials for SMC sampling from $p_{\mathrm{lm}}( \cdot \mid \mathrm{constraint})$. First, we show that constraints specified as finite automata can be tensorized for efficient execution on GPUs, which we use to construct globally constrained decoding (GCD) proposals. In addition, leveraging the fact that tensorized finite automata share the same circuit structure as hidden Markov models, we circuit-multiply them to obtain the probabilistic GCD (P-GCD) proposals encoding both logical and probabilistic information about the target distributions. We evaluate (P-)GCD on the tasks of function calling, keyword-based generation, and SQL generation. Experiments show that under the same SMC sampling setup, compared to LCD proposals, (P-)GCD converges faster to the target distribution with significantly fewer particles.

paragraphs: Enforcing an output constraint by masking invalid next tokens can distort a language model’s distribution over complete valid outputs. This paper targets sampling from the model’s distribution conditioned on satisfying the constraint. Sequential Monte Carlo can reduce the distortion, but its effectiveness depends on the proposals and potential functions used to guide candidate sequences.

The authors construct globally constrained decoding proposals from constraints represented as finite automata. They express those automata as tensor operations suitable for efficient GPU execution. They then exploit a shared circuit structure with hidden Markov models, combining the circuits to produce probabilistic globally constrained proposals. These incorporate both the logical requirements and probabilistic information about the desired output distribution.

Evaluations cover function calling, generation with keyword requirements, and SQL generation. Within the same sequential Monte Carlo setup, the proposed methods converge toward the target distribution faster and use significantly fewer particles than locally constrained proposals. The result concerns the quality and efficiency of constrained sampling: looking beyond immediate token legality gives the sampling process more useful guidance toward complete valid outputs.
summary.tldr: GPU-friendly global constraint proposals help sequential Monte Carlo sample valid language-model outputs with less bias and fewer particles.

title: Mitigating Bias in Locally Constrained Decoding via Tractable Proposals

abstract: The evaluation of large language models (LLMs) is increasingly performed by other LLMs, a setup commonly known as "LLM-as-a-judge", or autograders. While autograders offer a scalable alternative to human evaluation, they are not free from biases (e.g., favouring longer outputs or generations from their own model family). Here we propose a statistical framework based on Bayesian generalised linear models (GLMs) that enables researchers to address their primary research questions (e.g., LLM capability or risk assessment), while simultaneously identifying, quantifying and mitigating various biases in their autograders. Our approach can be applied to various evaluation formats (e.g., absolute scores or pairwise preferences) and augments traditional metrics (e.g., inter-rater agreement) by providing precise uncertainty estimates and clarifying sources of disagreement between graders. This framework also enables efficient counterfactual simulations without costly re-evaluation (e.g., assessing agreement after removing systematic biases). We demonstrate these capabilities through simulated examples, with all methods available in an open-source software package. Overall, we introduce a novel framework for autograder evaluation which allows researchers to detect, quantify and correct for various biases in a systematic way.

paragraphs: Using language models to grade other language models makes evaluation scalable, but graders can favor properties such as response length or their own model family. This paper proposes a statistical framework that examines those biases alongside the research question the evaluation was designed to answer, such as capability or risk.

The framework uses Bayesian generalized linear models and supports evaluation formats including absolute scores and pairwise preferences. It identifies and quantifies systematic grader effects while providing uncertainty estimates. This extends agreement-based summaries by helping explain why graders disagree and by supporting mitigation of modeled biases.

The fitted models also enable counterfactual simulations, such as estimating agreement after removing systematic bias, without paying for a fresh evaluation. The authors demonstrate these capabilities through simulated examples and provide the methods in an open-source package. The contribution is a systematic way to analyze autograder judgments together with their uncertainty and biases; the stated demonstrations establish these capabilities in simulation.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian statistical framework quantifies and corrects modeled LLM-grader biases while estimating uncertainty and simulating counterfactual evaluations.

title: Quantifying Biases in LLM-as-a-Judge Evaluations

abstract: In modern machine learning, parallelization of training is an important strategy for increasing scale. Asynchronous stochastic gradient descent (ASGD), which maximally utilizes available hardware, avoids having to wait for slow workers. However, with constant step sizes, the convergence of ASGD is nonetheless negatively effected by slow workers due to large delays in updates. At the same time, it has been empirically observed in asynchronous training of deep learning models that gradient clipping “stabilizes” training. In this work, we provide a theoretical justification for this behavior, as we show that clipping removes the dependence of the maximum delay in the oracle complexity. We employ a sub-Weibull model of gradient noise which generalize sub-Gaussian and sub-exponential disitributions to more heavy-tailed distributions, motivated by empirical observations in deep learning. We show convergence in expectation, and for the first time in asynchronous optimization, convergence with high probability.

At the same time, it has been empirically observed in asynchronous training of deep learning models that gradient clipping “stabilizes” training. paragraphs: Asynchronous stochastic gradient descent lets parallel workers contribute updates without waiting for the slowest worker. This improves hardware utilization, but some updates arrive after the model has already changed substantially. With a constant step size, these delays can still damage convergence even though they no longer hold up every other worker.

The paper gives a theoretical explanation for the observed stabilizing effect of gradient clipping in asynchronous training. Clipping limits the magnitude of updates. In the authors' analysis, it removes dependence on the maximum update delay from oracle complexity, the measure of how many gradient evaluations are required to reach the target optimization accuracy.

The guarantees use a sub-Weibull model of gradient noise, a family broad enough to include sub-Gaussian, sub-exponential, and heavier-tailed behavior. Under this model, the authors establish convergence both in expectation and with high probability, reporting the latter as a first for asynchronous optimization. The result explains a specific form of robustness to stragglers: the worst delay no longer appears in the stated oracle-complexity dependence.
summary.tldr: Under a sub-Weibull gradient-noise model, clipping removes maximum-delay dependence from asynchronous SGD's oracle complexity and enables high-probability convergence guarantees.

title: Clipping Makes Distributed and Federated Asynchronous SGD Robust to Stragglers

abstract: It is infeasible to encompass all possible disturbances within the training dataset. This raises a critical question regarding the robustness of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models when encountering unseen real-world visual disturbances, particularly under imperfect visual conditions. In this work, we conduct a systematic study based on recent state-of-the-art VLA models and reveal a significant performance drop when visual disturbances absent from the training data are introduced. To mitigate this issue, we propose a lightweight adapter module grounded in information theory, termed the Information Bottleneck Adapter (IB-Adapter), which selectively filters potential noise from visual inputs. Without requiring any extra data or augmentation strategies, IB-Adapter consistently improves over the baseline by an average of 30%, while adding fewer than 10M parameters, demonstrating notable efficiency and effectiveness. Furthermore, even with a 14x smaller backbone (0.5B parameters) and no pre-training on the Open X-Embodiment dataset, our model StableVLA achieves robustness competitive with 7B-scale state-of-the-art VLAs. With negligible parameter overhead ($<$10M), our approach maintains accuracy on long-horizon tasks and surpasses OpenPi under real-world visual disturbances. The code will be made publicly available.

abstract: Existing quantization methods are fundamentally limited by rigid, integer-based bit-widths (e.g., 2, 3-bit), resulting in a "deployment gap" where Large Language Models cannot be optimally fitted to specific memory budgets. To bridge this gap, we introduce LiftQuant, a novel framework that enables continuous bit-width control for true Pareto-optimal deployment. The core innovation is a "lift-then-project" mechanism which approximates low-dimensional weight vectors by projecting a simple 1-bit lattice from a higher-dimensional “lifted" space. Crucially, the effective bit-width is determined simply by the ratio of the lifted dimension to the original dimension, which allows the bit-width to be tuned quasi-continuous as the dimension is a flexible structural parameter. This projection generates a structured yet non-uniform codebook, capturing the expressive power of Vector Quantization (VQ). While beneficial over VQ, LiftQuant’s decoding path relies solely on linear transformations and 1-bit uniform quantizers, retaining hardware-friendly nature. This flexibility is transformative: LiftQuant enables a 70B LLM to be compressed to 2.4 bits to precisely fit a 24GB GPU, where its performance significantly surpasses state-of-the-art 2-bit models fitted on the same device. Our code and ckpt is available at https://github.com/Heliulu/LiftQuant.

LiftQuant introduces finer control over effective bit width through a lift-then-project representation of weight vectors.

The method represents low-dimensional weights by projecting a one-bit lattice from a higher-dimensional space. The ratio between the lifted and original dimensions determines the effective bit width, so changing that structural ratio enables quasi-continuous precision choices.
