Its decoding operations remain linear transformations and uniform one-bit quantizers, maintaining a hardware-friendly structure.

The reported deployment example compresses a 70-billion-parameter language model to 2.4 bits so that it fits a 24 GB GPU. On that device, it substantially outperforms state-of-the-art two-bit models. This demonstrates the practical value of using more of a specific memory budget: intermediate effective precision can preserve additional model performance while still meeting a hard deployment constraint.
summary.tldr: LiftQuant uses dimensional lifting and projection to tune effective weight precision more finely and fit language models to specific memory budgets.

title: LiftQuant: Continuous Bit-Width LLM via Dimensional Lifting and Projection

abstract: Process Reward Models (PRMs) enhance reasoning ability of LLMs by providing step-level supervision. However, their widespread adoption is limited due to expensive manual step-level annotation and poor generalization of static training data to novel errors. We introduce Adversarially Trained PRMs (APRM), where a Generator ($G$) learns to produce reasoning errors to deceive a PRM ($R$), while $R$ concurrently learns to detect them. This interaction yields progressively harder negatives for $R$, improving it’s robustness and generalization to novel errors without requiring manual step-level labels. Averaged across diverse mathematical reasoning benchmarks, APRM improves solver accuracy by $+3.4$ percentage points (pp) over the strongest PRM baseline. APRM achieves gains of $+5.3$ pp on out-of-distribution tasks.

paragraphs: Process reward models assess individual reasoning steps, providing supervision that can help language models solve problems. Building these evaluators is difficult because manually labeling intermediate steps is expensive. A fixed collection of training errors can also leave an evaluator poorly prepared for unfamiliar mistakes encountered later.

The paper proposes training the evaluator together with a generator that tries to fool it. The generator learns to introduce reasoning errors that escape detection, while the reward model learns to recognize those errors. As the two improve, the generator supplies progressively harder negative examples. This creates an evolving source of training challenges without requiring manual step-level labels.

Across the mathematical reasoning benchmarks studied, the resulting reward models improve solver accuracy by an average of 3.4 percentage points over the strongest process-reward baseline. The reported gain on out-of-distribution tasks is 5.3 percentage points. These results support the value of continually adapting the errors used in training: the benefit appears in the solver’s final accuracy, not only in the evaluator’s ability to detect mistakes.
summary.tldr: Training a reasoning-error generator against a process reward model improves mathematical solver accuracy without manual step-level labels.

title: Adversarial Training for Process Reward Models

abstract: Recent advances in end-to-end, multi-task robot policies based on transformer models have demonstrated impressive generalization to real-world embodied navigation tasks. Trained on vast datasets of simulated and real-world trajectories, these policies map multimodal observations directly to action sequences for physical execution. Despite promising real-world capabilities, these models are still data-driven and, therefore, lack explicit notions of behavioral correctness. We address this gap by introducing SafeDec, a constrained decoding framework for autoregressive, transformer-based robot navigation policies that enforces safety specifications expressed as Signal Temporal Logic (STL) formulas. Our method ensures that generated actions provably satisfy STL specifications under assumed dynamics at runtime without retraining while remaining agnostic of the underlying policy. We evaluate SafeDec on tasks from the CHORES benchmark for state-of-the-art embodied navigation policies across hundreds of procedurally generated environments and show that our decoding-time interventions are useful not only for filtering unsafe actions but also for conditional action generation. Videos are available at constrained-robot-fms.github.io.

paragraphs: Transformer-based navigation policies can generate actions directly from multimodal observations, but learning from trajectories does not itself give them explicit behavioral correctness rules. SafeDec adds such rules at decoding time, when an autoregressive policy constructs its action sequence. It operates without retraining the underlying policy.

Safety requirements are expressed in Signal Temporal Logic, a formal language for specifications involving signals over time. SafeDec constrains generated actions so that they provably satisfy those specifications under the assumed dynamics. That qualification matters: the guarantee is tied to the dynamics used by the framework, rather than being an unconditional claim about every physical execution.

The authors evaluate SafeDec with state-of-the-art navigation policies on CHORES tasks across hundreds of procedurally generated environments. Their results show that decoding interventions can support conditional action generation as well as filter unsafe actions. The contribution is a policy-agnostic way to connect explicit temporal specifications to action generation, bringing formal constraints into deployment without changing how the original navigation model was trained.
summary.tldr: SafeDec constrains robot-policy decoding to provably satisfy temporal safety specifications under assumed dynamics, without retraining.

title: SafeDec: Constrained Decoding for Safe Autoregressive Generalist Robot Navigation Policies

abstract: Language Models (LMs) have shown remarkable potential as role-playing chatbots, delivering consistent, stylized interactions when given a specification of a character or user persona. However, applying these capabilities to real-world applications (e.g., ecosystems with numerous NPCs interacting simultaneously) exposes a critical inefficiency due to the excessive computational cost. In this paper, we question the necessity of dedicating a full, generalist model to a single persona, hypothesizing that a specific character identity relies on only a fraction of the model’s total capacity. We observe that naïvely pruning LMs often severely degrades the role-playing performance for a specific persona; it does not distinguish between redundant knowledge and essential character traits. We propose Persona-Pruner, a framework that sculpts a lightweight role-playing model by isolating persona-specific sub-networks from a single description. Our experiments consistently show that Persona-Pruner preserves role-playing performance substantially more effectively than existing state-of-the-art LLM pruning techniques, reducing the performance drop from the dense model by up to 93.8% over the strongest baseline on RoleBench in LLM-as-a-judge score, while still maintaining general LLM capabilities. Code is available at https://github.com/jsu-kim/Persona-Pruner.

paragraphs: Running a full general-purpose language model for every character can be expensive, especially when many characters interact at once. Persona-Pruner investigates whether a particular persona can be supported by a smaller portion of a model's capacity. Ordinary pruning is problematic because it can remove abilities essential to maintaining that character's identity and style.

The framework uses a single persona description to isolate a subnetwork suited to that role. Its purpose is to distinguish capacity that can be removed from capacity important to the specified character. This makes the target persona part of the pruning objective, aligning compression with the behavior the resulting model is expected to preserve.

Experiments report stronger preservation of role-playing performance than existing pruning methods while maintaining general language-model capabilities. On RoleBench, Persona-Pruner reduces the performance loss relative to the dense model by up to 93.8% compared with the strongest baseline, measured using a language-model judge. That figure describes a reduction in performance degradation, not a model-size reduction. The findings support persona-specific pruning as a route to lighter character models.
summary.tldr: Persona-Pruner uses a character description to extract a smaller subnetwork that better preserves the model's role-playing performance.

title: Persona-Pruner: Sculpting Lightweight Models for Role-Playing

abstract: Sparse Mixture of Experts (MoE) models scale more efficiently than dense models by routing tokens to modular expert networks that are only active when relevant to the task. A leading hypothesis for the performance of MoE models is that each expert specialises in a single, coherent domain. However, interpretability efforts that assume this hypothesis have generally been unsuccessful. We propose and present evidence for an alternative account that we call the Superposed Specialisation Hypothesis (SSH): experts specialise in a disjoint union of fine-grained features rather than one broad domain. Leveraging the SSH, we introduce RouterInterp, a method for interpreting expert routing that identifies Sparse Autoencoder features most predictive of routing decisions and produces unified natural language explanations. On gpt-oss-20b, RouterInterp explains expert routing with 57% higher detection accuracy than prior token statistics based methods. This work provides a scalable method for generating concise and more accurate explanations of expert routing and increases our understanding of a previously uninterpretable component of foundation models.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts models route tokens to selected expert networks, making routing an important part of how their computation is organized. A common explanation is that each expert specializes in one broad, coherent domain. This paper presents evidence for a different account: an expert can specialize in several distinct, fine-grained features.

The authors call this the Superposed Specialisation Hypothesis and use it to build RouterInterp. The method finds sparse-autoencoder features that best predict routing decisions, then combines them into concise natural-language explanations. This shifts the interpretation target from assigning each expert one domain label to describing the collection of features associated with its selection.

On gpt-oss-20b, RouterInterp achieves 57% higher detection accuracy than previous methods based on token statistics. The result supports the usefulness of feature-based routing explanations in that model and provides evidence for the proposed specialization account. The broader contribution is a scalable method for explaining expert selection while accommodating more varied specialization than a single-domain description allows.
summary.tldr: RouterInterp explains expert routing through collections of fine-grained features, improving detection accuracy over token-statistics methods.

title: RouterInterp: Understanding Superposed Specialisation in Mixture of Experts Routing

abstract: Step-level caching accelerates diffusion models by exploiting temporal redundancy across denoising steps. Existing methods make per-step cache decisions using threshold-based heuristics, without directly optimizing for final output quality. As a result, their inference latency varies across inputs and is difficult to control at deployment. In this work, we propose BudCache, which inverts this formulation: rather than letting per-step error thresholds dictate the runtime cost, we fix the compute budget in advance and search for the cache policy that best preserves the final output. To tackle the combinatorial complexity of step selection, we combine Simulated Annealing with deterministic Hill Climbing. This offline search identifies high-quality cache policies within minutes and introduces no online search or thresholding overhead during inference. When the compute budget is very tight, we further introduce cache-aware schedule alignment, which adapts the time discretization to the selected cache policy to reduce cache-induced trajectory mismatch. Experiments on FLUX.1-dev and Wan2.1 show that BudCache achieves better generation quality than heuristic caching baselines under the same inference budgets.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can save computation by reusing information across denoising steps. Existing caching methods often decide whether to reuse it by comparing a per-step error with a threshold. This makes runtime depend on the input and does not directly optimize the quality of the finished output. BudCache instead starts with a fixed compute budget and searches for the best caching policy within it.

Choosing which steps should reuse cached information creates a large combinatorial search problem. BudCache combines simulated annealing with deterministic hill climbing to find useful policies offline within minutes. Inference then follows the selected policy without online search or thresholding overhead. This separates the work of selecting a policy from the cost of generating each output.

For especially tight budgets, the method also adjusts the denoising time discretization to fit the chosen cache policy, reducing mismatches in the generation trajectory caused by caching. Experiments on FLUX.1-dev and Wan2.1 report better generation quality than heuristic caching methods at the same inference budgets. The result supports directly optimizing final quality under a preset resource constraint.
summary.tldr: BudCache searches offline for diffusion caching policies that preserve output quality under a fixed compute budget.

title: Budget-Constrained Step-Level Diffusion Caching

abstract: Diffusion and flow policies are gaining prominence in online reinforcement learning (RL) due to their expressive power, yet training them efficiently remains a critical challenge. A fundamental difficulty that distinguishes online RL from standard generative modeling is the lack of direct samples from the target Boltzmann distribution defined by the Q-function. To address this, two seemingly distinct families of methods have been proposed for diffusion policies: a noise-expectation family, which uses a weighted average of noise as the training target, and a gradient-expectation family, which employs a weighted average of Q-function gradients. However, it remains unclear how these objectives are formally related, or whether they can be synthesized into a more general formulation. In this paper, we propose a unified framework, reverse flow matching (RFM), which rigorously addresses the problem of training diffusion and flow models without direct target samples. By adopting a reverse inferential perspective, we formulate the training target as a posterior mean estimation problem given an intermediate noisy sample. Crucially, we introduce Langevin Stein operators to construct zero-mean control variates, deriving a general class of estimators that share the same expectation. We show that existing noise-expectation and gradient-expectation methods are simply two specific instances within this broader class. This unified view yields two key advancements: it extends the capability of targeting Boltzmann distributions from diffusion to flow policies, and it enables the principled combination of Q-value and Q-gradient information to form an effective estimator, thereby improving training efficiency and stability. We instantiate RFM to train a flow policy in online RL and demonstrate improved performance on continuous-control benchmarks compared to diffusion policy baselines.

Existing diffusion-policy methods address this using either weighted noise averages or weighted Q-gradient averages. Reverse flow matching explains how these apparently different training targets fit together.

It uses Langevin Stein operators to construct zero-mean control variates: adjustments that preserve an estimator's expectation. This produces a broader family of estimators containing both existing noise-expectation and gradient-expectation approaches as special cases.

The authors report that this combination improves training efficiency and stability. They instantiate the approach with a flow policy and show improved continuous-control performance relative to diffusion-policy baselines. Its contribution is both conceptual and practical: a common estimation framework clarifies existing objectives and supports a new way to train expressive policies without direct target samples.
summary.tldr: Reverse flow matching unifies diffusion-policy training objectives and combines Q-value and Q-gradient information to train flow policies without direct target samples.

title: Reverse Flow Matching: A Unified Framework for Online Reinforcement Learning with Diffusion and Flow Policies

abstract: Interpretable machine learning requires models that are accurate and structurally faithful to the data. Existing explainability methods rely heavily on additive representations (e.g., Generalized Additive Models (GAMs), SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), functional ANOVA), which can suffer from signal cancellation and off-support extrapolation in the presence of strong interactions. We propose Tensor Separation Learning (TSL), a regression model that learns a sum of rank-1 products of univariate per-feature functions via a stagewise greedy procedure with orthogonal refitting. By enforcing separability, TSL avoids the information loss inherent in additive projections caused by marginalizing higher-order interactions. The learned TSL model can be fully reconstructed from first-order partial dependence functions, up to constant factors. This stage-wise correspondence ensures that the resulting visualizations are faithful to the fitted components. We establish approximation-rate guarantees for functions with bounded mixed $p$-th order partial derivatives and demonstrate that TSL competes with black-box models on regression benchmarks.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to make regression models interpretable when features interact strongly. Explanations based on additive effects can lose information through cancellation or evaluate combinations outside the data's support. The proposed Tensor Separation Learning model instead represents predictions as a sum of products, with each product assembled from functions of individual features.

Those products preserve a structured way for features to interact while keeping their individual functions available for inspection. The model is built through a stagewise greedy procedure with orthogonal refitting. A central result is that first-order partial dependence functions can reconstruct the learned model up to constant factors. The correspondence holds stage by stage, making the resulting visualizations faithful to the fitted components.

The paper also establishes approximation-rate guarantees for functions whose mixed partial derivatives of the specified order are bounded. That condition defines the scope of the theoretical result. Regression experiments show performance competitive with black-box models. Together, the findings support separability as a route to combining interaction modeling with explanations that retain the structure of the fitted predictor.
summary.tldr: Tensor Separation Learning models feature interactions through separable products while supporting faithful reconstruction from first-order partial dependence functions.

title: Beyond Additive Decompositions: Interpretability Through Separability

abstract: Autoregressive Models (ARMs) have long dominated the landscape of Large Language Models. Recently, a new paradigm has emerged in the form of diffusion-based Large Language Models (dLLMs), which generate text by iteratively denoising masked segments. This approach has shown significant advantages and potential. However, dLLMs suffer from high inference latency. Traditional ARM acceleration techniques, such as Key-Value caching, are incompatible with dLLMs due to their bidirectional attention mechanism. To address this specific challenge, our work begins with a key observation that dLLM inference involves a static prompt and a partially dynamic response, where most tokens remain stable across adjacent denoising steps. Based on this, we propose dLLM-Cache, a training-free adaptive caching framework that combines long-interval prompt caching with partial response updates guided by feature similarity. This design enables efficient reuse of intermediate computations without compromising model performance. Extensive experiments on representative dLLMs, including LLaDA 8B and Dream 7B, show that dLLM-Cache achieves up to 9.1$\times$ FLOPs reduction on LongBench-HotpotQA while maintaining competitive output quality. Notably, our method brings dLLM inference latency close to that of ARMs under many settings. The code for this work is publicly available at: https://github.com/maomaocun/dLLM-cache.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models generate text through repeated denoising of masked segments. Their bidirectional attention makes conventional autoregressive key-value caching incompatible with this process, contributing to high inference latency. This paper identifies a different opportunity for reuse: the prompt stays fixed, and most response tokens remain stable between neighboring denoising steps.

dLLM-Cache uses that stability in a training-free caching framework. It retains prompt computations over longer intervals and updates only selected response computations, guided by feature similarity. This separates the relatively static prompt from the partially changing response, allowing the system to reuse intermediate work while still responding to changes during generation.

Experiments include LLaDA 8B and Dream 7B. On LongBench-HotpotQA, the method achieves up to a 9.1-fold reduction in floating-point operations while maintaining competitive output quality. The authors also report inference latency approaching that of autoregressive models in many settings. The computation reduction and latency finding are distinct results: together, they show how adaptive reuse can reduce the practical cost of iterative text generation.
summary.tldr: dLLM-Cache reuses stable prompt and response computations to accelerate diffusion language models without additional training.

title: dLLM-Cache: Accelerating Diffusion Large Language Models with Adaptive Caching

abstract: In the big-world regime, agents cannot be universally capable and their ability is inevitably specialized across a world model in pieces. Consequently, standard uniform guarantees fail to distinguish between the understanding of critical bottlenecks and irrelevant failures. We first formalize this limitation by proving that general agents are not universal, rendering standard worst-case analysis uninformative. To overcome this, we introduce structural certification, a transition-local framework that maps bounded goal-conditioned performance to entry-wise guarantees on the agent’s internal world model. Our main contribution is constructive. We provide algorithms that filter specific transitions using deep compositional goals and prove that a general agent on these goals has a structural world model with a $\mathcal{O}(1/n)+\mathcal{O}(\delta)$ error bound. Conversely, this bound is tight in the small-$\delta$ regime, whose existence is explicitly guaranteed by our certification. These results enable the certifiable deployment of general agents by localizing the specific transitions where long-horizon planning is reliable.

A uniform worst-case guarantee can obscure whether the agent understands transitions crucial to a goal or fails on irrelevant parts of the environment. This paper formalizes that limitation by proving that general agents are not universal in the big-world regime.

Structural certification evaluates the internal world model transition by transition. It connects bounded goal-conditioned performance with guarantees on individual entries of that model. Constructive algorithms use deep compositional goals to filter specific transitions, allowing behavioral performance to provide localized evidence about the agent’s understanding of the world.

For an agent general on those goals, the authors prove a structural world-model error bound of O(1/n) + O(δ). They also establish tightness in a small-δ regime whose existence the certification guarantees. These results identify particular transitions where long-horizon planning is reliable, giving certification a more selective role than an all-purpose competence claim. The practical significance is the ability to distinguish reliable pieces of a world model from failures elsewhere.
summary.tldr: Structural certification translates goal-conditioned performance into local world-model guarantees that identify transitions supporting reliable long-horizon planning.

title: World Models in Pieces: Structural Certification for General Agents

abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) suffers from severe accuracy degradation in ultra-low-bit regimes. To address this challenge, we propose SHARP-Q, a unified framework grounded in Information Geometry that aligns the quantization objective with the intrinsic Fisher geometry. Following a "Rectify-then-Approximate" strategy, SHARP-Q first preconditions the optimization landscape via Hessian-Aware Rectification (HAR) and subsequently approximates the rectified Fisher Information Matrix through Dynamic Fisher-Subspace Compensation (DFSC). Our empirical evaluations reveal a pivotal insight: precise geometric alignment enables hardware-friendly uniform quantizers to outperform specialized non-uniform designs. Extensive experiments across representative convolutional networks, Vision Transformers, and State Space Models confirm that SHARP-Q establishes new state-of-the-art results, achieving substantial accuracy gains in the challenging W2A2 and W3A3 settings.

paragraphs: Post-training quantization reduces numerical precision in an already trained model, but very low bit widths can sharply reduce accuracy. SHARP-Q addresses this by aligning the quantization objective with Fisher information geometry. The approach makes the model's geometric sensitivity central to how quantization is optimized.

The order is central to the framework: the geometric approximation operates on a landscape that has already been adjusted, rather than treating these as unrelated corrections.

The authors report new state-of-the-art results and find that geometrically aligned uniform quantizers can outperform specialized non-uniform designs. That empirical finding suggests that improving the optimization geometry can make hardware-friendly quantization competitive even in demanding low-precision regimes.
summary.tldr: SHARP-Q improves ultra-low-bit post-training quantization by rectifying and approximating the model's Fisher geometry.

title: SHARP-Q: Spectral Hessian Alignment and Rectification for Post-training Quantization

abstract: Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) aims to reverse-engineer model behaviors by identifying functional sub-networks. Yet, the scientific validity of these findings depends on their stability. In this work, we argue that circuit discovery is not a standalone task but a statistical estimation problem built upon causal mediation analysis (CMA). We uncover a fundamental instability at this base layer: exact, single-input CMA scores exhibit high intrinsic variance, implying that the causal effect of a component is a volatile random variable rather than a fixed property. We then demonstrate that circuit discovery pipelines inherit this variance and further amplify it. Fast approximation methods, such as Edge Attribution Patching and its successors, introduce additional estimation noise, while aggregating these noisy scores over datasets leads to fragile structural estimates. Consequently, small perturbations in input data or hyperparameters yield vastly different circuits. We systematically decompose these sources of variance and advocate for more rigorous MI practices, prioritizing statistical robustness and routine reporting of stability metrics.

paragraphs: Mechanistic interpretability seeks subnetworks, often called circuits, that explain a model’s behavior. This paper argues that discovering a circuit should be treated as statistical estimation. A circuit’s scientific usefulness depends partly on whether it remains stable when the data or analysis choices change.

The authors trace instability to causal mediation analysis, which underlies component-effect measurements. Even exact scores for individual inputs have high intrinsic variance, meaning that a component’s measured causal effect varies substantially with the input. Circuit discovery then inherits this variation. Fast approximations such as Edge Attribution Patching add estimation noise, and aggregation across a dataset can produce fragile structural estimates.

The analysis shows that small changes to inputs or hyperparameters can yield very different circuits. By decomposing the sources of variance, the paper explains how uncertainty at the level of individual causal scores can propagate into uncertainty about an entire subnetwork. It advocates routine stability reporting and stronger statistical robustness practices so that circuit findings can be assessed as estimates with variability.
summary.tldr: Circuit discovery inherits and amplifies variable causal-effect estimates, motivating routine statistical stability checks in mechanistic interpretability.

title: Mechanistic Interpretability as Statistical Estimation: A Variance Analysis

abstract: Foundation models have revolutionized AI, but adapting them efficiently for multimodal tasks, particularly in dual-stream architectures composed of unimodal encoders, such as DINO and BERT, remains a significant challenge. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods like Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) enable lightweight adaptation, yet they operate in isolation within each modality, limiting their ability in capturing cross-modal interactions. In this paper, we take a step in bridging this gap with Cross-Modal Low-Rank Adaptation (CoLA), a novel PEFT framework that extends LoRA by introducing a dedicated inter-modal adaptation pathway alongside the standard intra-modal one. This dual-path design enables CoLA to adapt unimodal foundation models to multimodal tasks effectively, without interference between modality-specific and cross-modal learning. We evaluate CoLA across a range of vision-language (RefCOCO, RefCOCO+, RefCOCOg) and audio-visual (AVE, AVS) benchmarks, where it consistently outperforms LORA, achieving a relative gain of around 3% and 2%, respectively, while maintaining parameter efficiency. Notably, CoLA enables the first multi-task PEFT framework for visual grounding, bridging a key gap in efficient multimodal adaptation. Code is available at https://github.com/peterwisu/CoLA

paragraphs: Combining separate image, language, or audio encoders requires learning how their information fits together. Standard low-rank adaptation, or LoRA, provides an economical way to adapt individual models, but its updates operate separately within each modality. The paper argues that this separation limits the cross-modal relationships learned when adapting dual-stream systems.

CoLA adds a dedicated adaptation pathway between modalities alongside the usual pathway within each modality. This gives modality-specific learning and cross-modal learning their own routes, with the stated aim of avoiding interference between them. The approach retains parameter-efficient adaptation while explicitly addressing the interactions needed for multimodal downstream tasks.

On the evaluated vision-language and audio-visual benchmarks, CoLA consistently exceeds LoRA's performance, with relative gains of around 3% and 2%, respectively. The authors also report the first multi-task parameter-efficient fine-tuning framework for visual grounding. Together, these findings suggest that efficient multimodal adaptation benefits from allocating capacity to relationships between encoders, as well as to adjustments inside each encoder.
summary.tldr: CoLA extends LoRA with a separate cross-modal adaptation pathway, improving multimodal tasks while retaining parameter efficiency.

title: CoLA: Cross-Modal Low-rank Adaptation for Multimodal Downstream Tasks

abstract: Diffusion inversion, which maps images back to the Gaussian latent space of a diffusion model, is a critical task for image reconstruction and editing. While DDIM enables fast deterministic inversion, it inherently introduces deviations that accumulate into noticeable inversion errors. Existing methods often address this by solving a fixed-point problem but largely overlook how the selection of the diffusion timestep in the noise scheduler influences inversion fidelity. In this work, we reveal that the deviation scale in diffusion inversion is strongly dependent on the timestep size, and exhibits a parabolic trend, with larger errors concentrated at both small and large timesteps. Based on this finding, we propose a simple yet effective nonuniform timestep scheduler that integrates a global rescaling with a local dynamic programming based rescheduling, enabling a strategic allocation of computational effort that minimizes the overall inversion error and preserves higher inversion accuracy. Our method serves as an off-the-shelf enhancement for existing inversion techniques and requires no extra parameters or computational overhead. Through extensive experiments, we verify that integrating our scheduler consistently boosts the performance of existing inversion methods, achieving superior results in image reconstruction and editing.

title: Timestep Rescheduling in Diffusion Inversion

abstract: Continuous Normalizing Flows (CNFs) enable elegant generative modeling but remain bottlenecked by their iterative nature requiring costly sampling and lacking interpretability of the intermediate states. Recent approaches accelerate sampling by straightening trajectories or distilling endpoints, yet they treat the original generative process as a black box, discarding the teacher’s intermediate dynamics. We propose a fundamentally different perspective: globally linearizing flow dynamics via Koopman theory to achieve trajectory-preserving linearization. By lifting Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) into a higher-dimensional Koopman space, we represent its evolution with a single linear operator. Crucially, unlike boundary-only distillation, our method enforces infinitesimal consistency with the teacher’s vector field along the full generative path. We derive a practical, simulation-free training objective that ensures this global alignment and yields two key benefits. First, sampling becomes one-step and parallelizable. Second, because the linearization is faithful to the dynamics, the Koopman operator provides unique insights on the generation. We demonstrate that this structure enables novel applications unavailable in prior approaches, including discovery of semantically coherent editing directions, inversion with a teacher-aligned linear operator and class-conditional spectral signatures. Empirically, our approach achieves competitive sample quality, while enabling spectral analysis and control of the entire trajectories of generative flows.

title: Unfolding Generative Flows with Koopman Operators: Trajectory-Preserving Linearization

abstract: The impressive performance of generalist large language models (LLMs) such as GPT and Claude in healthcare raises a critical question: will domain-specific medical specialist models become obsolete? We argue that the future of medical artificial intelligence (AI) lies not in building monolithic medical foundation models, nor in replacing human expertise, but in orchestrating collaboration among generalist LLMs, domain-specific specialist models, and clinicians. We propose HetMedAgent, a heterogeneous medical multi-agent framework that enables conflict-aware evidence fusion, uncertainty-based clinician intervention triggering, and adaptive threshold calibration. Experiments on three real-world clinical decision-making tasks demonstrate that the synergy between generalist LLMs and domain-specific specialist models significantly outperforms using either type of model alone, validating the irreplaceable value of specialist models in modality-specific analysis. HetMedAgent represents a shift from building medical LLMs or foundation models to multi-agent collaboration, achieving a balance between general reasoning capabilities and domain-specific precision.

paragraphs: This paper asks what role medical specialist models should retain as general-purpose language models become more capable in healthcare. Its proposed answer is collaboration among generalist models, domain-specific models, and clinicians. The authors argue that broad reasoning ability and specialized analysis offer complementary strengths that a medical AI system should coordinate.

HetMedAgent implements that idea through a heterogeneous multi-agent framework. It combines evidence while accounting for conflicts, uses uncertainty to trigger clinician intervention, and adaptively calibrates thresholds. The authors interpret this as evidence for the continuing value of specialists in modality-specific analysis. The stated findings support the collaborative architecture in the evaluated tasks, showing that general reasoning and domain-specific precision can contribute jointly. They also make clinician participation part of the proposed workflow rather than treating model collaboration as a replacement for expertise.
summary.tldr: HetMedAgent combines generalist models, medical specialists, and clinician intervention, outperforming either model type alone on three clinical tasks.

title: Why Specialist Models Still Matter: A Heterogeneous Multi-Agent Paradigm for Medical Artificial Intelligence

abstract: Following the rise of large foundation models, Vision–Language–Action models (VLAs) emerged, leveraging strong visual and language understanding from Vision-Language Models for general-purpose policy learning. Yet, the current VLA landscape remains fragmented and exploratory. Although many groups have proposed their own VLA models, inconsistencies in training protocols and evaluation settings make it difficult to identify which design choices truly matter. To bring structure to this evolving space, we reexamine the VLA design space under a unified framework and evaluation setup. Starting from a simple VLA baseline similar to RT-2, which is the origin of VLA, we systematically dissect design choices along three dimensions: foundational components, perception essentials, and action modelling perspectives. From this study, we distill 12 key findings that together form a practical recipe for building strong VLA models. The outcome of this exploration is a simple yet effective model, VLANeXt. It outperforms the state-of-the-art methods on the LIBERO and LIBERO-plus benchmarks and demonstrates strong performance in real-world experiments. We release a unified and easy-to-use codebase to reproduce our findings, explore the design space, and develop new VLA variants on top of a shared foundation. The codebase is available at https://github.com/DravenALG/VLANeXt.

abstract: Language models are increasingly used not only as standalone predictors but also as components in larger inference systems, from test-time scaling to multi-agent collaboration. We study language model networks, where pre-trained language models serve as reusable nodes and intelligence emerges from their topology, communication, and optimization. Existing systems mostly communicate through natural language: easy to deploy, but discrete, inefficient, and hard to optimize from end-task supervision. We propose LMNet, a dense and differentiable realization of this paradigm. LMNet uses stripped LLMs as vertex modules and trainable seq2seq modules as communication edges, enabling intermediate nodes to exchange dense vectors while preserving natural-language input and output at the system boundary. By bypassing intermediate embedding and de-embedding, LMNet enables efficient information transfer, end-to-end gradient optimization, and learned communication beyond hand-designed protocols. Experiments show performance with small additional training cost and effective adaptation under limited supervision.

paragraphs: When several language models work together, they commonly communicate by generating text for one another. This is convenient, but the discrete messages can make information transfer inefficient and complicate optimization from the final task’s supervision. LMNet explores a network in which pretrained language models are reusable computational nodes connected by learned communication modules.

Bypassing intermediate embedding and de-embedding makes the internal communication differentiable and supports end-to-end gradient optimization.

The approach allows communication itself to be learned rather than fully specified through hand-designed protocols. The reported experiments show effective adaptation with limited supervision and a small additional training cost. The broader contribution is an architecture for treating model collaboration as a trainable network: its internal connections can carry learned representations while the user still interacts through ordinary language.
summary.tldr: LMNet connects language models through trainable dense-vector communication, enabling end-to-end adaptation with limited supervision.

title: Language Model Networks: Supervision-Efficient Learning through Dense Communication

abstract: Recent advances in Large Reasoning Models have significantly improved chain-of-thought (CoT) capabilities via reinforcement learning (RL). However, generated reasoning chains frequently suffer from structural redundancy (i.e., overthinking), incurring high computational overhead without improving answer correctness. Existing mitigation strategies typically rely on token-uniform length penalties, which provide coarse, segment-agnostic pressure toward shorter outputs and can inadvertently suppress useful reasoning alongside redundancy. To address this, we demonstrate that inefficiency concentrates in high-probability segments with low marginal utility. We derive a theoretical characterization of segment suboptimality under the correctness-length trade-off objective and propose SLAT (Segment-Level Adaptive Trimming), an RL framework that selectively suppresses redundant segments based on this criterion. Empirical results on standard benchmarks indicate that SLAT establishes a superior accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier, reducing reasoning length by 50% relative to uncompressed baselines while maintaining competitive accuracy. Overall, our results suggest that theoretically grounded, segment-aware trimming is a promising direction for efficient CoT reasoning in large language models.

paragraphs: Long reasoning outputs can contain substantial repetition or other material that adds little to answer correctness. Common length penalties pressure every token equally, which can remove useful reasoning along with redundancy. This paper studies how to target the specific segments responsible for inefficient reasoning instead.

The authors find that inefficiency concentrates in high-probability segments with low marginal utility. They derive a theoretical characterization of when a segment is suboptimal under an objective that trades off correctness against length. Competitive accuracy does not imply identical accuracy in every case; the finding concerns an improved overall trade-off. The results support analyzing reasoning at the segment level when training models to spend fewer tokens on material with limited value.
summary.tldr: SLAT selectively discourages low-value reasoning segments, cutting reported reasoning length by 50% while maintaining competitive accuracy.

title: SLAT: Segment-Level Adaptive Trimming for Efficient CoT Reasoning

abstract: Token merging accelerates Transformer inference by clustering similar tokens to reduce sequence length (retention ratio $r$), but distorts attention outputs, inducing covariate shift in residual streams and performance collapse under high compression. Existing heuristics, such as proportional attention, mitigate mild compression effectively but degrade sharply at aggressive ratios due to unaddressed energy drift and biased attention distributions. We reframe token merging as a statistical reconstruction problem in high dimensions and introduce an asymptotic radial-angular decomposition of the reconstruction error, an analytical framework decoupling magnitude and distributional distortions. Minimizing this decomposed risk under minimal assumptions of finite second moments and variance stationarity yields closed-form optimal corrections governed by a single scaling factor $\sqrt{r}$: scaling merged values and shrinking merged logits toward the cluster-size prior. This calibrates both energy balance and distributional fidelity. Extensive experiments on vision Transformers demonstrate superior accuracy and robustness across compression levels.

We reframe token merging as a statistical reconstruction problem in high dimensions and introduce an asymptotic radial-angular decomposition of the reconstruction error, an analytical framework decoupling magnitude and distributional distortions. Minimizing this decomposed risk under minimal assumptions of finite second moments and variance stationarity yields closed-form optimal corrections governed by a single scaling factor $\sqrt{r}$: scaling merged values and shrinking merged logits toward the cluster-size prior. This calibrates both energy balance and distributional fidelity. Extensive experiments on vision Transformers demonstrate superior accuracy and robustness across compression levels.

paragraphs: Token merging speeds up Transformer inference by grouping similar tokens and shortening the sequence. Aggressive merging can, however, distort attention outputs enough to disrupt the residual stream and collapse performance. The paper attributes this to both changes in output magnitude and biased attention distributions that existing heuristics do not fully correct.

The authors treat merging as a statistical reconstruction problem. Their asymptotic radial-angular decomposition separates magnitude errors from distributional errors. Under finite-second-moment and variance-stationarity assumptions, minimizing the decomposed risk produces closed-form corrections controlled by the square root of the retention ratio. These corrections scale merged values and shrink merged logits toward a prior based on cluster size.

The two adjustments jointly address energy balance and attention-distribution fidelity. Experiments on vision Transformers show improved accuracy and robustness across compression levels. The contribution is an analytical calibration rule for controlling the disruption caused by token merging, with its optimality derived under the stated statistical assumptions and its practical benefits demonstrated in vision-model experiments.
summary.tldr: A statistically derived scaling rule corrects magnitude and attention-distribution distortions caused by Transformer token merging.

title: Statistically Calibrated Scaling for Token Merging in Transformers

abstract: Modeling dynamic dependencies from irregularly sampled event sequences is a fundamental challenge in modern machine learning. In many real-world systems, individual-level states evolve continuously over time while being simultaneously influenced by population-level dynamics. However, existing methods typically model these processes in isolation or rely on discrete-time approximations that fail to capture long-range temporal irregularities and sparse observations. This paper studies the problem of learning coupled continuous-time latent dynamics from irregular events, where individual event sequences and global distributional processes evolve asynchronously and interact over time. We propose a Coupled Continuous-Time Latent Dynamics (CoCLD) framework that jointly models individual latent dynamics and population-level distributional shifts, and aligns them in a continuous-time latent space. CoCLD integrates a Diffusion-based Latent Interpolator with neural ordinary differential equations, enabling principled interpolation, generation, and alignment of latent states across arbitrary time points. We show that the proposed coupling mechanism yields a consistent estimator of continuous-time latent dynamics under sparse and irregular observations. Empirical evaluations show CoCLD effectively captures dynamic dependencies and generalizes across tasks like next-event prediction, mobility trajectory generation, and sequential behavior modeling, indicating that learning coupled continuous-time latent dynamics is a powerful paradigm for irregular event sequence modeling.

abstract: Mappings to structured output spaces (strings, trees, partitions, etc.) are typically learned using extensions of classification algorithms to simple graphical structures (eg., linear chains) in which search and parameter estimation can be performed exactly. Unfortunately, in many complex problems, it is rare that exact search or parameter estimation is tractable. Instead of learning exact models and searching via heuristic means, we embrace this difficulty and treat the structured output problem in terms of approximate search. We present a framework for learning as search optimization, and two parameter updates with convergence theorems and bounds. Empirical evidence shows that our integrated approach to learning and decoding can outperform exact models at smaller computational cost.

Unfortunately, in many complex problems, it is rare that exact search or parameter estimation is tractable. We present a framework for learning as search optimization, and two parameter updates with convergence theorems and bounds. paragraphs: The paper studies prediction problems whose outputs are structured objects, such as strings, trees, or partitions. Existing approaches often extend classification methods to simple graphical structures where exact search and parameter estimation are feasible. More complicated output spaces frequently make those exact computations impractical, creating a central obstacle for learning and prediction.

The authors make approximate search part of the learning formulation itself. Their framework treats learning as an optimization of the search process used to produce structured outputs. This brings parameter learning and decoding into a shared approach, so the learning problem reflects the approximate procedure that will actually be used to find predictions.

The paper provides two parameter-update methods together with convergence theorems and bounds. It also reports empirical evidence that this integrated approach can outperform exact models while using less computation. The performance statement is a demonstrated possibility, rather than a universal ranking of approximate and exact methods. The broader contribution is a framework that directly incorporates computationally feasible search into structured prediction.
summary.tldr: A structured-prediction framework integrates learning with approximate search and can improve performance while reducing computation.

title: Learning as search optimization: approximate large margin methods for structured prediction

abstract: Users of topic modeling methods often have knowledge about the composition of words that should have high or low probability in various topics. We incorporate such domain knowledge using a novel Dirichlet forest prior in a Latent Dirichlet Allocation framework. The prior is a mixture of Dirichlet tree distributions with special structures. We present its construction, and inference via collapsed Gibbs sampling. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate our model's ability to follow and generalize beyond user-specified domain knowledge.
originalAbstract: Users of topic modeling methods often have knowledge about the composition of words that should have high or low probability in various topics. We incorporate such domain knowledge using a novel Dirichlet forest prior in a Latent Dirichlet Allocation framework. The prior is a mixture of Dirichlet tree distributions with special structures. We present its construction, and inference via collapsed Gibbs sampling. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets demonstrate our model's ability to follow and generalize beyond user-specified domain knowledge.

paragraphs: People using topic models may already know which words should receive high or low probability within particular topics. This paper provides a way to incorporate that knowledge into Latent Dirichlet Allocation. The goal is to let user knowledge influence the learned topics through the probabilistic model itself.

The authors introduce a Dirichlet forest prior, constructed as a mixture of specially structured Dirichlet tree distributions. The prior is the mechanism that expresses the supplied knowledge about topic composition. They describe how to construct it and perform inference using collapsed Gibbs sampling, connecting the knowledge representation to a concrete learning procedure.

Experiments on synthetic and real datasets show that the model can follow user-specified knowledge and generalize beyond it. That combination matters because useful guidance should influence learning while still allowing the data to support additional structure. The contribution is therefore a probabilistic route for combining explicit domain knowledge with topic discovery, accompanied by evidence that the resulting model can do more than reproduce the supplied guidance.
summary.tldr: A Dirichlet forest prior lets LDA incorporate user knowledge about word probabilities while learning beyond that guidance.

title: Incorporating domain knowledge into topic modeling via Dirichlet Forest priors

abstract: In a dynamic social or biological environment, the interactions between the underlying actors can undergo large and systematic changes. Each actor in the networks can assume multiple related roles and their affiliation to each role as determined by the dynamic links will also exhibit rich temporal phenomenon. We propose a state space mixed membership stochastic blockmodel which captures the dependency between these multiple correlated roles, and enables us to track the mixed membership of each actor in the latent space across time. We derived efficient approximate learning and inference algorithms for our model, and applied the learned models to analyze an email network in Enron Corp., and a rewiring gene interaction network of yeast collected during its full cell cycle. In both cases, our model reveals interesting patterns of the dynamic roles of the actors.

We propose a state space mixed membership stochastic blockmodel which captures the dependency between these multiple correlated roles, and enables us to track the mixed membership of each actor in the latent space across time. We derived efficient approximate learning and inference algorithms for our model, and applied the learned models to analyze an email network in Enron Corp., and a rewiring gene interaction network of yeast collected during its full cell cycle. paragraphs: Networks can change because the roles of their participants change. An actor may also occupy several roles at once, with those roles related to one another. This paper proposes a model for representing both properties: mixed role membership and its evolution over time. The goal is to describe changing interactions without assigning each actor one permanent role.

The method combines a mixed-membership stochastic blockmodel with a state-space formulation. It captures dependencies among an actor's multiple roles and tracks their membership in a latent representation across time. The authors also derive efficient approximate procedures for learning the model and inferring these evolving memberships from observed network connections.

The model is applied to an Enron email network and a yeast gene-interaction network observed throughout a cell cycle. In both applications, the authors report interesting patterns in how actors' roles change. The findings support the model's use as an analytical tool for evolving networks, with attention to changing combinations of roles rather than only changes in individual links.
summary.tldr: A dynamic network model tracks actors' changing mixtures of correlated roles and reveals role patterns in email and gene-interaction networks.

title: Dynamic mixed membership blockmodel for evolving networks

abstract: We present a theoretical analysis of supervised ranking, providing necessary and sufficient conditions for the asymptotic consistency of algorithms based on minimizing a surrogate loss function. We show that many commonly used surrogate losses are inconsistent; surprisingly, we show inconsistency even in low-noise settings. We present a new value-regularized linear loss, establish its consistency under reasonable assumptions on noise, and show that it outperforms conventional ranking losses in a collaborative filtering experiment.
originalAbstract: We present a theoretical analysis of supervised ranking, providing necessary and sufficient conditions for the asymptotic consistency of algorithms based on minimizing a surrogate loss function. We show that many commonly used surrogate losses are inconsistent; surprisingly, we show inconsistency even in low-noise settings. We present a new value-regularized linear loss, establish its consistency under reasonable assumptions on noise, and show that it outperforms conventional ranking losses in a collaborative filtering experiment.

paragraphs: Supervised ranking algorithms often optimize a surrogate loss that is easier to work with than the ranking objective itself. This paper asks when that substitution is statistically sound in the large-data limit. It provides necessary and sufficient conditions for asymptotic consistency of ranking algorithms based on minimizing such surrogate losses.

The analysis finds that many commonly used surrogates are inconsistent. This can happen even when noise is low, so reducing noise does not by itself resolve the mismatch identified by the theory. The result highlights why the choice of training loss matters: optimizing a convenient objective need not lead to the desired ranking behavior asymptotically.

The authors introduce a value-regularized linear loss and establish its consistency under specified reasonable assumptions about noise. They also report that it outperforms conventional ranking losses in a collaborative filtering experiment. The contribution combines a diagnostic theory for existing objectives with a proposed alternative whose guarantee is conditional on noise assumptions and whose empirical benefit is demonstrated in the stated experiment.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes ranking consistency, identifies inconsistent common surrogate losses, and proposes an alternative consistent under noise assumptions.

title: On the Consistency of Ranking Algorithms

abstract: Riffled independence is a generalized notion of probabilistic independence that has been shown to be naturally applicable to ranked data. In the riffled independence model, one assigns rankings to two disjoint sets of items independently, then in a second stage, interleaves (or riffles) the two rankings together to form a full ranking, as if by shuffling a deck of cards. Because of this interleaving stage, it is much more difficult to detect riffled independence than ordinary independence. In this paper, we provide the first automated method for discovering sets of items which are riffle independent from a training set of rankings. We show that our clustering-like algorithms can be used to discover meaningful latent coalitions from real preference ranking datasets and to learn the structure of hierarchically decomposable models based on riffled independence.
originalAbstract: Riffled independence is a generalized notion of probabilistic independence that has been shown to be naturally applicable to ranked data. In the riffled independence model, one assigns rankings to two disjoint sets of items independently, then in a second stage, interleaves (or riffles) the two rankings together to form a full ranking, as if by shuffling a deck of cards. Because of this interleaving stage, it is much more difficult to detect riffled independence than ordinary independence. In this paper, we provide the first automated method for discovering sets of items which are riffle independent from a training set of rankings. We show that our clustering-like algorithms can be used to discover meaningful latent coalitions from real preference ranking datasets and to learn the structure of hierarchically decomposable models based on riffled independence.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to discover hidden groups of items from observed rankings. Its organizing idea is riffled independence: two disjoint groups receive their own independently generated rankings, and those rankings are then interleaved to produce a complete ordering. The analogy is shuffling two separately ordered portions of a deck together.

Interleaving makes the independence difficult to detect because the observed data contains the final combined rankings. The authors provide what they describe as the first automated method for identifying riffle-independent item sets from training rankings. Their algorithms resemble clustering, but the structure they seek is defined by this ranking-generation process.

On real preference-ranking datasets, the algorithms discover meaningful latent coalitions. They also learn the structure of models that can be decomposed hierarchically using riffled independence. The contribution therefore goes beyond dividing items into groups once: it supports discovering a hierarchy of such groupings. This gives a structured account of ranked preferences that accommodates independently ordered groups while allowing their items to appear interleaved.
summary.tldr: Clustering-like algorithms discover independently ranked groups hidden within interleaved preferences and learn hierarchical ranking-model structures.

title: Learning Hierarchical Riffle Independent Groupings from Rankings
